rows.label: abstract
rows.text:
**Abstract.** The Stieltjes measure of every integrable minimiser of the
zero-temperature Parisi functional for the pure, zero-field
Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model has full support on $[0,1)$ and a smooth
density that is strictly positive on $(0,1)$. We reconstruct OpenAI's quantitative
argument, organised around two uses of one spatial-moment inequality.
On a positive constant interval, it makes the derivative of the gradient
second moment strictly convex, contradicting the endpoint conditions
imposed by minimality. The same curvature and the bounded gradient
also exclude terminal gaps. Full support then gives moment identities and
smoothness; a local constant replacement transfers the inequality to the minimiser and
forces its density to be positive. H.-B. Chen previously proved full support
and smooth nonnegative density. We isolate the fixed-time spatial moment
and the positive margin that survives local replacement, while importing its
shape comparisons and full polynomial identity. We also derive the scalar value
identity and explain its classical optimisation consequence. For the quantum approximate
optimization algorithm (QAOA), we identify the rooted energy of a finite Gaussian
observable and the separate circuit theorem that approximates it. A further
second-moment theorem gives a measured near-optimal configuration on the same
random instance, with the circuit word fixed before the number of spins grows.

rows.label: contact
rows.text:
For an admissible coefficient, $\Phi$ is even, convex and one-Lipschitz
in space. Its positive-order spatial derivatives are bounded and
continuous on each strip $[0,T]\times\mathbb R$, $T<1$; the PDE
holds almost everywhere in time. The compact-strip approximation
theorem justifies the following Itô calculations even when $\gamma$
has jumps (see [OpenAI (2026a), Lemmas 2.1–2.2][FS]). The control method
has antecedents in [Jagannath and Tobasco (2016)][JT] at positive
temperature and [Auffinger and Chen (2017), Theorem 2 and
Corollary 2][AC] at zero temperature; see also [Chen, Handschy and
Lerman (2018), Proposition 2 and Theorem 5][CHL].

Fix a minimiser. Itô's formula cancels the drift of $u(t,X_t)$:
$$
du(t,X_t)=a(t,X_t)\,dB_t,
\qquad q(0)=0,\qquad q'(t)=\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^2].
$$
In particular $q'$ is continuous across coefficient jumps. Minimality
means that every allowed one-sided change has nonnegative first-order
cost. The one-sided variation formula gives the rate of change of the functional
when $\gamma$ is replaced by $\gamma+\varepsilon\eta$ as
$\varepsilon\downarrow0$:
$$
D_+\mathcal P(\gamma)[\eta]
=\tfrac12\int_0^1\eta(t)(q(t)-t)\,dt,                 \tag{1}
$$
for every integrable direction $\eta$ for which
$\gamma+\varepsilon\eta\in\mathcal U$ for all sufficiently small
$\varepsilon\geq0$ (see [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 6.1][FS]). Earlier
zero-temperature variation and support identities appear in
[Chen, Handschy and Lerman (2018), Propositions 3–4][CHL].

Adding a unit atom at $s$ raises the cumulative function at every
$t\geq s$, so its direction is $\eta=\mathbf1_{[s,1)}$. The
first-order cost is therefore a tail integral:
$$
G(s):=\int_s^1(q(t)-t)\,dt\geq0.
$$
Here $G(s)/2$ is the first-order cost of the added atom. Conversely,
let $\nu=\mu_\gamma|_K$ for a compact $K\subset[0,1)$.
For $0\leq\varepsilon\leq1$, the measure
$\mu_\gamma-\varepsilon\nu=(1-\varepsilon\mathbf1_K)\mu_\gamma$
is nonnegative, and its cumulative function is
$\gamma-\varepsilon\nu([0,\cdot])\in\mathcal U$. Minimality gives
$$
0\leq D_+\mathcal P(\gamma)[-\nu([0,\cdot])]
=-\tfrac12\int_K G(s)\,d\mu_\gamma(s).
$$
The change of integration order is justified by $|q-t|\leq1$ and
$\mu_\gamma(K)<\infty$. Since $G\geq0$, it vanishes almost
everywhere for $\mu_\gamma$, and continuity makes it vanish on
$S=\operatorname{supp}\mu_\gamma$. The variation removes a fraction of
all mass in $K$, not only atoms; no density or probability constraint is assumed.

At a support point $s>0$, $G$ has a minimum. Hence
$$
G'(s)=s-q(s)=0,\qquad G''(s)=1-q'(s)\geq0,
\quad\text{so}\quad q(s)=s,\quad q'(s)\leq1.       \tag{2}
$$
If $0\in S$, contact gives $G(0)=0$; independently, zero field
gives $q(0)=0$. Hence $G(h)=\tfrac12(1-q'(0))h^2+o(h^2)$; nonnegativity gives the
same slope bound at zero. These are the contact conditions of
[OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 6.2][FS].

rows.text: The quantity used in both arguments is a spatial moment. Recall $a=\Phi_{xx}$, write $b=\Phi_{xxx}$ and $d=\Phi_{xxxx}$, and, for $00$. For its associated diffusion, $$ \mathcal C_\gamma(t)\geq\frac{c^2}{1000} \mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^4]. $$ Neither minimality nor a constant neighbourhood of $t$ is required. This is the consequence of [OpenAI (2026a), Proposition 5.1 and Lemmas 2.1–2.2][FS] stated in the companion's [Proposition 4.1, §4.5](../long/reasoning-record.md#fixed-time-coercivity). We first explain the positive-plateau estimate, then obtain this fixed-time form by inserting a short plateau. For a smooth coefficient the identity connecting the two applications is $$ q'''+2\gamma'\mathbb E a^3=\mathcal C_\gamma. $$ On a plateau, $\gamma'=0$; at a smooth minimiser, full support gives $q=t$ and hence $q'''=0$. Section 4 proves the required smoothness before using the second identity. On a plateau with $\gamma=c>0$, put $r=c\Phi_x=c u$, $v=r_x=c a$, $w=r_{xx}$ and $z=r_{xxx}$. This rescaling makes the derivative identities polynomial. The PDE becomes $r_t=-\tfrac12r_{xx}-rr_x$, and the diffusion has spatial generator $\tfrac12\partial_{xx}+r\partial_x$. Differentiating in space and applying Itô's formula gives the drift and diffusion pairs $(0,v)$, $(-v^2,w)$ and $(-3vw,z)$ for $r,v,w$, respectively. All expectations in this section evaluate spatial functions at $(t,X_t)$. Starting with $c^2q'=\mathbb E v^2$, Itô's formula gives $$ \begin{aligned} c^2q''&=\mathbb E[w^2-2v^3],\\ c^2q'''&=\mathbb E[z^2-12vw^2+6v^4] =c^2\mathcal C_\gamma(t). \end{aligned} \tag{4} $$ For example, the drifts of $w^2$ and $v^3$ are $z^2-6vw^2$ and $3vw^2-3v^4$, respectively. The negative mixed term is the obstacle. Convexity, which gives $v\geq0$, does not control it. Indeed, for the smooth auxiliary terminal value $\log(2\cosh x)$ and coefficient $\gamma\equiv1$, the solution is $\Phi(t,x)=\log(2\cosh x)+(1-t)/2$. Thus $r=\tanh x$; at $r^2=1/2$, the polynomial in (4) equals $-19/8$. This is a finite-step smoothing example, not a minimiser of the absolute-value-terminal problem; its calculation is given in [long §4.1](../long/reasoning-record.md#curvature-moments). The same section gives a negative pointwise value with the actual $|x|$ terminal datum for a small positive constant coefficient ([long §4.1, pointwise obstruction](../long/reasoning-record.md#pointwise-curvature-obstruction)). The proof subtracts a weighted divergence whose expectation under the law of $X_t$ is zero. The resulting expression has a positive fourth-moment remainder. The backward value function and the forward density must satisfy joint shape restrictions for this decomposition to have the required signs. Those comparisons and the exact polynomial identity are the substantial inputs from [OpenAI (2026a), §§3–4][FS]. We explain their roles first for finite-step coefficients, then pass the integrated inequality to an integrable coefficient by approximation. Begin with a positive nondecreasing finite-step coefficient $\gamma_{\rm step}$: a function constant on each interval of a finite partition. Replace the terminal value $|x|$ by the smooth approximation $M^{-1}\log(2\cosh Mx)$, with $M\geq\|\gamma_{\rm step}\|_\infty$. On a step of height $c$, set $h=e^{c\Phi}$. Then $h_t=-h_{xx}/2$ and $r=h_x/h$. The same exponential removes the drift from the forward density equation. Indeed, writing $f=hg$ gives $$ \begin{aligned} f_t&=\tfrac12(hg)_{xx}-(h_xg)_x\\ &=-\tfrac12h_{xx}g+\tfrac12hg_{xx} =h_tg+\tfrac12hg_{xx}. \end{aligned} $$ Comparison with $f_t=h_tg+hg_t$ yields $g_t=g_{xx}/2$. Thus one backward heat factor and one forward heat factor determine the law against which the moment polynomial is integrated. For $s=-\partial_x\log g$, the source proves joint shape restrictions: on $x>0$, $r_x>0$ and $s_x\geq1/t$, both $r$ and $s$ are concave, and $H:=w/(2r)+v\leq0$ is nondecreasing. They also give $$ j:=s_x-(s/r)v=r\,\partial_x(s/r)\geq0. $$ The last inequality couples the backward gradient to the forward density; separate monotonicity and concavity do not supply it. On the first step, $s=x/t$, so concavity of $r$ gives $j\geq0$. A parabolic comparison propagates the sign within each step. At a forward jump with $k=c_+/c_-\geq1$, continuity of $\Phi$ and $f$ gives $$ r_+=kr_-,\qquad s_+=s_-+(k-1)r_-,\qquad j_+=(s_x)_+-\frac{s_+}{r_+}(r_x)_+=j_-. $$ The joint sign therefore survives coefficient jumps as well. The quotients $w/r$ and $s/r$ extend smoothly through zero because $r,s,w$ are odd and $r_x(0)>0$. The comparison's boundary controls and these extensions are analytic inputs from [OpenAI (2026a), Lemmas 3.2–3.4][FS], reconstructed in [long §4.3](../long/reasoning-record.md#shape-comparisons). The factorisation of the density gives $f_x/f=r-s$. For a suitable expression $F$ in the shape quantities, define $$ \mathcal W(F)=r\partial_xF+(v+r^2-rs)F. $$ Then $f\mathcal W(F)=\partial_x(rfF)$. The smooth extensions avoid an interior boundary term at zero, and the source's differentiated Gaussian tail estimates give $rfF\to0$ at both spatial infinities for the polynomial correction used below. Hence $\mathbb E_f\mathcal W(F)=0$, where $\mathbb E_f$ denotes integration against $f(x)\,dx$. The remaining step is algebra under these analytic restrictions. The correction polynomial below is chosen by first arranging a square and other nonnegative terms containing the highest derivative $z$, then cancelling their linear terms in $z$ through the weighted divergence. The residual depends only on lower derivatives and the shape quantities. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 4.1][FS] supplies an explicit polynomial $F_2$ and a decomposition $$ z^2-12vw^2+6v^4 =\mathcal W(F_2)+\kappa v^4+\mathcal R, \qquad \mathcal R\geq0,\qquad \kappa=\frac{1661507}{1521000000}>\frac1{1000}. $$ The coefficients of $F_2$ have both signs; no sign of $F_2$ or $\mathcal W(F_2)$ is needed, since the correction integrates to zero. In contrast, the shape inequalities make every term of $\mathcal R$ nonnegative. Two of its actual terms are $$ \frac{337}{10000}\,r^2j\,(-w/r-7v)^2, \qquad (2rH_x)v\left(\frac{2331}{10000}r^2+\frac{87}{2500}j\right). $$ The first needs the joint comparison $j\geq0$; the second also uses $H_x\geq0$ on the positive half-line. Reflection preserves these signs on the negative half-line. The remaining terms use $H\leq0$, forward concavity and the other shape bounds. Thus the decomposition is positive on the shapes supplied by the PDE, not on arbitrary spatial derivatives. Integration removes $\mathcal W(F_2)$ and keeps the fourth-moment margin, giving $$ \int_{\mathbb R}(z^2-12vw^2+6v^4)f\,dx \geq\frac1{1000}\int_{\mathbb R}v^4f\,dx. \tag{5} $$ We use (5) as an imported analytic estimate. The full polynomial and its decomposition are in [Lemma 4.1 and Table 1][certificate]; Proposition 4.2 integrates them using the signs and zero boundary flux supplied by Lemma 3.4. [Long §4.4, “How the signs make a correction with zero expectation useful”](../long/reasoning-record.md#curvature-algebra) reproduces the definitions and complete identity. To obtain Lemma 2 for an integrable coefficient, choose positive monotone step coefficients $\gamma_n$ retaining the plateau near a fixed interior time, with $\|\gamma_n-\gamma\|_1\to0$, and terminal parameters $M_n\geq\|\gamma_n\|_\infty$ with $M_n\to\infty$. Spatial derivatives through order four converge uniformly on a fixed strip below one, and the diffusions driven by the same Brownian motion converge (see [OpenAI (2026a), Lemmas 2.1–2.2 and Proposition 5.1][FS]). Only $v,w,z$ remain in (5), so no convergence theorem for the auxiliary logarithmic derivative $s$ is needed. Dividing by $c^2$ gives (3); strictness follows from $\Phi_{xx}>0$ on the plateau (see [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 2.3][FS]). The plateau-preserving approximants and their common strip bounds are specified in [long §4.5](../long/reasoning-record.md#plateau-limit). The zero plateau has the separate heat identity in Lemma 2. Its strictness uses a positive diffusion density and the fact that $\Phi_{xxx}$ cannot vanish identically: an even quadratic profile would contradict the one-Lipschitz bound and $|x|+O(1)$ growth. **Passage to a fixed time.** Now let $\gamma\in\mathcal U$ be continuous at $t\in(0,1)$, with $c=\gamma(t)>0$. For $0<\delta<\min(t,1-t)$ define $$ \gamma_\delta(s)= \begin{cases} c,&t-\delta\leq s0$, then $q'$ cannot attain an interior maximum. The endpoint slope bounds therefore give $q'<1$ inside the gap and the same strict area deficit. Proposition 3 supplies more for the next argument: it applies at the chosen comparison time without assuming $q''=0$, and its fourth-moment lower bound survives the local replacement. Bare strict positivity could be lost in that limit.

rows.label: density-consequence
rows.text: Full support does not force pointwise positive density. For instance, $\gamma(t)=\int_0^t(s-\tfrac12)^2\,ds$ has full Stieltjes support but $\gamma'(\tfrac12)=0$: every interval of positive length has a positive integral, although the integrand vanishes at one point. The quantitative remainder in (5) rules this out for a minimiser. First, the identity $\mathbb E a^2=1$ expresses $\gamma$ as a quotient of continuous moments and then gives smoothness. Only afterwards do we apply the fixed-time spatial estimate to obtain $\gamma'>0$. **Corollary 4 (smooth positive density; [OpenAI (2026a), Corollary 6.4][FS]).** Under the hypotheses of Theorem 1, $\gamma(0)=0$ and $\gamma\in C^\infty([0,1))$, with derivatives at zero taken from the right. Its Stieltjes measure is $\mu_\gamma(dt)=\gamma'(t)\,dt$, and $$ 2\gamma'(t)\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^3] \geq\frac{\gamma(t)^2}{1000}\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^4]>0 \qquad(0[long §9.1](../long/reasoning-record.md#smooth-density-consequence). Now the two differentiated moments are $$ \frac{d}{dt}\mathbb E b^2=\mathbb E[d^2-6\gamma ab^2], \qquad \frac{d}{dt}\mathbb E a^3=\mathbb E[3ab^2-3\gamma a^4]. $$ For a smooth time coefficient, differentiating $q''=\mathbb E b^2-2\gamma\mathbb E a^3$ therefore gives $$ q^{(3)}+2\gamma'\mathbb E a^3 =\mathcal C_\gamma(t). \tag{9} $$ This identity displays the two uses of the same spatial moment. On a plateau, $\gamma'=0$ and $(v,w,z)=c(a,b,d)$ recover (4). For the now smooth minimiser, $q=t$, so $q^{(3)}=0$ and the left side is $2\gamma'\mathbb E a^3$. Proposition 3 supplies the lower bound for this spatial moment. Apply Proposition 3 to the now smooth minimiser. Strict increase and $\gamma(0)=0$ give $\gamma(t)>0$ for $t>0$; (9) therefore gives (7). Strictness follows from $\gamma(t)>0$ and $\mathbb E a^4\geq(\mathbb E a^2)^2=1$. In particular, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $$ \mathbb E a^3\leq\sqrt{\mathbb E a^2\,\mathbb E a^4} =\sqrt{\mathbb E a^4}\leq\mathbb E a^4, $$ so the same inequality implies $\gamma'(t)\geq\gamma(t)^2/2000$ for $0[Long §§9.1–9.2](../long/reasoning-record.md#smooth-density-consequence) retain the smoothness argument and fixed-time transfer, including the common approximation bounds. **Earlier and related estimates.** The backward shape comparisons, transformed density and positive-temperature gap-crossing argument appear in [Lopatto (2026), v3, Propositions 3.6, 7.1 and 9.1][Lopatto]. [H.-B. Chen (2026), Proposition 4.2][Chen] proves the zero-temperature crossing implication $q''=0\Rightarrow q'''>0$ under the minimiser convention of §3.1. [Lopatto's v4, Proposition 5.1 and Corollary 5.6][Lopatto-v4] give qualitative crossing for arbitrary positive-temperature probability measures. In unit-noise coordinates, their cumulative coefficient is $\gamma_\beta=\beta\alpha_\nu$, where $\alpha_\nu(t)=\nu([0,t])$, and the terminal value is $\beta^{-1}\log\cosh(\beta x)$. Every bounded $\gamma\in\mathcal U$ has this form: choose $\beta>0$ with $\beta\geq\sup\gamma$ and put the remaining probability mass at one. Thus the coefficient classes alone do not distinguish the estimates; the terminal datum and the quantitative control through its zero-temperature limit matter. [Lopatto's external-field paper, Theorem 2.3 and §8][Lopatto-field] also uses a fixed-time spatial inequality for support and positive density. At a continuity point, monotonicity supplies its one-sided coefficient bounds; on a smooth full-support interval of the minimiser, its scalar conditions become equalities. Appendix B gives the positive-temperature, zero-field strict-density result. The bound used here instead applies at a nonstationary comparison time and retains an explicit fourth-moment margin through the local replacement with terminal datum $|x|$. The rescaling and exact hypothesis comparisons are in [long §2.3, finite-temperature dictionary](../long/reasoning-record.md#finite-temperature-dictionary).

rows.label: evidence-scope
rows.text: This AI-assisted article reconstructs the cited analytic arguments. The integrated estimate (5), its shape hypotheses and compact-strip approximation are substantial imported inputs. OpenAI's retained [full-support formal statement][support-challenge] asserts the support and moment conclusions conditional on an admissible minimiser, and constructs its associated diffusion. A separate [scalar formal statement][value-challenge] covers value identities and finite Gaussian approximation, with minimiser and diffusion premises for those clauses. Its third clause identifies the ground-state and Parisi values from a minimiser, constructing the diffusion internally. The two formal models have not been transported into one another in this record. Neither statement includes the positive-density corollary or QAOA convergence. Their [full-support][support-lean] and [scalar][value-lean] implementations use [Lean][Lean4] and [mathlib][mathlib]. A source-bound local build of the Support implementation completed on 26 October 2026, and dependency extraction recorded its conditional full-support root. Dependencies outside the selected extraction scope remain boundaries. Comparator acceptance and the scalar-target results remain pending. Exact versions, checking outcomes and correspondence are retained in the long record's [§12, “What the formal statements establish”](../long/reasoning-record.md#formal-interfaces) and [§13, “Source checks and finite calculation”](../long/reasoning-record.md#verification).

rows.label: gap-proof
rows.text: **Lemma 2 (constant-interval curvature; [OpenAI (2026a), Proposition 5.1][FS]).** Let $\gamma\in\mathcal U$, with its associated diffusion and moment $q$. If $\gamma=c$ on an open interval $I\subset(0,1)$, called a plateau, then for $t\in I$ $$ q'''(t)\geq\frac{c^2}{1000}\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^4]>0 \quad\text{if }c>0. \tag{3} $$ If $c=0$, then $q''(t)=\mathbb E[\Phi_{xxx}(t,X_t)^2]>0$. Minimality is not a hypothesis of this lemma. Section 3 derives its moment polynomial and explains the integrated estimate imported from the source. **Proof of Theorem 1, assuming Lemma 2.** A complementary interval with two support endpoints admits two contact conditions; an initial interval without support at zero has coefficient zero. For terminal gaps, the bound $q\leq1$ replaces the missing right contact condition. Suppose $(\ell,r)$ is a support gap with endpoints in $S$ and $r<1$. The coefficient is a positive constant there: support at $\ell$ and absence of mass immediately to its right force $\mu_\gamma([0,\ell])>0$. Strict convexity of $q'$ and (2) give $$ q'(t)<\frac{r-t}{r-\ell}q'(\ell) +\frac{t-\ell}{r-\ell}q'(r)\leq1 \qquad(\ell0$, hence $q'(t)1$. Convexity then gives $q'(s)>q'(t)>1$ for $s>t$. Consequently $q(s)>t+(s-t)q'(t)>1$ for $s<1$ sufficiently close to one, contrary to $q\leq1$. Thus $q(t)[long §5, “A shorter qualitative exclusion”](../long/reasoning-record.md#qualitative-terminal-gap) gives the full endpoint discussion. The stronger boundary estimate $1-q(t)\geq C\sqrt{1-t}$ for arbitrary coefficients constant near one is proved in [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 6.3][FS] and [long §5, terminal boundary estimate](../long/reasoning-record.md#terminal-gap); [Chen (2026), Proposition 4.5, equations (4.27)–(4.38)][Chen] gives the square-root asymptotic under the terminal-gap hypothesis. The zero-coefficient heat argument and late-step variation have antecedents in [Chen, Handschy and Lerman (2018), Theorem 6][CHL]. These cases exhaust the complement of the relatively closed set $S$. Consequently $S=[0,1)$, contact gives $q(t)=t$, and differentiation gives $\mathbb E a^2=1$, including the right-hand value at zero. Moreover, $\gamma(t_2)-\gamma(t_1)=\mu_\gamma((t_1,t_2])>0$. This proves Theorem 1 using the stated analytic inputs.

rows.label: main-result
rows.text: [Auffinger, Chen and Zeng (2020), Theorem 1][ACZ] proved infinite support. This need not be full support: the measure $\sum_{k\geq1}2^{-k}\delta_{1-2^{-k}}$ has infinitely many atoms and many gaps. [H.-B. Chen (2026), Theorem 1.3][Chen] subsequently proved full support and smooth nonnegative density. We follow OpenAI's quantitative proof of the support conclusion and its further strict-positivity result. The feature used twice is a lower bound valid throughout every positive constant interval of an admissible coefficient, without a minimising assumption. **Theorem 1 (full support; quantitative proof following [OpenAI (2026a), Theorem 1.1][FS]).** If $\gamma\in\mathcal U$ minimises $\mathcal P$, then $$ \operatorname{supp}\mu_\gamma=[0,1),\qquad \gamma(t_2)>\gamma(t_1)\quad(0\leq t_10$, with probability tending to one there are configurations $\sigma,\tau$ with $|R(\sigma,\tau)-\rho|<\delta$ and both energies at least $n(P_*-\eta)$. This follows from [Auffinger, Chen and Zeng (2020), Proposition 1, equation (5)][ACZ], using the Gaussian normalisation above. Our purpose is to isolate the spatial moment common to the support and density arguments, explain why it needs an integrated estimate, and identify what survives the local-replacement limit. The conclusions and the quantitative method are those of the cited sources. The proof compares two demands on a gap with two support endpoints. Minimality forces $q$ to agree with time there, with endpoint slopes at most one. On a positive constant interval a quantitative estimate makes $q'$ strictly convex, so its integral is smaller than the interval's length. This contradicts the required change in $q$. After excluding all gaps, the identity $q'=1$ supplies the equation from which the same estimate will force $\gamma'>0$. A qualitative crossing criterion already suffices for a bounded gap. The density argument needs more: an estimate for a local constant replacement that need not minimise, at a time where $q''$ need not vanish, and a positive lower bound that survives the limit. The second aim, in §5, is to follow the support identities to a finite Gaussian observable whose rooted energy a QAOA circuit approximates, then identify the additional concentration input for a measured configuration. These optimisation consequences use full support; strict density positivity is a further analytic conclusion. Readers interested in optimisation may accept Theorem 1 and continue to §5. Sections 2–4 assume Itô calculus and martingale convergence; the circuit construction is a separate imported theorem. Omitted proofs are linked to *From Parisi full support to deterministic QAOA circuits: A long reasoning record*, the [companion edition of 26 October 2026](../long/reasoning-record.md); original-source citations remain beside the imported inputs.

rows.label: model
rows.text:
For independent standard Gaussian couplings $J_{ij}$, the pure,
zero-field [Sherrington–Kirkpatrick (SK) Hamiltonian][SK] is
$$
H_n(\sigma)=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}\sigma_i\sigma_j,
\qquad \sigma\in\{-1,1\}^n.
$$
The limiting ground-state energy per spin, with the maximisation
convention, is
$$
P_*:=\lim_{n\to\infty}n^{-1}\mathbb E\max_\sigma H_n(\sigma).
$$
The Parisi formula expresses $P_*$ as a minimum over nondecreasing
functions. Our subject is the structure of a minimiser: its increments
charge every interval of overlap scales below one, and in fact have
strictly positive density at each interior scale. The proof uses one
quantitative bound twice, first to exclude constant intervals and then,
after an approximation, to prove pointwise positivity.

For two configurations, their overlap is
$R(\sigma,\tau)=n^{-1}\sum_i\sigma_i\tau_i$. It determines the
energy covariance: $\mathbb E[H_n(\sigma)H_n(\tau)]=nR^2/2-1/2$.
Thus the Gaussian law of the energies is encoded by the overlaps.
We use the covariance convention $\xi(t)=t^2/2$, so $\xi''=1$;
adding one independent centred Gaussian of
variance $1/2$ to every configuration's energy gives covariance
$n\xi(R)$ and leaves the expected maximum unchanged. This is the
normalisation of the ground-state Parisi formula of
[Auffinger and Chen (2017), Theorem 1][AC]. There are no higher-order
interactions and no external field.

Let $\mathcal U$ consist of the nonnegative, nondecreasing,
right-continuous functions $\gamma:[0,1)\to[0,\infty)$ satisfying
$\int_0^1\gamma(t)\,dt<\infty$. Define the locally finite Stieltjes
measure by
$$
\mu_\gamma([0,t])=\gamma(t),\qquad 0\leq t<1.
$$
Thus $\mu_\gamma((s,t])=\gamma(t)-\gamma(s)$: the measure records
the increments of $\gamma$. A point mass (atom) of size $\gamma(0)$
is allowed at zero, and the total mass need not be finite or equal
to one. All support statements use the relative topology of $[0,1)$.
A support gap is a relatively open interval of positive length with
zero mass; the cumulative coefficient is constant on such an interval.

The Parisi functional $\mathcal P(\gamma)$ is defined using an
auxiliary value function $\Phi_\gamma(t,x)$, where $x\in\mathbb R$
is a spatial variable and $t$ is the overlap parameter, treated as
time in the equation. Write $\Phi=\Phi_\gamma$ and use subscripts
for partial derivatives. The backward equation, terminal condition
and functional are
$$
\Phi_t=-\tfrac12\bigl(\Phi_{xx}+\gamma(t)\Phi_x^2\bigr),
\qquad \Phi(1,x)=|x|,
\qquad
\mathcal P(\gamma)=\Phi_\gamma(0,0)-\tfrac12\int_0^1t\gamma(t)\,dt.
$$
The terminal value $|x|$ is the zero-temperature value of one spin
in a field $x$. For an integrable
coefficient, the PDE solution is interpreted by approximation from
bounded monotone coefficients. The exact control
definition and stability theorem are [OpenAI (2026a), §1 and
Lemmas 2.1–2.2][FS]. To turn minimality of $\mathcal P$ into a
condition on $\gamma$, we use a random process whose gradient moment
measures the first-order cost of changing $\gamma$. Write $u=\Phi_x$ for the spatial gradient
and $a=\Phi_{xx}$ for its spatial derivative. Let $B$ be standard
Brownian motion and define the diffusion $X$ and its self-consistency function $q$ by
$$
dX_t=\gamma(t)u(t,X_t)\,dt+dB_t,\qquad X_0=0,
\qquad q(t)=\mathbb E[u(t,X_t)^2].
$$
The discrepancy $q(t)-t$ enters the first variation of $\mathcal P$;
minimality will force $q(t)=t$ on the support of $\mu_\gamma$.
The SDE has a unique strong solution. All
stochastic calculations below take place on compact time intervals
ending before one, unless an endpoint limit is justified explicitly.

rows.label: qaoa-boundary
rows.text: ### 5.3 A fixed QAOA circuit before the thermodynamic limit The remaining consequence uses a separate circuit approximation theorem, stated as Proposition 5 below. We give its finite Gaussian input and identify the energy it approximates. Its operator and control construction is developed in the companion; the support and density proofs above do not require those additional prerequisites. Let $\widehat Z_i,\widehat X_i$ be Pauli operators, and define the cost and mixer by $$ C_{n,J}=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i0$ there is one finite $W$ with $v(W)\geq P_*-\varepsilon$, whose depth and angles depend on $\varepsilon$ but not on $n$ or $J$. The instance still determines $C_{n,J}$. Here depth counts global cost–mixer layers; their elementary gate counts depend on the implementation. This order of limits differs from the fixed-instance depth limit in [Farhi, Goldstone and Gutmann, §VI][FGG], which permits instance-dependent choices. The common-circuit conclusion was conjectured by [Basso, Farhi, Marwaha, Villalonga and Zhou (2022), §7, equation (7.2)][BFMVZ]. **The finite Gaussian input.** Fix the minimiser and its diffusion, a cutoff $0[long §7, “A finite Gaussian spin and its adjacent correlations”](../long/reasoning-record.md#finite-gaussian-approximation). **Proposition 5 (circuit approximation; a consequence of [OpenAI (2026b), §§2–5][Q]).** For each fixed $T,N$ in the preceding construction with finite positive normalisers, and every $\eta>0$, there is a finite ordinary QAOA word $W$, with deterministic angles independent of $n$ and $J$, such that $$ |v(W)-S_{T,N}|<\eta. $$ **Why the adjacent pairing is the energy.** We use the rooted Gaussian representation of [OpenAI (2026b), §2 and Lemma 3.1][Q], building on the spin–boson description of [Boulebnane et al. (2026)][spin-boson]. Its classical sector consists of square-integrable functions built recursively from a local Gaussian seed and child-generated Gaussian coordinates, with inner product given by expectation. For any finite list of fixed centred real child directions, their coordinates at the receiving root have a joint centred Gaussian law. For two such directions $f,g$, $$ \mathbb E[\mathsf G(f)\mathsf G(g)]=\langle f,g\rangle. $$ The directions are fixed elements of the child space, even when their values depend on the child's Gaussian coordinates. The receiving root's seed is independent of these coordinates; compatible embeddings preserve them as the recursive depth grows. The root shift $\mathsf L$ inserts a child direction into the first Gaussian chaos (the linear Gaussian part) with constant receiving-root state. Its adjoint projects onto that part and returns the child direction. The [one-pair calculation at the start of long §8](../long/reasoning-record.md#depth-one-calibration) checks this representation's energy against the finite SK circuit before the general construction in §8.1. Start with a standard normal receiving-root seed $g_0$ and recursively put $Z_{j+1}=\mathsf G(g_j)$. The orthonormal child directions give independent standard Gaussian lifts, reproducing the scalar law. The finite spin $F_N$ depends only on those lifts. Projection therefore gives the exact rooted-energy identity $$ \begin{aligned} \mathsf L^*F_N&=\sum_{j=0}^N\mathbb E[F_NZ_{j+1}]g_j,\\ \mathcal E(F_N):=\operatorname{Re}\langle F_N,\mathsf L F_N\rangle &=\sum_{j=0}^N\mathbb E[F_Ng_j]\,\mathbb E[F_NZ_{j+1}] =S_{T,N}. \end{aligned} \tag{12} $$ Independence of the receiving-root seed removes the $j=0$ term. This identity concerns the finite Gaussian formula in a limiting rooted space, not a finite-$n$ circuit. The unshifted pairing can have the same scalar limit without identifying this energy. The construction and projection are proved in [long §8.1](../long/reasoning-record.md#rooted-energy). The shift records the lift from a child direction $g_j$ to the receiving coordinate $Z_{j+1}$. A one-step example distinguishes it from the unshifted pairing. For the nonminimising heat coefficient $\gamma=0$, take $T=4/5$ and $N=1$. Then $g_1=Z_1$ and $F_1=\operatorname{sgn}(2Z_1+Z_2)$, so Gaussian regression gives $$ S_{T,1}=\frac4{5\pi},\qquad \mathbb E[F_1g_1]\,\mathbb E[F_1Z_1]=\frac8{5\pi}. $$ This tests the finite representation, not the minimiser-dependent limit in (11). The calculation is in [long §10.4, “An exact one-step calculation”](../long/reasoning-record.md#one-step-example). **Construction underlying Proposition 5.** [OpenAI (2026b), §§3–5][Q] smooths the spin and approximates every transmitted function by a bounded smooth map, preserving oddness; smoothing the final sign alone is insufficient. Its class exclusions prevent return through a traversed branch and reserve helper classes on which the output is zero, with positive probabilities fixed during synthesis. The resulting finite formula is approximated in energy using temporary Gaussian controls, with the same sitewise seeds throughout the word. Removing those controls produces an ordinary word, whose limiting energy is $v(W)$ by the fixed-word transfer. The approximation errors are absolute and can be chosen successively for each fixed $S_{T,N}$, before it is chosen close to $P_*$. The preserved quantity is energy; the measured-configuration conclusion below uses a further concentration theorem. The complete error bound is in [long §8.6, finite-formula energy approximation](../long/reasoning-record.md#finite-formula-energy-error), with the constructions and their hypotheses in [long §§8.1–8.6](../long/reasoning-record.md#qaoa-construction). The deduction of near-optimality is now explicit: $$ P_*-v(W)\leq (P_*-I_T)+|I_T-S_{T,N}|+|S_{T,N}-v(W)|. \tag{13} $$ Choose $T$ so that $1-T<\varepsilon/3$, then $N$ so that the second term is below $\varepsilon/3$, and finally use Proposition 5 with $\eta<\varepsilon/3$. These finite choices give $v(W)>P_*-\varepsilon$ before $n$ tends to infinity. The source's Appendix A supplies an alternative positive-temperature input to the same synthesis. This construction supplies no bounds on depth or cost-angle magnitudes in terms of accuracy, and no efficient procedure for finding angles. A separate estimate for the expected energy of a specified word is described in [long §11.5](../long/reasoning-record.md#finite-size-comparison). Its threshold depends on the word's depth and cost angles. Without bounds on those parameters it gives no threshold in optimisation accuracy alone; it also supplies no rate for measurement concentration. **Corollary 6 (a measured configuration on the same instance).** For every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a finite ordinary QAOA word $W_\varepsilon$, chosen independently of $n$ and $J$, such that one computational-basis measurement $\Sigma$ satisfies $$ \Pr_{J,\Sigma}\!\left\{ \max_\sigma H_{n,J}(\sigma)-H_{n,J}(\Sigma)\leq\varepsilon n \right\}\longrightarrow1 \qquad(n\to\infty). \tag{14} $$ **Proof.** For a fixed word, put $Y_n=H_{n,J}(\Sigma)/n$ and $K_n=\max_\sigma H_{n,J}(\sigma)/n$. [Farhi, Goldstone, Gutmann and Zhou, §4, equations (13)–(22)][FGGZ] prove $$ \mathbb E_{J,\Sigma}Y_n\to v(W),\qquad \mathbb E_{J,\Sigma}Y_n^2\to v(W)^2. $$ The second moment is $\mathbb E_J\langle(C_{n,J}/n)^2\rangle$, so it includes measurement variance as well as disorder fluctuations. Thus $Y_n\to v(W)$ in joint $L^2$. Gaussian concentration of the maximum and its defining mean limit give $K_n\to P_*$ in probability. Choose $W$ with $P_*-v(W)<\varepsilon/3$. With probability tending to one, both $K_n-P_*<\varepsilon/3$ and $v(W)-Y_n<\varepsilon/3$, which proves (14). The two energies use the same $J$; no independence between them is needed. The companion's [§11.2, “What is averaged, and a fixed-word probability consequence”](../long/reasoning-record.md#fixed-word-probability) gives the concentration argument and its further probability consequences.

rows.label: scalar-value
rows.text: ### 5.1 A martingale formula for the ground-state value The support identities give a scalar representation of $P_*$. Set $M_t=u(t,X_t)$, the bounded gradient martingale satisfying $dM_t=a(t,X_t)\,dB_t$. The quadratic variations distinguish the two Hessian moments: $$ d\langle M\rangle_t=a(t,X_t)^2\,dt, \qquad d\langle M,B\rangle_t=a(t,X_t)\,dt. $$ Full support gives $\mathbb E a(t,X_t)^2=1$, hence each increment $M_t-M_s$ has unconditional variance $t-s$. This normalises the discrete increments below. The first moment of $a$ instead gives covariance with the driving noise. Let $U$ be the almost-sure and $L^2$ limit of $M_t$. The value identity is $$ P_*=\mathbb E[UB_1] =\int_0^1\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)]\,dt. \tag{10} $$ Boundedness gives $|U|\leq1$, while $\mathbb E M_t^2\to1$ gives $\mathbb E U^2=1$; therefore $U^2=1$ almost surely. To see the cancellation behind (10), the terminal convergence of the convex value functions gives $UX_1=|X_1|$ (the equality is automatic on $X_1=0$), while Itô's formula gives $\mathcal P(\gamma)=\mathbb E|X_1|-\int_0^1t\gamma(t)\,dt$. Multiplying $X_1=B_1+\int_0^1\gamma(t)M_t\,dt$ by $U$ cancels that integral because $\mathbb E[UM_t]=t$. The Parisi formula then gives (10). The endpoint limits and stochastic-integral covariance are proved in [OpenAI (2026a), Corollary 7.1][FS] and the long record, [§6, “Recovering the value from a martingale”](../long/reasoning-record.md#scalar-value-identities). This argument uses full support, not the density corollary. In particular, convexity and Cauchy–Schwarz give $0\leq\mathbb E a\leq1$, so $$ 0\leq P_*-\int_0^T\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)]\,dt\leq1-T. $$ One can therefore fix the terminal cutoff before discretising the diffusion. The gradient-martingale and value methods have antecedents in [Montanari, preprint v2, Lemmas 3.2–3.4][Montanari], under its positive-temperature support assumption, and in the zero-temperature calculations of [El Alaoui, Montanari and Sellke, preprint v1, Lemmas 6.5 and 6.13][EAMS]. [Sellke, preprint v4, Proposition 3.10 and Lemma 3.11, p. 17][Sellke] gives the closely related finite-cutoff cancellation by applying Itô's formula to $\Phi$ and $x\Phi_x$. ### 5.2 The classical algorithm Full support and existence give an attained, strictly increasing minimiser in the monotone zero-temperature class. This is Assumption 2 of [El Alaoui, Montanari and Sellke, preprint v1][EAMS]. Their Corollary 2.2 then gives, for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, a randomised algorithm returning a configuration within $\varepsilon n$ of the finite SK maximum with probability tending to one over couplings and algorithmic randomness. Its cost is $C(\varepsilon)n^2$ real-arithmetic operations with the prescribed scalar functions and normalisers available; this includes no separate numerical-preprocessing or finite-precision bound. [OpenAI (2026a), Corollary 7.3][FS] and [long §9.4](../long/reasoning-record.md#classical-algorithm-consequence) check the Gaussian convention and operation count. Chen already records the classical consequence in [§1, p. 4][Chen]. Their incremental approximate message-passing iterates use the coupling matrix. Their scalar description uses the martingale multiplier and state drift $$ u_{\rm EAMS}(t,x)=a(t,x),\qquad v_{\rm EAMS}(t,x)=\gamma(t)u(t,x). $$ Thus their noise multiplier is the Hessian, whereas our $u$ is the gradient. The bounded martingale $M_t$ and $\mathbb E a^2=1$ give the required variance normalisation. With the fixed-strip regularity and discretisation estimates, [their Theorem 2][EAMS] achieves energy arbitrarily close to the truncated first-moment integral in (10). Strict positivity of the density is unnecessary.

rows.label: changed-case-answer
rows.text: ### 7.4 Answers to the questions **[Question 1](#question-1).** Adding mass at $1/2$ gives cumulative heights $0,2,2+\varepsilon,3+\varepsilon$, in their successive intervals; removing it at $1/4$ gives heights $0,2-\varepsilon,3-\varepsilon$. Both functions remain nonnegative and nondecreasing. Removing mass at $1/2$ instead lowers the height from $2$ to $2-\varepsilon$ there, creating a downward jump, so it is forbidden even though all values remain nonnegative. Scaling both weights preserves all admissibility conditions. These tests concern allowed candidates; a smaller ordinary area alone does not establish a smaller Parisi value. **[Question 2](#question-2).** For $\gamma=0$, the state is $X_{1/4}=B_{1/4}$, a centred Gaussian with variance $1/4$, so it has the law of $Z/2$. The remaining independent Gaussian noise $B_1-B_{1/4}$ has variance $3/4$ and standard deviation $\sqrt3/2$. Thus $$ q_0(1/4)=\int_{\mathbb R} \left(2F_{\mathrm G}(z/\sqrt3)-1\right)^2\varphi(z)\,dz. $$ The two variances agree at half time, but not here. For nonzero $z$, the magnitude of the response is now smaller, so $q_0(1/4)<1/3$. The arcsine formula in Section 7.1 also gives this comparison. Changing the coefficient after $1/2$ leaves $X_{1/4}=B_{1/4}$: its drift has been zero up to that time. The remaining Brownian noise still has variance $3/4$, but the value now includes future control terms. Its slope must be recomputed before averaging the square against the unchanged state law. Thus the displayed integral using $u_0$ is no longer justified. Knowing the future coefficient schedule does not reveal future random noise. **[Question 3](#question-3).** A strictly convex $f'$ lies below its endpoint chord. That chord has mean height $(1/2+3/2)/2=1$, hence integral three. Therefore $f(5)-f(2)=\int_2^5f'(t)\,dt<3$, contradicting the prescribed values. With non-strict convexity the data are possible: $f(t)=2+(t-2)/2+(t-2)^2/6$ has affine derivative and satisfies all four endpoint values. The argument needs a strict loss of area; the common endpoint upper bound of one in Figure 2 is convenient, not essential. This is a calculus example, not a candidate SK moment function. With the right slope changed to $2$, the chord has mean $5/4$, so a strict loss of area can leave the required mean one. Indeed, $$ f(t)=2+\frac{t-2}{2}+\frac{(t-2)^3}{18} $$ has the required endpoint values, slopes $1/2$ and $2$, and $(f')''=1/3>0$. Thus these changed data are compatible. Strict convexity produces the contradiction only when the chord cannot supply enough area. **[Question 4](#question-4).** Set $h=q'-1$. Since $q(r)=r$, reaching or passing the diagonal at $t$ means $\int_r^t h\ge0$. Strict convexity places $h$ below its endpoint chord, so that integral is less than $(t-r)(h(r)+h(t))/2$. With $h(r)\le0$, this forces $h(t)>0$. The chord rule on $[r,s]$, solved for $h(s)$, keeps every later value at least $h(t)$. Integrating gives $q(s)\ge t+(s-t)(1+h(t))>1$ for a suitable $s<1$, violating the bound. If $q$ never reaches the diagonal, then $G(r)<0$ instead. Thus both possibilities contradict the conditions on a minimiser. For the proposed polynomial, $q(0)=0$, $q'(0)=1$, $q'''=6>0$, and direct integration gives $G(s)=s^3(1-s)/4\ge0$, with $G(0)=0$. Its derivative has minimum $13/16$, so $q$ increases to $5/4$ as $t\uparrow1$. It is bounded, but $q(9/10)=2043/2000>1$. The other reduced conditions therefore do not replace the exact cap supplied by $|u|\le1$. **[Question 5](#question-5).** Choose $r=0.4$ and $\varepsilon=0.02$. The theorem gives a pair differing on between 29% and 31% of sites. Reverse every sign of the second configuration. Its energy is unchanged, its overlap changes sign, and the differing-site fraction becomes its complement, between 69% and 71%. This operation uses the same successful instance and causes no further probability loss. The theorem fixes $\eta>0$ before $n$ grows; it supplies no rate justifying $\eta=1/n$. This stronger choice is not established by the stated result.

rows.label: changed-cases
rows.text: ### 5.5 Two checks on the gap argument **Question 3: tilt the chord.** Suppose a differentiable function $f$ on $[2,5]$ has $f(2)=2$, $f(5)=5$, $f'(2)=1/2$ and $f'(5)=3/2$. If $f'$ is strictly convex, can these data hold? What changes if strict convexity is weakened to convexity? The endpoint chord is now tilted, so a pointwise comparison with the constant one is unavailable. Finally, keep the endpoint values and left slope fixed but change $f'(5)$ to $2$. Are these data compatible with strict convexity of $f'$? **Question 4: the missing right endpoint.** Put the proof aside and explain why a terminal plateau cannot minimise. Identify what replaces the missing right contact point and why the contradiction occurs before time one. Then check whether the exact bound $q\le1$ could be replaced by mere boundedness: test the calculus function $q(t)=t-3t^2/4+t^3$ on $[0,1)$ against the remaining contact and curvature conditions at $r=0$. This test concerns the calculus argument; the polynomial is not asserted to arise from an SK coefficient. [Answers 3](#answer-3) and [4](#answer-4).

rows.label: contact-and-gap
rows.text:
Adding a small atom at scale $s$ raises the cumulative function at
*every* later scale. It is always allowed: the total mass is not
fixed, so no compensating removal is required. Its direction is
$\eta(t)=\mathbf1_{[s,1)}(t)$, equal to zero before $s$ and one
from $s$ onward. Thus

$$
D\mathcal P(\gamma)[\mathbf1_{[s,1)}]
=\frac12\int_s^1(q(t)-t)\,dt=:\frac12G(s).
$$

For the candidate in Figure 1, adding $\varepsilon$ mass at $s=1/2$
creates a jump of height $\varepsilon$ there and raises the entire
remaining curve by $\varepsilon$. The coefficient changes only on
that tail, but its optimised value and feedback must be recomputed:
earlier starting states also face a changed future control problem. The
first-variation theorem accounts for this dependence. Its formula
has a tail integral because that is where the coefficient changes:
$G(s)/2$ is the marginal cost of placing mass at $s$. At a minimiser,
$G(s)\ge0$ for every $s<1$.

For the two weights in Section 2, the same accounting gives

$$
\int_0^1\gamma(t)(q(t)-t)\,dt
=2G(1/4)+G(3/4).
$$

Each weight is charged for its entire remaining tail. The $q$ and $G$
in this identity belong to that candidate; no optimality has been assumed.
Reducing both weights by a fraction $\varepsilon$ multiplies the
cumulative function by $1-\varepsilon$.

Suppose temporarily that this two-weight candidate minimised
$\mathcal P$. Addition would give two nonnegative costs,
$G(1/4)\ge0$ and $G(3/4)\ge0$, while the allowed reduction would give

$$
0\le-\frac12\bigl(2G(1/4)+G(3/4)\bigr).
$$

Both costs must be zero: their positive-weighted sum is nonnegative,
and the reduction forces it to be nonpositive. This is a necessary
condition under the temporary minimiser assumption, not a claim that
the two-weight candidate attains the minimum.

Now fix a general minimiser $\gamma$ and its own $q$, $G$ and
$\mu_\gamma$. The same argument replaces the finite sum by an integral.
The direction $\eta=-\gamma$
is integrable, and $(1-\varepsilon)\gamma$ remains admissible for
$0\le\varepsilon\le1$. It scales all existing mass by the same
factor. For the continuous candidate in Figure 1, it multiplies the
two nonzero slopes and the plateau height by $1-\varepsilon$;
it works for diffuse mass as well as atoms. To see the order of
integration, each weight at $s$ contributes for exactly the times
$t\ge s$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^1\gamma(t)(q(t)-t)\,dt
&=\int_0^1\int_{[0,1)}\mathbf1_{\{s\le t\}}(q(t)-t)\,\mu_\gamma(ds)\,dt\\
&=\int_{[0,1)}G(s)\,\mu_\gamma(ds).
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the allowed reduction gives

$$
0\le D\mathcal P(\gamma)[-\gamma]
=-\frac12\int_{[0,1)}G(s)\,\mu_\gamma(ds).
$$

The exchange of integration order is valid even if the total mass is
infinite. Its absolute integral is bounded by the area from Section 2:

$$
\int_{[0,1)}\int_s^1|q(t)-t|\,dt\,\mu_\gamma(ds)
=\int_0^1\gamma(t)|q(t)-t|\,dt
\le\int_0^1\gamma(t)\,dt<\infty.
$$

Since $G\ge0$, its integral must be zero. If $G$ were positive at a
support point, continuity would bound it below by a positive number
on a neighbourhood carrying positive mass, contradicting that zero
integral. Hence $G=0$ on the support. This is **contact**: the
nonnegative function touches zero there. The scaling argument is the
variational argument of [Chen, Proposition 3.2, equations (3.11)–(3.12)][chen-support],
applied with the integrable-direction formula above.

Scaling removes only mass that exists. In Figure 1, even the supported
point $1/4$ has no atom: intervals around it carry mass, but the point
itself does not. Subtracting $\varepsilon\delta_{1/4}$ would create a
downward jump. For $0<\varepsilon<1/4$ the cumulative values would
remain nonnegative, but the function would no longer be nondecreasing.
Support alone does not permit atom removal. We have proved contact
on the support, not that every zero of $G$ must carry mass.

### 5.2 Contact gives endpoint conditions

We need information about $q$ at the ends of a possible gap. An interior
support point $s$ is a minimum of $G$. Since
$G'(s)=s-q(s)$ and $G''(s)=1-q'(s)$, ordinary calculus gives

$$
q(s)=s,\qquad q'(s)\le1.
$$

At zero, if it belongs to the support, contact and symmetry give
$G(0)=q(0)=0$. If $q'(0)>1$, continuity would give $q'(t)>1$
for small positive $t$. Integration would then give $q(t)>t$, so
$G'(t)=t-q(t)<0$. Starting from $G(0)=0$, this would force $G(t)<0$,
a contradiction. Hence $q'(0)\le1$. This one-sided argument includes
an atom at zero.

### 5.3 Strict curvature creates an impossible integral

The support is relatively closed in $[0,1)$. Starting at a missing
point, enlarge its mass-free interval until it reaches support or a
boundary of the domain. Such a maximal interval has two
support endpoints, starts at zero outside the support, or reaches one.
We treat these three cases in order; the last includes empty support.

First suppose $(r,s)$ has both endpoints in the support, with
$0\le r<s<1$. Its constant height $c$ is necessarily positive:
for $t$ inside the gap, a small relative neighbourhood of $r$ lies in
$[0,t]$ and has positive mass, so $c=\mu_\gamma([0,t])>0$.
If $r=0$, this mass is an atom at zero. Contact imposes

$$
q(r)=r,\quad q(s)=s,\quad q'(r)\le1,\quad q'(s)\le1.
$$

The first two conditions require area $s-r$ under $q'$ across the gap.
A calculus model shows how strict convexity can prevent this. On the
earlier interval $[1/3,2/3]$, put $x=3t-1$ and consider the slope
$1-x(1-x)$. Its endpoints equal one, but

$$
\int_{1/3}^{2/3}[1-(3t-1)(2-3t)]\,dt
=\frac13\int_0^1[1-x(1-x)]\,dx=\frac5{18}.
$$

The missing area is $1/3-5/18=1/18$. This is a calculus model, not a
computed SK moment curve. The next input forces the actual $q'$ below
its endpoint chord in the same way.

**Strict-curvature input ([OpenAI (2026a), Proposition 5.1][support-curvature]).**
For any admissible coefficient equal to $c>0$ on an open interval,
its moment curve satisfies, strictly inside that interval,

$$
q'''(t)\ge\frac{c^2}{1000}\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^4]>0
\qquad(r<t<s).
$$

Section 7.3 explains how this sign is obtained after expectation.
The gap argument uses its strict sign; it does not use the particular
number $1/1000$.
The final inequality uses $a(t,x)>0$, proved by Gaussian smoothing
on the constant interval ([OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 2.3][support-regularity]);
convexity of $\Phi$ alone would only give $a\ge0$.
Because $q'''=(q')''$, the function $q'$ is strictly convex: between
two points its graph lies strictly below their joining chord.
The moment identity makes $q'$ continuous at the endpoints, even if
$\gamma$ jumps there; higher derivatives are needed only inside the gap.
Hence

$$
q'(t)<\frac{s-t}{s-r}q'(r)+\frac{t-r}{s-r}q'(s)\le1
\qquad(r<t<s).
$$

<!-- Modified 2026-10-25: equal endpoint slopes isolate strictness. -->
\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}[x=1cm,y=1cm,font=\small,line cap=round]
  \fill[black!8] (0,3.1) -- (8,3.1) -- (8,3.1)
     .. controls (5.333333,2.066667) and (2.666667,2.066667) .. (0,3.1) -- cycle;

slopes equal one, so the chord alone loses no area. A strictly convex
slope lies below it. Contact would require zero shaded area, but
$\int_r^s(1-q'(t))\,dt>0$. The drawn calculus model is
$1-x(1-x)$ with $x=(t-r)/(s-r)$; its mean is $5/6$, while the constant
slope one has mean one. Neither is asserted to be an SK moment curve.
The proof also allows unequal endpoint slopes, each at most one. Adapted from
\href{https://github.com/openai/math/blob/adc7f1241b42e322a6451854ab7e4b4c146bf78a/preprints/Full-support-of-the-zero-temperature-Sherrington-Kirkpatrick-order-parameter-September-27-2026/build/gap-convexity.tex}{Figure 1 of OpenAI (2026a)}, OpenAI/math (Apache 2.0).}
\end{figure}

Integration gives $q(s)-q(r)<s-r$, contradicting contact. For the candidate in Section 2,
a minimising plateau on $(1/3,2/3)$ would require the same increment
to be both equal to and strictly less than $1/3$.

rows.label: control-derivations
rows.text:
### 7.2 The value equation and the moment identity

At $t=1$ there is no noise or response left to accumulate, so the value
is $|x|$. At earlier times it includes the best remaining response.
Its partial differential equation (PDE) runs backward from that final value:

$$
\partial_t\Phi_\gamma
=-\frac12\left(\partial_{xx}\Phi_\gamma
+\gamma(t)(\partial_x\Phi_\gamma)^2\right),
\qquad \Phi_\gamma(1,x)=|x|.
$$

With the spatial derivatives $u$ and $a$ defined in Section 3.3,
the equation expresses
a recursive choice: choose a response for a short first step, then
use the best continuation from the state reached. At a continuity
point of $\gamma$, this gives the formal first-order relation

$$
\Phi_\gamma(t,x)
=\sup_{|v|\le1}\left\{
\mathbb E\Phi_\gamma(t+h,x+\gamma(t)vh+\sqrt hZ)
-\tfrac12\gamma(t)v^2h\right\}+o(h).
$$

Subtract the present value, divide by $h$, and Taylor-expand.
The identities $\mathbb EZ=0$ and $\mathbb EZ^2=1$ give

$$
0=\Phi_t+\tfrac12\Phi_{xx}
  +\sup_{|v|\le1}\gamma(t)(v\Phi_x-v^2/2).
$$

The square completion from Section 3.3 gives a supremum of
$\gamma u^2/2$, attained at $v=u$, and hence the stated PDE. This calculation explains the equation;
justifying the recursion and the Taylor expansion requires the
control representation and regularity results. See
[Auffinger–Chen, Theorem 2 and Corollary 2][auffinger-chen] for the zero-temperature
control formula and [Jagannath–Tobasco, Lemma 18][jt-control] for the
control method with finite-temperature terminal data. The extension after
Auffinger–Chen's Corollary 2 covers integrable coefficients. The regularity
used here is in
[OpenAI (2026a), Lemmas 2.1–2.2][support-regularity].

Itô's rule is the chain rule for Brownian paths. Along
$dX_t=b_t\,dt+dB_t$, the coefficient of $dt$ (the **drift**)
in a smooth $f(t,X_t)$ is
$f_t+b_tf_x+f_{xx}/2$, and its noise term is $f_x\,dB_t$.
Differentiate the PDE in $x$ and take $b_t=\gamma u$. The drift of
the slope cancels:

$$
du(t,X_t)
=\underbrace{(u_t+\gamma u u_x+u_{xx}/2)}_{0}\,dt
+a(t,X_t)\,dB_t.
$$

Thus $M_t=u(t,X_t)$ is a bounded **martingale**: its conditional
expected later value, given observations up to time $t$, is its present
value. Zero field gives symmetry and $M_0=u(0,0)=0$. Applying Itô's rule once more
to $M_t^2$ gives

$$
d(M_t^2)=2M_ta(t,X_t)\,dB_t+a(t,X_t)^2\,dt.
$$

The noise term has mean zero because its coefficient is nonanticipating
and bounded on each strip ending before one. Taking expectations and
integrating yields $q(t)=\int_0^t\mathbb E[a(s,X_s)^2]\,ds$,
which gives the asserted derivative. Since $\mathbb EM_t=0$,
$q(t)$ is also the variance of the slope response.

For each fixed $T<1$, the required spatial derivatives are bounded on
$[0,T]\times\mathbb R$, and step-coefficient and smooth-terminal
approximations justify the identities. The bounds depend on the coefficient
and strip. The PDE holds almost everywhere in time. These are not
bounds up to time one.

rows.label: correction-example
rows.text:
For a small example of this operation, let $Z$ be standard normal and
$F(x)=2x$. Its density has logarithmic derivative $-x$, so
$\mathbb E[2-2Z^2]=0$. Although $2x^2-1$ is negative near zero,
adding that zero-mean correction gives

$$
(2x^2-1)+(2-2x^2)=1.
$$

Hence $\mathbb E[2Z^2-1]=1>0$. The boundary term vanishes because a
polynomial times the Gaussian density tends to zero. This illustrates
how a correction changes the visible sign without changing the
expectation; it supplies none of the SK-specific sign estimates.

rows.label: curvature-mechanism
rows.text:
### 7.3 Where the strict-curvature input comes from

The proof in Section 5 used strict curvature on a positive constant
interval. We now explain how a correction with expectation zero makes
the estimate usable once the required density bounds and algebraic
identity are supplied. The sources construct the correction and prove
those bounds. Take any admissible
coefficient with $\gamma=c>0$ on an open interval, without assuming
minimality. Set $b=\Phi_{xxx}$ and $d=\Phi_{xxxx}$ there.
Differentiating the PDE and applying Itô's rule gives

$$
q''=\mathbb E[b^2-2ca^3],\qquad
q'''=\mathbb E[d^2-12cab^2+6c^2a^4].
$$

The negative middle term prevents a pointwise positivity argument.
The source instead averages with the spatial probability density
$f_t(x)$ of $X_t$ at positive time. As in the half-time example,
for any integrable function $F$, grouping paths by their reached position gives

$$
\mathbb E[F(X_t)]=\int_{\mathbb R}F(x)f_t(x)\,dx.
$$

These are probability weights on states $x$, distinct from the
Stieltjes weights $\mu_\gamma(ds)$ on overlap scales. The proof needs
bounds relating this density to the spatial derivatives of the value.
The factorisation and comparison arguments establishing those bounds
are given in [OpenAI (2026a), §3][support-signs].

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}

The operation can be written directly for the positive density $f_t$;
here $f_t'$ means differentiation in the state variable $x$, with $t$ fixed.
For a smooth function $F$ with integrable terms and vanishing boundary
product $Ff_t$,

$$
\mathbb E\!\left[F'(X_t)+F(X_t)\frac{f_t'(X_t)}{f_t(X_t)}\right]
=\int_{\mathbb R}(Ff_t)'(x)\,dx=0.
$$

rows.label: curvature-transfer
rows.text: The source first uses positive nondecreasing finite-step coefficients with terminal approximation $M^{-1}\log(2\cosh(Mx))$, choosing $M$ at least as large as every step height. The source's sign comparisons use this bound as well as smoothness. At this stage, write $R_c=d^2-12cab^2+6c^2a^4$. The source constructs a correction $C$ from the spatial derivatives and density, with $$ \mathbb E[C(t,X_t)]=0,\qquad R_c(t,x)+C(t,x)\ge\frac{c^2}{1000}a(t,x)^4. $$ A rational polynomial identity gives the second inequality by writing the remainder as a sum of nonnegative terms. The density bounds and vanishing boundary products justify the first. Consequently $$ q'''(t)=\mathbb E[R_c(t,X_t)] =\mathbb E[(R_c+C)(t,X_t)] \ge\frac{c^2}{1000}\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^4]. $$ This is how the correction produces a useful lower bound for the expectation even though $R_c$ can be negative at particular states. To reach an arbitrary admissible coefficient, fix a time inside the plateau and approximate in $L^1$ by step coefficients, keeping the same value $c$ near that time. Uniform convergence of spatial derivatives through order four on a fixed strip below one, together with convergence of the coupled paths, passes the quantitative inequality to the limit. Strictness is then established for the limit itself: the constant-coefficient heat formula expresses $a$ as a nonnegative mean plus $c$ times a strictly positive variance of a nonconstant slope under a positively weighted Gaussian law. Hence $a(t,x)>0$ and its fourth moment is positive. Positivity of the approximants alone would not suffice. The auxiliary logarithmic derivatives need not converge: they have already been removed by integration. The analytic details are [OpenAI (2026a), §§3–5][support-manuscript] and the companion *Long Reasoning Record*, [§4.4, “How the signs make a correction with zero expectation useful”](../long/reasoning-record.md#curvature-algebra), and [§4.5, “A fixed-time inequality and its plateau application”](../long/reasoning-record.md#plateau-limit).

rows.label: density-and-approximation
rows.text: Full support alone does not give a density. Additional differentiation of the identities $q=t$ and $\mathbb E[a^2]=1$, followed by another use of the integrated curvature estimate on locally constant comparison coefficients, proves that $\gamma$ is smooth, $\gamma(0)=0$, and $\mu_\gamma=\gamma'(t)\,dt$ with $\gamma'(t)>0$ for $0[§§9.1–9.2](../long/reasoning-record.md#smooth-density-consequence), supplies this additional argument; Chen's earlier theorem had already given smooth nonnegative density and full support.

Then $\gamma=0$ there, so the positive-coefficient bound supplies no strictness. Instead the zero-coefficient heat identity gives $$ q''(t)=\mathbb E[\Phi_{xxx}(t,X_t)^2]>0\qquad(00$ throughout $(0,1)$: it is $q$ itself that is strictly convex. Recall that $q(0)=0$ and $q\le1$. For $00$. **The excess slope persists and violates the bound.** To control a later slope, use the same chord rule on the larger interval $[r,s]$, where $t0. $$ The bound holds at every time after $t$, so integration gives $q(s)\ge t+(s-t)(1+h(t))$. Choose any time $$ t+\frac{1-t}{1+h(t)}0$, and the lower bound now gives $q(s)>1$, contradicting $q(s)\le1$ strictly before time one. Thus $q(t)[§5, terminal estimate](../long/reasoning-record.md#terminal-gap). [Auffinger–Chen–Zeng, Remark 7][acz] had already recorded the absence of terminal plateaus. These cases exhaust the complement of the support. Contact now gives $q(t)=t$ for every interior time, and symmetry includes zero. Differentiating gives $\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^2]=1$, completing the theorem.

rows.label: first-variation
rows.text:
## 5. Why a flat interval cannot minimise

We now prove the theorem. The identities $q=t$ and $q'=1$ are
conclusions still to be established. We begin with the first-order cost
of an allowed change, obtain conditions at support points, and then
exclude every possible gap.

### 5.1 Allowed changes and their first-order cost

The **first variation** in a direction $\eta$ is the derivative at
zero of $\varepsilon\mapsto\mathcal P(\gamma+\varepsilon\eta)$.
At a minimum its right derivative is nonnegative whenever small
$\varepsilon\ge0$ leave the candidate admissible. It need not vanish:
the opposite change may violate nonnegativity or monotonicity.
Precisely, let $\eta\in L^1(0,1)$, meaning $\int_0^1|\eta(t)|\,dt<\infty$, and suppose
$\gamma+\varepsilon\eta$ stays admissible for every
$0\le\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0$, for some $\varepsilon_0>0$.
The formula is

$$
D\mathcal P(\gamma)[\eta]
=\frac12\int_0^1\eta(t)(q(t)-t)\,dt.
$$

Here $q$ belongs to the unperturbed candidate $\gamma$.
The term $-t/2$ comes from the outer correction in $\mathcal P$;
$q(t)/2$ is the sensitivity of the reoptimised control value. The latter
is the analytic content of the formula, not differentiation with a fixed
control. [Chen–Handschy–Lerman (2018), Proposition 4][chl-optimality]
gives the derivative along the segment joining any two admissible
coefficients. Taking the second endpoint to be
$\gamma+\varepsilon_0\eta$ and rescaling the segment parameter gives
the formula above. The detailed proof in
[OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 6.1][support-variation] compares value functions
and bounds the terminal remainder by the $L^1$ tail of $\eta$.

rows.label: full-support-statement
rows.text:
## 4. The full-support theorem

**Source theorem ([OpenAI (2026a), Theorem 1.1][support-manuscript]).**
In the pure, zero-field model with $\xi(t)=t^2/2$, let $\gamma$ be an
admissible integrable minimiser of $\mathcal P$. Its Stieltjes measure
has full relative support on $[0,1)$, and $\gamma$ is strictly increasing.
For every associated diffusion and every $0\le t<1$,

$$
\mathbb E[u(t,X_t)^2]=t,\qquad
\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^2]=1.
$$

The theorem requires a minimiser,
not merely an admissible candidate. Zero field supplies $q(0)=0$;
$\xi''=1$ enters the curvature estimate. The statement does not cover
nonzero field or general mixed-spin covariance functions.

rows.label: opening
rows.text:
The Sherrington–Kirkpatrick (SK) model asks us to choose signs that
maximise a random sum of pair interactions. The Parisi formula expresses
the limiting maximum through a nondecreasing function, the **order
parameter**. We explain why a minimising order parameter cannot be
constant on any interval below one.

The proof compares two consequences of a hypothetical gap. Minimality
fixes the values and bounds the slopes of an auxiliary curve at its
endpoints. An analytic estimate makes the derivative strictly convex
between them, leaving too little area to connect the required values.
Initial and terminal gaps need separate arguments. We then return to
the spins: a theorem about their energies gives nearly optimal sign
choices differing on any prescribed positive fraction of positions up to one half,
with arbitrarily small error in that fraction.

We follow the quantitative proof in [OpenAI (2026a)][support-manuscript];
[Hong-Bin Chen (2026), Theorem 1.3][chen-support] had already proved
full support by a different method. The estimate used here makes the
final contradiction a direct comparison of areas. We assume algebra
and elementary calculus, and introduce probability and cumulative mass
through calculations. The deeper analytic facts are stated where the
proof needs them. By the end of Sections 1–6, the reader should be able
to reconstruct how minimality and those inputs exclude each kind of gap,
then translate the result into a statement about spin configurations.
Section 7 gives optional calculations and answers to the short questions
in the text; the full analytic proofs remain in the cited sources.

rows.label: order-parameter-example
overlap-payoff
rows.text: ## 6. Return to the spins At a fixed finite size, almost surely the only exact maximisers are a configuration and its global reversal. Indeed, two configurations that are neither equal nor global reversals differ in some pair product. Their energy difference is then a Gaussian with positive variance, so a tie has probability zero; there are only finitely many pairs. Intermediate separations become possible when we allow a small loss per spin and let the system grow. A separate theorem of [Auffinger–Chen–Zeng, Proposition 1, equation (5)][acz] applies at each point in the minimiser's support. Combining it with full support: for every fixed overlap $r\in[0,1)$ and tolerances $\varepsilon,\eta>0$, with probability over the couplings tending to one exponentially fast as $n\to\infty$, there exist configurations $\sigma,\tau$ with $$ |R(\sigma,\tau)-r|<\varepsilon, \qquad H_n(\sigma)/n,\ H_n(\tau)/n\ge P_*-\eta. $$ If $k$ sites differ, $k/n=(1-R)/2$. The overlap tolerance therefore gives $$ \left|\frac{k}{n}-\frac{1-r}{2}\right|<\frac\varepsilon2. $$ For example, fix an energy loss $\eta>0$ per spin and take $r=1/2$ and $\varepsilon=0.02$. With probability tending to one exponentially fast, the same instance has two configurations with energies per spin at least $P_*-\eta$ and a differing-site fraction between $0.24$ and $0.26$. No numerical threshold for $n$ is asserted. At target zero, the differing-site fraction can be arbitrarily close to one half. The pair may depend on the chosen target and the couplings. This is existence for each fixed target, not a statement about typically sampled pairs or a procedure for finding them. The companion *Long Reasoning Record*, [§9.3, “Near-ground configurations at a prescribed overlap”](../long/reasoning-record.md#near-ground-overlaps), gives the probability bound, covariance adjustment and exact finite-size comparison. The threshold $P_*-\eta$ refers to the limiting value, whereas an exact maximiser attains its particular finite instance's maximum. **Question 5: use the spin conclusion.** Fix an energy loss $\eta>0$. How can the theorem give two configurations differing on between 69% and 71% of sites, although it is stated for nonnegative overlap targets? Which earlier symmetry is needed? Does the stated theorem also permit the choice $\eta=1/n$? [Answer 5](#answer-5).

rows.label: qaoa-boundary
rows.text: The separate circuit theorem in [OpenAI (2026b)][qaoa-manuscript] resolves the eventual-optimality conjecture for the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) in [Basso–Farhi–Marwaha–Villalonga–Zhou, §7, equation (7.2)][bfmvz]. The *Long Reasoning Record*, [§8](../long/reasoning-record.md#qaoa-construction), develops its circuit construction and the order of limits. It requires additional arguments beyond full support.

rows.label: scalar-identities
rows.text: Further martingale arguments recover the ground-state value from the terminal slope response. They use the first curvature moment $\mathbb E[a]$, distinct from the second moment $\mathbb E[a^2]=1$ used here. See [OpenAI (2026a), Corollary 7.1][support-consequences] and the *Long Reasoning Record*, [§6](../long/reasoning-record.md#scalar-value-identities).

The empty-support and terminal convexity arguments in Section 5.4 are ordinary deductions from the stated analytic inputs; the finite no-tie argument in Section 6 follows from the Gaussian Hamiltonian. These arguments are not claimed to have been replayed in Lean. The Lean [implementation][support-proof], [challenge statement][support-interface] and [Comparator configuration][support-config] concern a minimiser's support and moment identities. The support statement assumes a minimiser; it does not prove the external Parisi formula or attainment. The separate scalar [implementation][value-proof] and [statement][value-interface] concern the value identity and finite Gaussian approximation. Neither selected statement covers positive density, the external near-ground overlap theorem used in Section 6, or the complete QAOA circuit theorem. The implementations use [Lean 4 (de Moura–Ullrich, 2021)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-79876-5_37) and [mathlib (The mathlib Community, 2020)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3372885.3373824).
