rows.label: spins-and-overlap
rows.text:
## 1. The finite optimisation problem

At each of $n$ positions, or **sites**, we choose a sign $\sigma_i\in\{-1,1\}$,
called a **spin**. A configuration is the vector
$\sigma=(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_n)$.
For each unordered pair choose an independent standard Gaussian
$J_{ij}$, a normal random variable with mean zero and variance one.
Independence means that learning the other couplings does not change
the probability distribution of this one.
These coefficients, or **couplings**, are drawn once and then held
fixed while we maximise the energy, or **Hamiltonian**,

$$
H_n(\sigma)=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}J_{ij}\sigma_i\sigma_j.
$$

A positive coupling rewards equal signs; a negative one rewards opposite
signs. For example, positive couplings on pairs $12$ and $23$ favour
$\sigma_1=\sigma_2=\sigma_3$, which conflicts with a negative coupling
on pair $13$. This inability to maximise every pair's contribution
simultaneously is called **frustration**. The factor $n^{-1/2}$ fixes
the model's scale.

For two spins, $H_2(\sigma)=J_{12}\sigma_1\sigma_2/\sqrt2$.
Choosing equal or opposite signs according to the sign of $J_{12}$ gives
$\max_\sigma H_2(\sigma)=|J_{12}|/\sqrt2$.

\Needspace{9\baselineskip}

To average over the couplings, we first need their probabilities.
A **probability density** assigns probability by area. For a standard
Gaussian random variable $Z$, the density is
$\varphi(z)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-z^2/2}$; it is nonnegative, has total
integral one, and for $a\le b$ gives

$$
\Pr(a\le Z\le b)=\int_a^b\varphi(z)\,dz.
$$

In particular, a single point has probability zero. The density's height
is not the probability of that point. To average a score $f(Z)$, weight
it by this same density. Its **expectation** is

$$
\mathbb E f(Z)=\int_{\mathbb R}f(z)\varphi(z)\,dz.
$$

For the standard Gaussian, $\mathbb EZ=0$ and $\mathbb EZ^2=1$.
For a mean-zero random variable, its **variance** is this mean square;
thus $\sqrt h Z$ has variance $h$ for $h>0$. Symmetry gives the zero mean, whereas
$\mathbb E|Z|=2\int_0^\infty z\varphi(z)\,dz=\sqrt{2/\pi}$.
Thus the expected two-spin maximum is $1/\sqrt\pi$. For any signs
chosen before seeing the coupling, the expected energy is instead zero.
The order matters: we choose signs for each realised coupling, then average
the achieved maximum. For many spins, we seek the limiting expected
maximum **per spin**,

$$
P_*:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\mathbb E\max_\sigma H_n(\sigma),
$$

where expectation averages over the couplings after taking the maximum.
**Zero temperature**, or **ground-state value**, refers here to this
maximisation problem. The model is **pure** because every term contains
exactly two spins, and has **zero external field** because there is
no additional term $h\sum_i\sigma_i$.

The maximum is one question; the arrangement of nearly optimal choices
is another. To compare two configurations for the *same couplings*,
define their **overlap**
$R(\sigma,\tau)=n^{-1}\sum_i\sigma_i\tau_i$, their average agreement
with a disagreement counted as $-1$. If they disagree at $k$ positions,
then $R=1-2k/n$. For example, $(+,+,+,+)$ and $(+,+,+,-)$ have
overlap $1/2$; two disagreements would give zero. We will ask whether
two nearly optimal configurations can differ on roughly one quarter
of their sites, and more generally at any prescribed fraction up to
one half.

Our normalisation gives the covariance function $\xi(t)=t^2/2$ in the
variational problem below. **Optional normalisation calculation.**
For fixed $\sigma,\tau$, put $v_i=\sigma_i\tau_i$. When we expand the product
of energies, different couplings have mean product zero by independence
and their zero means; a coupling multiplied by itself has mean one.
Together with $v_i^2=1$, this gives

$$
\mathbb E[H_n(\sigma)H_n(\tau)]
=\frac1n\sum_{i<j}v_iv_j
=\frac{(\sum_i v_i)^2-n}{2n}
=\frac n2 R(\sigma,\tau)^2-\frac12.
$$

Dividing by $n$ gives the limiting covariance
$\xi(t)=t^2/2$. For exact covariance
$n\xi(R)$, add the same independent centred Gaussian of variance $1/2$
to every energy; this leaves the expected maximum unchanged.

**Back to the spin question.** Reversing one configuration's signs
preserves its energy and reverses its
overlap with another. We next define deterministic candidate values
indexed by nonnegative overlap scales $t$. The Parisi theorem in
Section 3 identifies their minimum with the limiting spin optimum;
that connection is an external input, not a change of variables in
the finite maximisation.

rows.label: value-and-diffusion
rows.text: ## 3. How a candidate receives its value To rule out a candidate, we will look for an allowed change that lowers its value. Adding mass at one scale changes the cumulative coefficient at every later scale. We therefore need both a value for each candidate and a way to compute the cost of that change. The auxiliary optimisation below supplies the value; its response to the starting state will enter the first-variation formula in Section 5.1. ### 3.1 First evaluate the zero coefficient The variational problem assigns each $\gamma$ a value by a one-dimensional auxiliary optimisation. Its final reward at state $x$ is $|x|$: this is the best one-spin score $\max_{\sigma\in\{-1,1\}}x\sigma$. First take $\gamma=0$, when only noise changes the state. The imported control representation uses noise with variance rate $\xi''$ ([Auffinger–Chen, Theorem 2][auffinger-chen]). Our normalisation $\xi(t)=t^2/2$ gives rate one, so the noise is **Brownian motion** $B$: a continuous random path starting at zero. Its increments over disjoint time intervals are independent; over an interval of length $h$, an increment has the law of the centred Gaussian $\sqrt h Z$. Starting at time $t$ in state $x$, the remaining noise $B_1-B_t$ therefore has the law of $\sqrt{1-t}Z$. The expected final reward is $$ \Phi_0(t,x)=\mathbb E|x+\sqrt{1-t}Z| =\int_{\mathbb R}|x+\sqrt{1-t}z|\varphi(z)\,dz. $$ At $(t,x)=(0,0)$ this is the calculation already performed: $\Phi_0(0,0)=\sqrt{2/\pi}$. At $t=1$ no noise remains and the value is $|x|$. The function gives an expected payoff at a specified starting state; it is not a probability density. ### 3.2 Allowing a response to the noise For a general $\gamma$, a response can bias the future state, with a quadratic cost. Here the overlap scale $t$ plays the role of time; the path is auxiliary, not a motion of the spins. The noise is the Brownian motion introduced above. A **control** $\alpha_s\in[-1,1]$ chooses a response at each time using only noise already observed since the starting time. The whole deterministic schedule $\gamma$ is known, but future noise is not. A rule chosen in advance can still give different responses on different observed paths. To see why this matters, let a sign $W=\pm1$, each with probability $1/2$, be revealed after a single choice $v\in[-1,1]$. The expected score $|W+v|-v^2/2$ is $1-v^2/2$, maximised at $v=0$. A choice $v=W$ would score $3/2$, but uses information unavailable at the time of choice. The continuous control problem repeats decisions with this same restriction; the finite example only illustrates that restriction. For a starting position $x$, the value is $$ \Phi_\gamma(t,x)=\sup_\alpha\mathbb E\left[ \left|x+B_1-B_t+\int_t^1\gamma(s)\alpha_s\,ds\right| -\frac12\int_t^1\gamma(s)\alpha_s^2\,ds \right]. $$ Inside the absolute value, noise and the accumulated bias change the state before its final reward is paid. The second integral is the running control cost. The supremum chooses the best permitted rule; its formal information condition is progressive measurability. Expectation now averages over Brownian paths for a fixed $\gamma$, rather than over spin couplings. At $\gamma=0$ both control terms vanish, recovering Section 3.1. The **Parisi functional** subtracts an explicit correction from this optimised value: $$ \mathcal P(\gamma)=\Phi_\gamma(0,0) -\frac12\int_0^1t\gamma(t)\,dt. $$ The inner supremum chooses a response for fixed $\gamma$; the outer problem minimises $\mathcal P$ over $\gamma$. The ground-state Parisi formula and attainment give $$ P_*=\min_{\gamma\text{ admissible}}\mathcal P(\gamma). $$ Each candidate supplies an upper bound, and minimisation finds the sharpest one. This equality and attainment are external inputs from [Auffinger–Chen (2017), Theorem 1 and the proof of Lemma 3][auffinger-chen]; Gaussian concentration gives the expected-value form used here. The no-gap theorem assumes a minimiser and proves a property of it. The value $\mathcal P(0)=\sqrt{2/\pi}$ alone does not establish that the zero candidate minimises. ### 3.3 The response, the state and the averaged square First consider the value as a function of the starting state, holding $t$ and $\gamma$ fixed; we also write $\Phi=\Phi_\gamma$. For any permitted control, use the same responses to each Brownian history at two starting states $x$ and $y$. The costs are unchanged, and the triangle inequality bounds the change in the terminal reward by $|x-y|$. Taking the supremum over controls gives $$ |\Phi_\gamma(t,x)-\Phi_\gamma(t,y)|\le |x-y|. $$ The value is also **convex**: between two states its graph lies at or below the chord joining their values. Indeed, each fixed-control payoff is an average of translated absolute-value functions, hence convex. Its chord lies at or below the chord of the best endpoint payoffs; taking the supremum preserves that upper bound. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemmas 2.1–2.2][support-regularity] supply spatial differentiability below time one. Let $u(t,x)=\partial_x\Phi_\gamma(t,x)$ be the slope as the starting state changes. A small shift $\delta$ changes the best expected payoff by approximately $u(t,x)\delta$. Write $a(t,x)=\partial_{xx}\Phi_\gamma(t,x)$ for the rate at which that slope changes. The displayed bound gives $|u|\le1$, and convexity gives $a\ge0$. These are spatial derivatives: time is held fixed. For the zero coefficient, the slope can be computed directly. Put $F_{\mathrm G}(z)=\Pr(Z\le z)=\int_{-\infty}^z\varphi(y)\,dy$. Moving $x$ slightly raises $|x+\sqrt{1-t}Z|$ when the final state is positive and lowers it when the final state is negative. Consequently $$ u_0(t,x)=2F_{\mathrm G}\!\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-t}}\right)-1. $$ Differentiating the integral is legitimate: the difference quotients of the absolute value are bounded by one, and the Gaussian has zero probability of hitting its corner. Thus the slope is the probability of a positive final state minus the probability of a negative one. For general $\gamma$, the control theorem says that the slope response attains the value. To see why this is the right response, consider a short step of length $h$ from $(t,x)$. A response $v$ adds displacement $h\gamma(t)v$, whose first-order contribution to the continuation value is $h\gamma(t)vu(t,x)$. Its running cost is $h\gamma(t)v^2/2$. The response-dependent gain per unit time is therefore $$ \gamma vu-\tfrac12\gamma v^2 =\tfrac12\gamma u^2-\tfrac12\gamma(v-u)^2. $$ Since $\gamma\ge0$ and $|u|\le1$, $v=u$ attains its maximum. The optimised contribution $\gamma u^2/2$ also explains why a squared slope will enter the sensitivity to $\gamma$. The control theorem and the first-variation formula in Section 5.1 make these connections rigorous; the square completion alone does not justify differentiating an optimised value. The control representation and feedback are justified for integrable coefficients in [OpenAI (2026a), Lemmas 2.1–2.2][support-regularity]; see also [Auffinger–Chen, Corollary 2 and the extension after (13)][auffinger-chen]. We first fix $\gamma$ and obtain the deterministic value and slope by optimising the expected future payoff. We then use that slope as a rule along a random path. Computing an expected future payoff does not reveal future noise: at time $t$, the rule needs only $t$ and the state already reached. Following it generates the state $$ X_t=B_t+\int_0^t\gamma(s)u(s,X_s)\,ds,\qquad X_0=0. $$ This is the **associated diffusion**. The cited regularity theorem gives its existence and uniqueness for a fixed Brownian motion. The rule is called **feedback** because it uses the slope at the currently reached state. With $\gamma$ and $u$ supplied, a short forward step of length $h$ from state $x$ at time $t$, with $t+h<1$, is approximated by $$ x+h\gamma(t)u(t,x)+\sqrt h Z. $$ The response is evaluated before the fresh independent noise $Z$ is observed. This discrete approximation explains the order of operations; the integral equation defines the continuous process. Its drift accumulates through time, so even a jump of $\gamma$ does not make $X$ jump. Fix $\gamma$, follow a path to $X_t$, evaluate the slope there, square it, and average over paths. This defines a deterministic curve $$ q(t):=\mathbb E[u(t,X_t)^2]. $$ Here $\Phi_\gamma$ and $u$ are deterministic functions; $X_t$ and the response evaluated at it are random. Squaring before averaging retains the size of both positive and negative responses. \Needspace{22\baselineskip} **A calculation at half time.** For $\gamma=0$, $X_t=B_t$ and $B_{1/2}$ has the same distribution as $Z/\sqrt2$. We can average over paths by grouping them according to the state reached. At half time the reached state has density $e^{-x^2}/\sqrt\pi$. This density describes its **law**, assigning probability to positions on the real line. The law has total mass one even though the order-parameter measure $\mu_0$ is zero. The two measures describe different objects. Average $u_0(1/2,x)^2$ with this density. Substituting $x=z/\sqrt2$ gives $$ \begin{aligned} q_0(1/2) &=\int_{\mathbb R}(2F_{\mathrm G}(z)-1)^2\varphi(z)\,dz\\ &=\int_0^1(2v-1)^2\,dv=\frac13, \qquad v=F_{\mathrm G}(z),\quad dv=\varphi(z)\,dz. \end{aligned} $$ The response at zero is zero, but its mean square at the random state is $1/3$. Thus $q(t)=t$ is not automatic. Although every control is optimal at $\gamma=0$, $q_0$ uses the value slope $u_0$. Section 7.1 uses the whole curve to find a feasible decrease of $\mathcal P(0)$; a discrepancy at one time does not suffice. **Question 2: change the time and the future.** Still take $\gamma=0$ everywhere, but now set $t=1/4$. What variance has the state accumulated, and what variance remains in its future reward? Write the Gaussian integral for $q_0(1/4)$ without evaluating it. Now take $\gamma=0$ before $1/2$ and $\gamma=1$ afterward. Does that same integral still compute $q(1/4)$? Identify what remains unchanged and what must be recomputed. [Answer 2](#answer-2). The analytic facts needed in the proof are $$ q\in C^1([0,1)),\qquad q(0)=0,\qquad 0\le q(t)\le1, \qquad q'(t)=\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^2]. $$ Here $C^1$ means continuously differentiable, with derivatives at zero from the right. In particular, $q'$ stays continuous across jumps of $\gamma$. Spatial curvature controls the growth of the squared response. These facts hold for every admissible candidate and follow from [OpenAI (2026a), Lemmas 2.1–2.2][support-regularity]. The initial value has a direct symmetry explanation: reflecting the starting state, noise history and response rule together preserves reward and cost, so $\Phi_\gamma(t,x)$ is even in $x$. Hence $u(t,0)=0$, and the zero-field starting state $X_0=0$ gives $q(0)=0$. Section 7.2 explains the stochastic calculation for $q'$. In Section 5, $q(t)-t$ will determine the first-order cost of changing cumulative weight. An added mass persists at every later time, so its cost requires a tail integral.

rows.label: zero-candidate
rows.text:
\Needspace{11\baselineskip}

### 7.1 Why the zero candidate does not minimise

Return to the Gaussian value and slope from Section 3. With $\gamma=0$,
the state is $B_t$. Differentiating the slope once more gives

$$
X_t=B_t,\qquad
u_0(t,x)=2F_{\mathrm G}\!\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-t}}\right)-1,
\qquad
a_0(t,x)=\sqrt{\frac2{\pi(1-t)}}e^{-x^2/(2(1-t))}.
$$

A Gaussian integral gives
$\mathbb E e^{-B_t^2/(1-t)}=\sqrt{(1-t)/(1+t)}$. Substituting
into $q_0'=\mathbb E[a_0(t,B_t)^2]$ and integrating from zero yields

$$
q_0'(t)=\frac2{\pi\sqrt{1-t^2}},\qquad
q_0(t)=\frac2\pi\arcsin t.
$$

This recovers the half-time value $1/3$. It also shows that
$q_0(t)\to1$ while $q_0'(t)\to\infty$: convergence of a function
at one does not bound its derivative there.
The constant direction $\eta=1$ is admissible and adds an atom at zero.
Its cost is

$$
D\mathcal P(0)[1]
=\frac12\int_0^1\left(\frac2\pi\arcsin t-t\right)dt
=\frac14-\frac1\pi<0.
$$

So a small positive constant coefficient improves the zero candidate.
This calculation uses the heat and variation formulas, not a minimiser
hypothesis; see also [Chen–Handschy–Lerman, proof of Theorem 6][chl-optimality].

rows.label: approximation-choices
rows.text:
### 2.5 Order of approximation

The same symbol for a small error must not conceal changing background
objects. The following account fixes those objects before the indicated
limit. A single admissible minimiser and its associated diffusion are
retained throughout the scalar construction.

**Compact-strip regularity.** Fix a derivative order $k\ge1$, a cutoff
$T<1$ and a common coefficient $L^1$ bound. Coefficients converge in $L^1$
within that bound; spatial derivatives converge uniformly on the strip.

**Shape inequalities on a plateau.** Fix the height $c>0$ and a closed
interior neighbourhood. Choose step coefficients equal to $c$ there and
smooth terminal values with $M_m\ge\|\gamma_m\|_\infty$ and
$M_m\to\infty$. The coefficient and terminal approximations may be
chosen as one compatible sequence.

**First variation.** Fix $\gamma$, a feasible $\eta\in L^1$ and initially
$\epsilon>0$. Remove the terminal cutoff before letting
$\epsilon\downarrow0$. The terminal remainder divided by $\epsilon$ is
bounded by an $L^1$ tail of $\eta$.

**Terminal value.** Keep the chosen minimiser and diffusion fixed. Bounded
martingale convergence and integrability of $\gamma$ justify
$t\uparrow1$; no terminal derivative bound is needed.

**Finite Gaussian coefficients.** Fix $\gamma,X$ and $T<1$. Refine $N$
using the fixed-strip bounds, then control the remaining value tail by $1-T$.

For the plateau transfer, tail estimates for a fixed approximant may depend
on that approximant. The passage to the limit uses the integrated
polynomial in the scaled second, third and fourth spatial derivatives of
the value function and the common strip bounds; it does not require
uniform bounds on the auxiliary density scores. Sections 3 and 4 explain
the variation and plateau-transfer arguments, and §7 gives a complete scalar error
budget. The further choices used to produce a circuit appear in §8.6.
[OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 2.1, Lemma 6.1, Proposition 5.1 and
Proposition 7.2][fs-main].

rows.label: coefficient-budget
rows.text: **A coefficient budget from the first curvature moment.** Full support also bounds the minimizing coefficient. Put $m(t)=\mathbb E a(t,X_t)$. The compact-strip identity $$ da(t,X_t)=-\gamma(t)a(t,X_t)^2\,dt+b(t,X_t)\,dB_t $$ holds before any smoothness conclusion for $\gamma$; the bounded strip derivatives make its stochastic integral a martingale. [OpenAI (2026a), proof of Corollary 6.4][fs-density]. At zero, $X_0=0$, $a(0,0)\ge0$ and $\mathbb E a(0,X_0)^2=1$ give $a(0,0)=1$. Taking expectations and using $\mathbb E a(t,X_t)^2=1$ therefore yields $$ m(t)=1-\int_0^t\gamma(s)\,ds,\qquad 0\le t<1. $$ Convexity gives $m(t)\ge0$. Letting $t\uparrow1$ and using monotonicity of $\gamma$ on every tail gives $$ \int_0^1\gamma(s)\,ds\le1,\qquad 0\le\gamma(t)\le\frac{m(t)}{1-t}\le\frac1{1-t}. $$ Indeed, $(s-t)\gamma(t)\le\int_t^s\gamma\le m(t)$ for $t **Proposition 6.2 (terminal normalization in zero field).** For the minimizer and diffusion of Theorem 5.1, $$ \lim_{t\uparrow1}m(t)=0,\qquad \int_0^1\gamma(s)\,ds=1,\qquad m(t)=\int_t^1\gamma(s)\,ds, $$ and consequently $$ P_*=\int_0^1s\gamma(s)\,ds. $$ Thus $\gamma(s)\,ds$ has total mass one; this does not normalize the Stieltjes measure $d\gamma$. This is an ordinary analytic consequence, separate from the selected formal endpoints. **Proof.** The backward comparison in §4.3 gives $\Phi_{xxx}(t,x)\le0$ for $x>0$ in every positive finite-step approximation. Compact-strip convergence of the third spatial derivative passes this inequality to $\gamma$. Together with evenness and convexity, it says that $a(t,x)$ is nonnegative, even and nonincreasing in $|x|$. These inputs are [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 3.2][fs-signs] and [Lemma 2.1][fs-reg]; they do not require differentiability of $\gamma$. Uniform terminal convergence to $|x|$ and convex difference quotients give $u(t,x)\to1$ at every fixed $x>0$. For each $\delta>0$, $$ 0\le a(t,\delta) \le\frac2\delta\int_{\delta/2}^{\delta}a(t,x)\,dx =\frac2\delta\bigl(u(t,\delta)-u(t,\delta/2)\bigr) \longrightarrow0. $$ The spatial monotonicity is essential here: convergence of convex functions alone would not imply convergence of their second derivatives. It remains to control the probability of the shrinking region where curvature can be large. Oddness and monotonicity give $u(t,x)\ge0$ for $x\ge0$, so the drift points away from zero. Tanaka's formula for $R_t=|X_t|$ gives $$ R_t=W_t+V_t+L_t,\qquad W_t=\int_0^t\operatorname{sgn}(X_s)\,dB_s,\qquad V_t=\int_0^t\gamma(s)u(s,R_s)\,ds. $$ Here $L$ is the local time of $X$ at zero. The occupation-time formula and $d\langle X\rangle_s=ds$ imply $\int_0^t\mathbf1_{\{X_s=0\}}\,ds=0$. Thus $\langle W\rangle_t=t$, and the continuous martingale $W$ is Brownian motion. The process $V$ is nondecreasing and starts at zero; $L$ increases only when $R=0$. The reflection formula therefore gives, pathwise, $$ R_t=W_t+V_t-\min\left(0,\inf_{s\le t}(W_s+V_s)\right) \ge W_t-\min\left(0,\inf_{s\le t}W_s\right)=:R_t^0. $$ Indeed $0\le V_s\le V_t$ bounds the subtracted minimum by $\min(0,\inf_{s\le t}W_s)+V_t$. No independence of $V$ and $W$ is needed. Reflected Brownian motion $R_t^0$ has the one-time law $|B_t|$, so for $t>0$, $$ \Pr(|X_t|\le\delta) \le\Pr(|B_t|\le\delta) \le\sqrt{\frac2\pi}\frac{\delta}{\sqrt t}. $$ Splitting at $|X_t|=\delta$, using spatial monotonicity outside and Cauchy–Schwarz with $\mathbb E a(t,X_t)^2=1$ inside, yields $$ 0\le m(t)\le a(t,\delta) +\sqrt{\Pr(|X_t|\le\delta)}. $$ First let $t\uparrow1$ and then $\delta\downarrow0$. This proves $m(1-)=0$. The compact-strip identity for $m$ now gives total mass one and the tail formula. Tonelli and (6.1) give the stated expression for $P_*$. In particular, $$ 0\le P_*-I(T)=\int_T^1(s-T)\gamma(s)\,ds \le(1-T)m(T)=o(1-T). $$ No numerical rate for $m(T)\to0$ or for the required spatial derivative bounds follows from this proof. The endpoint distinction also matters when comparing editions. [Sellke, arXiv:2105.03506v4, Lemma 2.9, equation (2.7)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.03506v4) states the expected-Hessian tail equality. In [version 6, Lemma 2.9, equation (2.8), and Remark 2.10](https://arxiv.org/html/2105.03506v6#S2.SS3), the general statement is an inequality; the remark obtains equality indirectly for even mixtures. The specialized zero-field proof above supplies its own endpoint argument from the shape and contact identities, rather than substituting $t=1$ into a compact-strip formula or relying on the older equality in its full stated generality.

rows.label: contact
rows.text: **Proposition 3.1 (variational contact).** For an admissible minimizer, the potential $G(s)=\int_s^1(q(t)-t)\,dt$ is nonnegative on $[0,1)$ and vanishes on $S=\operatorname{supp}\mu_\gamma$. At every $s\in S$, $q(s)=s$ and $q'(s)\le1$, with a right derivative at zero. The minimisation takes place over nonnegative Stieltjes measures with an integrable cumulative function. Their total mass is free. We first derive the variation of the functional, then use changes of measure which preserve this admissible class. The result will be contact on the *existing* support; the exclusion of gaps comes afterwards. ### 3.1 The moment function before minimisation Fix any $\gamma\in\mathcal U$, without yet assuming that it minimises $\mathcal P$. Compact-strip regularity and Itô's formula give $$ u(t,X_t)=\int_0^t a(s,X_s)\,dB_s,\qquad q(t):=\mathbb E u(t,X_t)^2 =\int_0^t\mathbb E a(s,X_s)^2\,ds. $$ The initial term vanishes because zero field makes $\Phi$ even and $u(0,0)=0$. Thus $q(0)=0$, $0\le q(t)\le1$, and $$ q'(t)=\mathbb E a(t,X_t)^2\qquad(0\le t<1), $$ with a right derivative at zero. The integrand is continuous on each compact time strip, so $q\in C^1[0,1)$. These facts hold for every admissible coefficient. They do not yet say that $q(t)=t$. The source proves them by smooth approximation on $[0,T]$, $T<1$; it never differentiates the terminal cusp $|x|$ at time one. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemmas 2.1–2.2][fs-reg]. ### 3.2 The feasible right derivative Let $\eta\in L^1(0,1)$ and suppose that $\gamma+\varepsilon\eta\in\mathcal U$ for $0\le\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0$, where $\varepsilon_0>0$. This is a feasibility hypothesis: an arbitrary signed bump in $\gamma$ need not preserve monotonicity. Since $\mathcal U$ is convex, it is enough to check that the endpoint $\gamma+\varepsilon_0\eta$ is admissible. The formula below is the zero-field, $\xi''=1$ specialization of [Chen, Handschy and Lerman, arXiv:1609.04368v4, Proposition 4](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.04368v4). Their chord $\gamma_\theta=(1-\theta)\gamma+\theta\gamma_1$ gives this direction by taking $\gamma_1=\gamma+\varepsilon_0\eta$ and $\theta=\varepsilon/\varepsilon_0$. Their class $\mathcal U$ permits unnormalized cumulative measures with finite cumulative integral, so this change of parameter also covers the scaling direction $-\gamma$. We reconstruct the detailed PDE proof from OpenAI's Lemma 6.1. For $0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0$, put $\beta=\gamma+\varepsilon\eta$, $\widetilde u=\Phi_{\beta,x}$ and $D=\Phi_\beta-\Phi_\gamma$. Subtracting the two PDEs gives $$ D_t=-\frac12D_{xx} -\frac12\beta(\widetilde u+u)D_x -\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\eta u^2. $$ The choice of diffusion $$ dY_t^\varepsilon =\frac12\beta(t)(\widetilde u+u)(t,Y_t^\varepsilon)\,dt+dB_t, \qquad Y_0^\varepsilon=0, $$ cancels the first-order spatial term when Itô's formula is applied to $D(t,Y_t^\varepsilon)$. Its drift has absolute value at most $\beta(t)$, which is integrable. On $[0,T]$ the resulting identity is $$ D(0,0)=\mathbb E D(T,Y_T^\varepsilon) +\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\int_0^T \eta(t)\mathbb E[u(t,Y_t^\varepsilon)^2]\,dt. $$ At coefficient jumps the time derivatives need only exist almost everywhere. The source obtains this identity by approximating both coefficients by monotone step functions with the same smooth terminal datum, and then passing to the limit using the compact-strip estimates. The control representation, applied with the same control on each side, gives the time-local difference bound $$ \sup_x|D(T,x)|\le\frac{3\varepsilon}{2} \int_T^1|\eta(t)|\,dt. $$ Hence $T\uparrow1$, at fixed $\varepsilon$, removes the terminal term even after division by $\varepsilon$. We obtain the exact finite-change identity $$ \frac{\Phi_{\gamma+\varepsilon\eta}(0,0)-\Phi_\gamma(0,0)} {\varepsilon} =\frac12\int_0^1\eta(t) \mathbb E[u(t,Y_t^\varepsilon)^2]\,dt. $$ As $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, the coefficients converge in $L^1$ and have uniformly bounded $L^1$ norms. On each fixed strip, their gradients converge uniformly and have common spatial Lipschitz bounds. Coupling with the same Brownian motion and applying Gronwall's inequality therefore gives $Y^\varepsilon\to X$ uniformly on that strip. The integrand converges to $\eta(t)q(t)$ for each $t<1$, and its absolute value is at most $|\eta(t)|$. Dominated convergence, followed by subtraction of the linear Parisi penalty, now yields $$ D_+\mathcal P(\gamma)[\eta] :=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0} \frac{\mathcal P(\gamma+\varepsilon\eta)-\mathcal P(\gamma)} {\varepsilon} =\frac12\int_0^1\eta(t)(q(t)-t)\,dt. $$ If $\gamma$ is a minimiser, this derivative is nonnegative for every feasible direction. It need not vanish: the minimisation has one-sided constraints. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 6.1, equations (6.1)–(6.2)][fs-var]. ### 3.3 Which changes of measure are allowed? Write $\mu=\mu_\gamma$ and $S=\operatorname{supp}\mu$, with support relative to $[0,1)$. Tonelli's theorem gives the useful identity $$ \int_0^1\gamma(t)\,dt =\int_{[0,1)}\!\int_s^1dt\,\mu(ds) =\int_{[0,1)}(1-s)\,\mu(ds)<\infty. $$ This is weighted finiteness, not a bound on $\mu([0,1))$. In particular, there is no normalisation constraint requiring mass added at one point to be removed elsewhere. Define the tail potential $$ G(s)=\int_s^1(q(t)-t)\,dt\qquad(0\le s<1). $$ It is continuous, satisfies $|G(s)|\le1-s$, and has $G'(s)=s-q(s)$ and $G''(s)=1-q'(s)$ on compact strips, with one-sided interpretations at zero. The following two competitors suffice. | Change to the Stieltjes measure | Direction in the cumulative function | Allowed parameter | Consequence at a minimiser | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Add $\varepsilon\delta_s$, $0\le s<1$ | $\eta(t)=\mathbf1_{[s,1)}(t)$ | $\varepsilon\ge0$ | $G(s)\ge0$ | | Remove $\varepsilon\nu$, where $\nu=\mu|_K$ and $K\subset[0,1)$ is compact | $\eta_K(t)=-\nu([0,t])$ | $0\le\varepsilon\le1$ | $\int_KG(s)\,\mu(ds)\le0$ | For atom addition, the new cumulative function is nonnegative, nondecreasing and right-continuous. Its integral increases by $\varepsilon(1-s)$, so it remains in $\mathcal U$. This includes $s=0$: an atom there adds a constant to $\gamma$ on all of $[0,1)$. The point $1$ is outside the measure's domain and is not an additional competitor. The derivative formula gives $D_+\mathcal P(\gamma)[\mathbf1_{[s,1)}]=G(s)/2$, proving $G\ge0$ everywhere below one. For removal, choose $T<1$ with $K\subset[0,T]$. Then $\nu(K)\le\gamma(T)<\infty$. The measure $\mu-\varepsilon\nu$ is nonnegative for $0\le\varepsilon\le1$, so its cumulative function is nonnegative, nondecreasing and right-continuous. It lies between zero and $\gamma$, hence is integrable; also $|\eta_K|\le\nu(K)$. Fubini is justified quantitatively by $$ \int_K\!\int_s^1|q(t)-t|\,dt\,\mu(ds) \le\int_K(1-s)\,\mu(ds)\le\nu(K)<\infty. $$ It follows that $$ 0\le D_+\mathcal P(\gamma)[\eta_K] =-\frac12\int_0^1\nu([0,t])(q(t)-t)\,dt =-\frac12\int_KG(s)\,\mu(ds). $$ Since $G\ge0$, its integral on every compact $K$ is zero. The compact intervals $[0,T]$ exhaust $[0,1)$, so $G=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere. If a support point $s$ had $G(s)>0$, continuity would give a relative neighbourhood on which $G$ stays positive. After restricting to a compact interval containing that neighbourhood, the defining property of support would give it positive $\mu$-mass, contradicting the zero integral. Therefore $$ G(s)=0\qquad(s\in S). $$ This step applies to atoms, diffuse mass and singular continuous mass. Removing individual atoms alone would not establish it. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 6.2][fs-var]. ### 3.4 Contact values and endpoint slopes At $s\in S\cap(0,1)$, the function $G$ has an interior minimum of value zero. Thus $G'(s)=0$ and $G''(s)\ge0$, giving $$ q(s)=s,\qquad q'(s)\le1. $$ If $0\in S$, the argument needs the zero-field initial condition in addition to the one-sided minimum. We have $G(0)=0$ and $q(0)=0$, so $$ G(h)=G(0)+\int_0^h(t-q(t))\,dt =\frac12(1-q'(0))h^2+o(h^2). $$ Nonnegativity for $h>0$ implies $q'(0)\le1$. This works whether or not zero is an atom. The equality $q(0)=0$ comes from symmetry, rather than from differentiating a one-sided minimum. If $0\notin S$, no condition $G(0)=0$ has been obtained or used. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 6.2][fs-var]. We have now proved, without any no-gap assumption, $$ G\ge0\text{ on }[0,1),\qquad G=0\text{ on }S,\qquad q(s)=s\text{ and }q'(s)\le1\text{ for }s\in S. $$ These are precisely the contact data used in §5. They make no assertion that every zero of $G$ belongs to $S$, or that $q(t)=t$ at a point outside $S$. Terminal, interior and initial gaps remain to be excluded. ### 3.5 What the first-order criterion does, and does not, establish The contact data needed for the gap proof are already available. Readers following that proof can continue to [the curvature argument in §4](#curvature-and-gap-certificate). This subsection gives an alternative contact proof and the converse optimality criterion. There is also a global alternative to compact mass removal. Atom addition still gives $G\ge0$. Now replace $\mu$ by $(1-\varepsilon)\mu$, or equivalently $\gamma$ by $(1-\varepsilon)\gamma$, for $0\le\varepsilon\le1$. This preserves admissibility, and its direction $-\gamma$ lies in $L^1$, although it may be unbounded. The first variation in §3.2 therefore applies. The signed interchange is justified by $$ \int_{[0,1)}\!\int_s^1|q(t)-t|\,dt\,\mu(ds) =\int_0^1\gamma(t)|q(t)-t|\,dt \le\int_0^1\gamma(t)\,dt<\infty. $$ Consequently $$ 0\le D_+\mathcal P(\gamma)[-\gamma] =-\frac12\int_{[0,1)}G(s)\,\mu(ds). $$ Together with $G\ge0$, this gives $\int G\,d\mu=0$. Continuity then gives $G=0$ on relative support, including zero, as in §3.3. Finite weighted mass is sufficient throughout; no finite total mass or density of $\mu$ has been assumed. This ordinary argument uses the same integrable-direction first variation as the local removal proof. For the actual moment function associated with $\gamma$, the two potential conditions $G\ge0$ and $G=0$ on $S$ are also sufficient for minimality. This ordinary deduction explains exactly how much variational information has been extracted. For another admissible coefficient $\beta$, let $\nu=\mu_\beta$. The weighted identity above and $|G(s)|\le1-s$ make both measure integrals absolutely convergent, even when either measure has infinite total mass. Fubini gives $$ 2D_+\mathcal P(\gamma)[\beta-\gamma] =\int_{[0,1)}G(s)\,\nu(ds) -\int_{[0,1)}G(s)\,\mu(ds)\ge0. $$ Here the second integral is zero because $\mu$ is concentrated on its relative support. The control formula also shows that $\mathcal P$ is convex in its coefficient: for a fixed control, the terminal absolute value is convex in the coefficient and both penalties are linear; taking the supremum over the same control class preserves convexity. Therefore $$ \mathcal P(\beta)-\mathcal P(\gamma) \ge D_+\mathcal P(\gamma)[\beta-\gamma]\ge0. $$ This proves the converse. It agrees with the chord optimality criterion of [Chen, Handschy and Lerman, arXiv:1609.04368v4, Proposition 4, printed p. 14](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.04368v4). Chen's zero-temperature treatment obtains the same contact integral by testing $0$ and $2\gamma$ and then using weighted Fubini [Chen (2026), Proposition 3.2, equations (3.11)–(3.12)][chen2026]. The compact-removal proof above keeps the local mass operation explicit. The converse concerns $G$ built from the PDE and diffusion of the same $\gamma$. It does not say that an arbitrary curve with these contact properties comes from a Parisi solution. Nor does it prove full support: the missing input is the strict curvature on an interval where the coefficient is constant, established next. The formal chord statement and the ordinary derivative bridge are distinguished in §12.1.

rows.label: curvature
rows.text: The gap argument needs a property of the derivative $q'$, rather than convexity of the spatial function $\Phi$. We establish the following analytic input before using minimality. Let $\gamma\in\mathcal U$ be constant with value $c$ on an open interval $I\subset(0,1)$, and let $X$ be its diffusion started at zero. Then $$ \begin{cases} q'''(t)\ge \dfrac1{1000c^2} \mathbb E\bigl[(c\Phi_{xx}(t,X_t))^4\bigr]>0,&c>0,\\[4pt] q''(t)=\mathbb E[\Phi_{xxx}(t,X_t)^2]>0,&c=0, \end{cases}\qquad t\in I. $$ Thus $q'$ is strictly convex for $c>0$ and strictly increasing for $c=0$. The coefficient may jump outside $I$ and may be unbounded near one, provided it is nonnegative, nondecreasing, right-continuous and integrable. No support property or minimising assumption enters this statement. The positive-time restriction matters when a diffusion density is used; interval endpoints are handled later by continuity. [OpenAI (2026a), Proposition 5.1][fs-curv]. The proof has two stages. In §§4.1–4.4 the coefficient is a positive monotone finite-step function with smooth terminal data. Shape comparisons and boundary estimates justify the [polynomial correction](#curvature-algebra) and its zero expectation. In [§4.5](#plateau-limit), approximants $\gamma_n,\Phi_n,X^n$ approach an arbitrary admissible coefficient. Only the integrated expression in spatial derivatives passes to the limit; the auxiliary forward scores need not converge. Bounds depend on a fixed compact strip and a common coefficient mass bound. The strictly positive right side is then justified for the limiting solution itself. ### 4.1 Why the uncorrected expression has no pointwise sign On a positive constant interval put $r=c\Phi_x$, $v=r_x$, $w=r_{xx}$ and $z=r_{xxx}$. In forward time, $r_t=-\tfrac12r_{xx}-rr_x$ and $dX_t=r(t,X_t)\,dt+dB_t$. Differentiating the PDE and applying Itô's formula gives $$ dr(t,X_t)=v(t,X_t)\,dB_t, $$ $$ dv(t,X_t)=-v(t,X_t)^2\,dt+w(t,X_t)\,dB_t, \qquad dw(t,X_t)=-3v(t,X_t)w(t,X_t)\,dt+z(t,X_t)\,dB_t. $$ Since $q'=c^{-2}\mathbb E v^2$, the drift of $v^2$ yields $c^2q''=\mathbb E(w^2-2v^3)$. The drifts of $w^2$ and $v^3$ are, respectively, $z^2-6vw^2$ and $3vw^2-3v^4$. Therefore $$ c^2q'''=\mathbb E\bigl[z^2-12vw^2+6v^4\bigr]. $$ These are interior-time identities. On a smaller constant interval the heat formula gives classical time smoothness and bounded spatial derivatives of sufficiently high order, so the local martingale terms have zero mean and the expectation differentiations are justified. Nothing here assigns a sign to $q''$. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 2.3][fs-reg]. There is a concrete obstruction to reading the last display pointwise. For the smooth finite-step problem $c=M=1$ on $[0,1)$, with terminal value $\log(2\cosh x)$, the exact solution is $$ \Phi(t,x)=\log(2\cosh x)+\frac{1-t}{2},\qquad r=\tanh x. $$ Indeed, $\Phi_{xx}+\Phi_x^2=1$. Writing $R=r^2$ gives $v=1-R$, $w=-2rv$ and $z=-2v^2+4Rv$. At $R=1/2$, $v=1/2$, $w^2=1/2$ and $z=1/2$, so $$ z^2-12vw^2+6v^4=-\frac{19}{8}<0. $$ This example lies in the smooth analytic class used below. Its diffusion density is $f_t(x)=e^{-t/2}\cosh(x)p_t(x)$, obtained from the heat transition formula, and integrates to one because $\mathbb E\cosh(B_t)=e^{t/2}$. It illustrates the necessity of the integration argument; it uses a smooth terminal value and makes no claim to be the zero-temperature minimiser. The displayed negative value is an exact elementary calculation. The heat formula itself is [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 2.1][fs-reg]. The same pointwise obstruction occurs with the actual terminal datum $|x|$. For the admissible constant coefficient $\gamma_c\equiv c>0$, write $\tau=1-t>0$ and use the same heat formula: $$ \Phi_c(t,x)=c^{-1}\log\mathbb E e^{c|x+\sqrt\tau Z|}. $$ At $c=0$ its continuous extension is the heat value, whose derivatives are $$ a_0=\sqrt{\frac2{\pi\tau}}e^{-x^2/(2\tau)},\qquad b_0=-\frac{x}{\tau}a_0,\qquad d_0=\left(\frac{x^2}{\tau^2}-\frac1\tau\right)a_0. $$ At $x=\sqrt\tau$, $d_0=0$ and $b_0^2=a_0^2/\tau>0$. For fixed $t,x$, Gaussian convolution may be differentiated in $x$ through its kernel and expanded in $c$ near zero: exponential moments dominate every resulting polynomial factor. The apparent singularity of $c^{-1}\log\mathbb E e^{c|x+\sqrt\tau Z|}$ is removable, and its spatial derivatives through order four are smooth in $c$. Hence $$ d_c^2-12c a_cb_c^2+6c^2a_c^4 =-\frac{12a_0^3}{\tau}c+O(c^2)<0 $$ for all sufficiently small positive $c$, at that fixed point. This is an ordinary consequence of the constant-coefficient formula, not an arbitrary assignment of unrelated derivative values. It neither asserts minimality of $\gamma_c$ nor contradicts the positive expectation proved below; it shows why that expectation cannot be replaced by a pointwise inequality even in the absolute-value-terminal model. ### 4.2 The smooth finite-step problem and its boundary control Take $0=t_0<\cdots ### 4.3 Backward and forward comparisons, including jumps Use backward time $\tau$ on a single step. The equation is $r_\tau=\tfrac12r_{xx}+rr_x$. The logarithmic heat formula preserves strict positivity of $v$: its second spatial derivative is the tilted mean of the old second derivative plus the tilted variance of the old first derivative. Initially $v=cM\operatorname{sech}^2(Mx)>0$, and positive rescaling at a backward jump preserves this property. Consequently $r(x)>0$ for $x>0$. Twice differentiating gives $w_\tau=\tfrac12w_{xx}+rw_x+3vw$. At the terminal endpoint $w=-2cM^2\operatorname{sech}^2(Mx)\tanh(Mx)\le0$ for $x>0$. The boundary value at zero is zero, and the differentiated tails make the far boundary tend uniformly to zero. Comparison applied to $-w$ gives $w\le0$ on the positive half-line. Define $$ H=\frac{r_\tau}{r}=\frac{w}{2r}+v. $$ Oddness and $r_x(0)=v(0)>0$ make $w/r$, hence $H$, smooth and even at zero. Direct differentiation gives $$ H_\tau=\tfrac12H_{xx}+(v/r+r)H_x+vH, $$ $$ (H_x)_\tau=\tfrac12(H_x)_{xx}+(v/r+r)(H_x)_x +((v/r)_x+2v)H_x+wH. $$ The terminal signs are $H=(cM-M^2)\operatorname{sech}^2(Mx)\le0$ and $H_x\ge0$ on $x>0$, using $M\ge c$. For the first comparison write $v/r+r=1/x+\eta(x)$, where $\eta$ is smooth and odd near zero. The radial extension $H(|y|)$ to $\mathbb R^3$ turns $\tfrac12H_{xx}+x^{-1}H_x$ into $\tfrac12\Delta H$. It is smooth at the origin, as is the extra drift, and $H$ tends uniformly to zero at infinity. Comparison on expanding balls proves $H\le0$. For the second comparison, $wH\ge0$ and $(v/r)_x=w/r-v^2/r^2<0$, so the zeroth-order coefficient has upper bound $2\sup v$. On $[\varepsilon,A]$, the two lateral errors are $H_x(\varepsilon)=O(\varepsilon)$ and $H_x(A)=o_A(1)$, uniformly on the closed step. Taking $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ and $A\to\infty$ gives $H_x\ge0$. At a backward jump $r_{\rm new}=\alpha r_{\rm old}$ with $0<\alpha\le1$, $$ H_{\rm new}=H_{\rm old}-(1-\alpha)v_{\rm old},\qquad (H_x)_{\rm new}=(H_x)_{\rm old}-(1-\alpha)w_{\rm old}. $$ Thus both signs survive every jump. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 3.2][fs-signs]. For the forward score use $a_s=s_x$, temporarily distinguishing it from the Hessian $a=\Phi_{xx}$. The forward heat equation gives $$ s_t=\tfrac12s_{xx}-ss_x,\qquad (a_s)_t=\tfrac12(a_s)_{xx}-s(a_s)_x-a_s^2, $$ $$ (s_{xx})_t=\tfrac12(s_{xx})_{xx}-s(s_{xx})_x-3a_s s_{xx}. $$ The first step has $s=x/t$. Thereafter $a_s-1/t$ satisfies the linear equation with drift $-s$ and zeroth-order coefficient $-(a_s+1/t)$. For fixed smooth data this coefficient is bounded above on a closed step, independently of spatial truncation; this uses the tail bound and continuity, before asserting its sign. Comparison gives $a_s\ge1/t$. The last displayed equation then gives $s_{xx}\le0$ on $x>0$. At a forward jump, $$ s_+=s_-+\delta\Phi_x,\quad (a_s)_+=(a_s)_-+\delta\Phi_{xx},\quad (s_{xx})_+=(s_{xx})_-+\delta\Phi_{xxx}. $$ The backward signs and $\delta\ge0$ preserve the forward signs. A further comparison, not concavity alone, is needed. On $x>0$ set $d_s=s_x/s$, $d_r=r_x/r$ and $\rho=d_s-d_r$. The heat equation gives $s_t=\tfrac12s_{xx}-ss_x$, whereas $r_t=-rH$. Taking logarithmic derivatives yields $$ (d_s)_t=\tfrac12(d_s)_{xx}+d_s(d_s)_x-s_{xx},\qquad (d_r)_t=-H_x. $$ Since $\tfrac12(d_r)_{xx}+d_r(d_r)_x=\tfrac12(w/r)_x=H_x-w$, substitution of $d_s=d_r+\rho$ gives its equation $$ \rho_t=\tfrac12\rho_{xx}+d_s\rho_x+(d_r)_x\rho +2H_x-w-s_{xx}. $$ All three terms in the source are nonnegative by the comparisons already proved, and $(d_r)_x<0$. On the first step, concavity gives $r(x)=\int_0^xv(y)\,dy\ge xv(x)$, so $\rho=1/x-v/r\ge0$. Odd Taylor expansions give $d_s=1/x+O(x)$, $d_r=1/x+O(x)$ and $\rho=O(x)$ near zero; the tail estimates give $\rho\to0$ at infinity. Comparison on $[\varepsilon,A]$ therefore proves $\rho\ge0$ on each subsequent step provided its initial sign is preserved. Define $$ j=s\rho=s_x-(s/r)v. $$ At a forward jump, with $\alpha=c_+/c_-$ and $\lambda=(c_+-c_-)/c_-$, $r_+=\alpha r_-$, $v_+=\alpha v_-$, $s_+=s_-+\lambda r_-$ and $(s_x)_+=(s_x)_-+\lambda v_-$. Substitution cancels the added terms and gives $j_+=j_-$. Since $s_+>0$ on $x>0$, the sign of $\rho$ is preserved. The quotient $s/r$ extends smoothly and evenly across zero, with $j(0)=0$; reflection gives $j\ge0$ everywhere. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 3.3][fs-signs]. ### 4.4 How the signs make a correction with zero expectation useful Here the coefficient is a positive constant $c$ on the step containing the chosen time. The variables are the rescaled spatial derivatives $$ r=c\Phi_x,\qquad v=c\Phi_{xx},\qquad w=c\Phi_{xxx},\qquad z=c\Phi_{xxxx}. $$ Write $h=e^{c\Phi}$ and factor the forward diffusion density as $f=hg$; its auxiliary score is $s=-\partial_x\log g$. These are the backward and forward quantities compared in §4.3. On the positive half-line, where $r,s>0$, set $$ H=\frac{w}{2r}+v,\qquad j=s_x-\frac{s}{r}v,\qquad \rho=\frac{s_x}{s}-\frac vr, \qquad j=s\rho. $$ In this certificate only, $b=-w/r$ is a quotient; it is not the derivative $\Phi_{xxx}$ denoted by $b$ in the unscaled curvature formula. At a fixed positive time inside the step define $$ R=r^2,\quad K=rs,\quad b=-w/r,\quad B=b-2v, \quad L=-rs_{xx},\quad S_1=z+bv-2Rb. $$ The subscript on $S_1$ distinguishes it from the support set. The previous comparisons give $$ R,K,v,B,j,L,S_1\ge0,\qquad b=B+2v\ge0,\qquad Rb^2=w^2, $$ because $B=-2H$ and $S_1=2rH_x$. Here $s=-\partial_x\log g$ belongs to the forward heat factor, while $\partial_x\log f=r-s$ is the logarithmic derivative of the diffusion density. The signs have separate sources: $B\ge0$ comes from $H\le0$, $S_1\ge0$ from $H_x\ge0$ on the positive half-line, $j=s\rho\ge0$ from the relative-slope comparison, and $L=-rs_{xx}\ge0$ from forward concavity. Reflection extends these signs. The quotients were defined for $x>0$, where $r>0$ and $v>0$ by the tilted mean-and-variance argument in [§4.3](#shape-comparisons). At zero, $r$ and $w$ are odd, $r_x(0)=v(0)>0$, and division by $r$ is therefore division by a function with a simple zero. This gives the smooth even extension $b(0)=-z(0)/v(0)$; the other comparison identities give $j(0)=0$ and $S_1(0)=0$. Thus zero is not an omitted boundary of the integration. For $\mathcal D=r\partial_x$, direct differentiation gives $$ \mathcal D(R,K,v,b,j) =(2Rv,\ 2vK+Rj,\ -Rb,\ -z-bv,\ -jv+Kb-L). $$ Also $f_x/f=r-s$. Hence $\mathcal W(F)=\mathcal DF+(v+R-K)F$ satisfies $$ f\mathcal W(F)=\partial_x(rfF). $$ This identity does not itself make the integral vanish. The tails give $r=O(1)$; exponential decay of $v,w,z,b$ and their derivatives; $s=x/t+O(1)$; $j=1/t+O((1+x)e^{-\kappa x})$; and $K=O(1+x)$. Every polynomial $F$ in $R,K,v,b,j$ and its differentiated expression therefore has at most polynomial growth. Meanwhile $f(t,x)\le C\exp(-x^2/(2t)+C|x|)$. Thus every term used below is absolutely integrable and $rfF\to0$ at both infinities. Smooth extension across zero prevents an interior boundary term. Integrating on $[-A,A]$ and taking $A\to\infty$ now gives $\mathbb E_f\mathcal W(F)=0$. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 3.4][fs-signs]. The proof has four separate checks: the comparisons supply these signs; the tail estimates make the correction integrate to zero; the rational identity below gives a positive remainder; and [§4.5](#plateau-limit) passes the resulting expectation inequality to the original coefficient. The polynomial check verifies the third step. Set $$ (A,C,k,T_0,g_0,h_0)= \left(\frac1{13},\frac{53}{24},\frac{19}{16},\frac{73}{48}, \frac{2331}{10000},\frac{87}{2500}\right), $$ $$ (x_0,y,m,n_0)= \left(\frac{4663}{5000},\frac{6853}{10000}, -\frac{1051}{400},-\frac{1073}{500}\right). $$ Define $$ Q=Avb+Cv^2+kKv-2kRb+T_0Rv,\qquad T_1=v(g_0R+h_0j), $$ $$ \begin{aligned} F_2={}&(Av-2kR)b^2 +b\bigl(2Cv^2+2kKv+(g_0+2T_0)Rv+h_0jv\bigr)\\ &+x_0v^2j+yv^3+mKv^2+n_0Rv^2. \end{aligned} $$ The choice is motivated by the terms containing $z$. In fact, $$ \begin{aligned} \partial_bF_2 &=2(Av-2kR)b+2Cv^2+2kKv+(g_0+2T_0)Rv+h_0jv\\ &=2Q+T_1,\\ {}[z]\mathcal W(F_2)&=-\partial_bF_2=-(2Q+T_1). \end{aligned} $$ Here $[z]$ means the coefficient of $z$; only $\mathcal Db=-z-bv$ contributes it. The square $(z+Q)^2$ and $S_1T_1$ contribute $2Q+T_1$, so these terms cancel exactly. Therefore subtracting $(z+Q)^2+S_1T_1+\mathcal W(F_2)$ from the curvature expression cancels every term involving $z$. The other favourable derivative is $\partial_jF_2=x_0v^2+h_0bv\ge0$: the $-L$ in $\mathcal Dj$ leaves a nonnegative correction. Put $$ \begin{aligned} P_0&=Rj(b-7v)^2,& P_1&=RB(b-\tfrac73v)^2,\\ P_2&=Kv(b-\tfrac92v)^2,& P_3&=vB(K+\tfrac14R-\tfrac17v)^2,\\ P_4&=(vb-\tfrac{14}{5}v^2-\tfrac{13}{4}Kv+\tfrac43Rv)^2, \end{aligned} $$ $$ (p_0,p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4)= \left(\frac{337}{10000},\frac{183}{2500},\frac{411}{10000}, \frac{11461}{5000},\frac{647}{10000}\right). $$ Exact expansion, with $b=B+2v$, gives $$ z^2-12Rvb^2+6v^4 =(z+Q)^2+S_1T_1+\sum_{i=0}^4p_iP_i +\mathcal W(F_2)+L(x_0v^2+h_0bv)+P_{\rm rem}. $$ For completeness, the entire remainder is specified by this table; every unlisted coefficient is zero. | Monomial | Coefficient | Monomial | Coefficient | | --- | ---: | --- | ---: | | $R^2v^2$ | $223/160000$ | $R^2vB$ | $4007/240000$ | | $R^2B^2$ | $1097/120000$ | $RKv^2$ | $83/80000$ | | $RKvB$ | $3343/24000$ | $Rv^3$ | $16259/23400000$ | | $Rv^2B$ | $30179/5460000$ | $Rv^2j$ | $26/625$ | | $RvB^2$ | $107/15000$ | $RvBj$ | $3/2500$ | | $RB^3$ | $121/32500$ | $RB^2j$ | $11/10000$ | | $K^2v^2$ | $579/20000$ | $K^2vB$ | $207/2500$ | | $Kv^3$ | $911/975000$ | $Kv^2B$ | $349/420000$ | | $Kv^2j$ | $5011/5000$ | $KvB^2$ | $133/130000$ | | $KvBj$ | $87/2500$ | $v^4$ | $1661507/1521000000$ | | $v^3B$ | $633799/621075000$ | $v^2B^2$ | $10657/1690000$ | All square prefactors $Rj,RB,Kv,vB,1$ are nonnegative, as are $S_1T_1$, $L(x_0v^2+h_0bv)$ and every remainder monomial. Integration removes only $\mathcal W(F_2)$, giving $$ \mathbb E_f[z^2-12vw^2+6v^4] \ge\frac{1661507}{1521000000}\mathbb E_fv^4 \ge\frac1{1000}\mathbb E_fv^4. $$ The surplus of the first coefficient over $1/1000$ is exactly $140507/1521000000>0$. The rational identity and positive table can be checked by finite arithmetic. Their application to this diffusion also uses the signs, quotient behaviour, integrability and vanishing flux proved above. Dividing the integrated inequality by $c^2$ returns $$ \mathbb E[\Phi_{xxxx}^2-12c\Phi_{xx}\Phi_{xxx}^2 +6c^2\Phi_{xx}^4] \ge\frac{c^2}{1000}\mathbb E\Phi_{xx}^4. $$ This is the unscaled estimate needed by the gap argument. Section 4.5 passes it to the original coefficient and supplies strictness for the limiting solution. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 4.1 and Proposition 4.2][fs-cert].

rows.text: ### 9.1 Smoothness of the minimizing coefficient Full support does not by itself prove that the Stieltjes measure has a density. In the source manuscript, that conclusion uses the PDE again after the gap contradiction has established $\mathbb E a(t,X_t)^2=1$. We reconstruct the additional argument here because it explains a further conclusion of the original paper. It is not a clause of the selected full-support formal statement. Put $f_k=\partial_x^k\Phi_\gamma$, so $f_1=u$ and $f_2=a$. All formulas in this subsection are on a fixed compact time strip, where every finite collection of spatial derivatives is bounded. Differentiating the PDE and applying Itô's formula along the associated diffusion gives $$ df_k(t,X_t)= -\frac{\gamma(t)}2\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\binom{k}{j} f_{j+1}(t,X_t)f_{k-j+1}(t,X_t)\,dt +f_{k+1}(t,X_t)\,dB_t. $$ The sum is empty when $k=1$. This identity needs no derivative of $\gamma$. For an initially nonsmooth coefficient, apply it to finite-step approximations and pass to the integrated identity: the coefficient converges in $L^1$, the spatial factors converge uniformly, and the stochastic integrals converge by the Itô isometry. [OpenAI full-support manuscript, smooth-density proof, lines 35–50][fs-density]. Set $b=f_3$. The case $k=2$ gives $da=-\gamma a^2dt+b\,dB_t$, and consequently $$ 0=\frac d{dt}\mathbb E a^2 =\mathbb E b^2-2\gamma(t)\mathbb E a^3 \quad\text{for almost every }t<1. $$ Convexity gives $a\geq0$; the already established second moment gives $\mathbb E a^3\geq(\mathbb E a^2)^{3/2}=1$. Thus the quotient $$ \widetilde\gamma(t)=\frac{\mathbb E b(t,X_t)^2} {2\mathbb E a(t,X_t)^3} $$ is well defined and continuous, before any continuity of $\gamma$ is known. It equals $\gamma$ almost everywhere. Approaching an arbitrary $t<1$ from the right through the full-measure equality set, continuity of $\widetilde\gamma$ and right continuity of $\gamma$ give equality at that $t$ as well. This proves continuity of $\gamma$. At zero, $X_0=0$, and evenness of $\Phi(0,\cdot)$ gives $b(0,0)=0$; hence $\gamma(0)=0$. [OpenAI full-support manuscript, lines 52–66][fs-density]; [Chen, Proposition 4.6, pp. 25–26][chen26]. The bootstrap must treat all polynomial moments simultaneously. For a polynomial $P$ in finitely many variables, write $$ M_P(t)=\mathbb E P(f_1(t,X_t),\ldots,f_m(t,X_t)). $$ The preceding stochastic identities and Itô's product rule provide polynomials $Q_P,R_P$, involving only finitely many additional derivatives, such that $$ M_P(t)-M_P(0)=\int_0^t\bigl(M_{Q_P}(s)+\gamma(s)M_{R_P}(s)\bigr)\,ds. $$ Explicitly, if $$ D_k(y)=-\tfrac12\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\binom{k}{j}y_{j+1}y_{k-j+1}, $$ then $$ Q_P=\tfrac12\sum_{k,l}\partial_{kl}P\,y_{k+1}y_{l+1}, \qquad R_P=\sum_k\partial_kP\,D_k. $$ All these moments start continuous. Once $\gamma$ is continuous, the integral formula makes every moment $C^1$, and the quotient formula makes $\gamma$ itself $C^1$. If all moments and $\gamma$ are $C^r$, the same argument makes them $C^{r+1}$. Induction proves $\gamma\in C^\infty([0,1))$, with derivatives at zero taken from the right. Since $\gamma(0)=0$, there is no atom at zero; its Stieltjes measure is $\gamma'(t)\,dt$, and monotonicity gives $\gamma'\geq0$. This is the polynomial-moment method credited by the source to Auffinger–Chen and to Chen's zero-temperature treatment. [OpenAI full-support manuscript, lines 68–101][fs-density]; [Auffinger and Chen, proof of Theorem 2(ii), p. 16][ac-properties]; [Chen, Appendix B.6, p. 38][chen26]. The exact arXiv edition of Auffinger–Chen's polynomial-moment proof has a local display discrepancy: p. 16 of arXiv:1303.3573v1 prints a square in $F_3$ below (40), whereas Proposition 3, p. 9, has the cube. The identity $d(a^2)=(-2\gamma a^3+b^2)dt+2ab\,dB$ requires the cube used above; the moment induction itself is unchanged.

rows.text: ### 9.2 Why the density is strictly positive away from zero This is a further consequence of full support, not an input to it or to §6. A smooth increasing function can have zero derivative at an interior point. For example, $g(t)=(t-\tfrac12)^3+\tfrac18$ on $[0,1)$ is nonnegative and strictly increasing, and $dg$ has full support, although $g'(\tfrac12)=0$. This example is not a minimizing coefficient; it disproves only the inference from strict increase to a positive derivative. The minimizing density needs a further estimate. The coefficient is now smooth, so Proposition 4.1 applies at this time to the same diffusion. Its proof uses nonminimizing local constant replacements, with compact-strip bounds independent of the widths of the inserted plateaus. rows.text: ### 2.1 Structure of the argument The proof begins with regularity on strips bounded away from terminal time. It makes the diffusion $X$ and the gradient moment $q$ available, so a first variation can show where the minimizer is in contact. On a constant interval, the shape inequalities and the rational certificate give the strict curvature needed to contradict that contact. The zero-interval case uses a separate heat argument, and the possible terminal plateau needs its own exclusion. These steps lead to full support and the two moment equalities. In this manuscript route, the value argument then uses bounded-martingale convergence and the attained Parisi formula to express $P_*$ as a terminal Brownian correlation and an integral of expected curvature. Section 6 defines the terminal martingale variable and proves these equalities. The fixed-$T$ Gaussian approximation recovers this integral through Euler coupling, orthogonal normalization and mean-preserving rounding. The QAOA theorem additionally requires rooted energy identification, classical synthesis, removal of temporary seeds and transfer to fixed angles. The main route is §§3–5, then §§6–7, then §§8.1–8.6; §12 compares the two formal interfaces. The original analytic details are in [OpenAI (2026a), §§2–7][fs-main], and the circuit construction is in [OpenAI (2026b), §§2–6][q-intro]. The density theorem in §§9.1–9.2 is a further consequence of support and the PDE, not a premise of the scalar or circuit construction. The positive-temperature route in §11.1 independently supplies the same bounded classical input used for synthesis. The probability consequence in §11.2 requires a separate fixed-word second-moment theorem. These branches explain why the two selected formal statements are not a formal proof of the complete circuit theorem. These destinations separate premises of the support proof from its consequences. They locate the detailed arguments behind the short paper's support and density theorem. **The diffusion and moment identity.** For any admissible $\gamma$, the compact-strip estimates justify defining $X,q$ and computing $q'=\mathbb E a^2$; see [§2.4](#strip-estimates) and [§3.1](#gradient-moment). **Variational contact.** Minimality, admissible mass addition and compact mass removal give $G\ge0$, its vanishing on support and the contact slopes. The steps are in [§3.2](#feasible-variation), [§3.3](#measure-contact) and [§3.4](#contact-slopes). **Strict curvature.** Admissibility and a positive constant $c$ on an interval suffice; minimality is not needed. The shape comparisons, algebra and limiting argument are in [§4.3](#shape-comparisons), [§4.4](#curvature-algebra) and [§4.5](#plateau-limit). **Exclusion of gaps.** Combine contact with the appropriate positive, zero or terminal argument. The cases have separate destinations: [terminal](#terminal-gap), [bounded](#bounded-gaps) and [initial](#initial-gaps) gaps. **Positive density.** Full support comes first. Differentiated moments then give [smoothness in §9.1](#smooth-density-consequence), and a local comparison gives [strict positivity in §9.2](#positive-density). **Value and circuits.** Retain the same minimizer and diffusion through [the value identity in §6](#scalar-value-identities) and [the finite Gaussian construction in §7](#finite-gaussian-approximation). [The circuit argument in §8](#qaoa-construction) requires additional theorems. ### 2.2 The regularity available before the proof starts **Proposition 2.1 (compact-strip regularity).** For $\gamma\in\mathcal U$ and $0\le T<1$, the value has bounded, jointly continuous spatial derivatives of every positive finite order on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R$. If admissible coefficients converge in $L^1$ and their smooth, even, convex, one-Lipschitz terminal values converge uniformly to $|x|$, these spatial derivatives converge uniformly on each such strip. The bounds depend on the derivative order, the fixed strip and a common coefficient mass bound. Time derivatives need only exist almost everywhere across coefficient jumps. On an open constant interval, the heat formula supplies the additional time smoothness used in §4. The terminal estimate is $$ |x|\le\Phi_\gamma(t,x) \le |x|+\sqrt{2(1-t)/\pi}+\frac12\int_t^1\gamma(s)\,ds. $$ It controls approach to $|x|$ without differentiating that cusp. ### 12.1 The support statement and the derivative bridge

The first formal statement assumes a Brownian system and an admissible
minimizer. It supplies a Stieltjes measure, an associated diffusion, full
relative support and strict increase, and the two moment identities for
every associated diffusion. Its proof assembles contact, exclusion of a
terminal plateau, curvature for positive and zero constant intervals,
and uniqueness to transfer the moments between associated diffusions.
This describes the inspected proof's mathematical route; no successful
research-target replay is claimed. Its quantifiers are
$\forall W\,\forall\gamma$, followed by the minimizer hypothesis;
it supplies both witnesses on the given Brownian system. The moment
conclusion is universal over every diffusion satisfying the specified
equation, and covers exactly $0\le t<1$. The diffusion equation itself
holds through time one, simultaneously for all those times outside
one null set. Controls are progressive for the natural filtration of
Brownian increments and bounded by one pointwise. These are not
additional regularity or minimizer-existence assumptions. See the
[exact support statement][support-type] and the companion
[source-interface review](https://github.com/wcook04/lean-exposition/blob/21b1f9e995c4276fdad02377b378f11541a3d5e9/papers/qaoa-sk/source-review/full-support-interface.md).

There is one useful distinction between the manuscript's first variation
and its formal counterpart. The formal result initially gives a derivative
along chord lengths $1/(n+1)$. For this particular control functional,
that sampled limit determines the ordinary feasible right derivative.
With a control fixed, the terminal absolute value is convex in the
coefficient while the penalty is linear. The supremum over the same
control class, and then subtraction of the linear Parisi penalty,
preserve convexity. The secant slopes therefore vary monotonically as
the chord shortens; each intervening chord lies between two successive
sampled chords and has the same limiting slope. If $\eta$ is an
integrable feasible direction, choose $\varepsilon_0>0$ so that
$\gamma+\varepsilon_0\eta$ is admissible and rescale the chord. This
bridge is an ordinary deduction from the definitions and sampled limit,
not an additional formally named theorem.

At the origin, the manuscript smoothly extends auxiliary quotient
variables. The formal coercivity proof for the spatial diffusion density instead works on the positive
half-line, controls the zero flux at the origin and reflects. What must
agree is the resulting integrated inequality; auxiliary values at zero
need not coincide. In particular, the declared generic flux lemma has
a global derivative hypothesis that is not the supplier used here:
the finite-density proof uses the Gaussian half-line coercivity lemma
and reflection. A totalized quotient value at zero cannot silently
satisfy the generic global hypothesis. The precise source spans are in
the correspondence record.
The [fixed-time supplier `actual_coercivity`][support-fixed-time] assumes
positive time and continuity of the coefficient at that time. Its scaled
polynomial inequality is (4.1) multiplied by $c^2$; division requires
$c>0$. This gives a direct source destination for Proposition 4.1 without
adding a minimizing or plateau premise.

rows.text: ### 12.3 Relating the two statements The support and scalar models encode closely related control problems. A direct formal application still needs a specified map of their objects. The following contract identifies the obligations, rather than asserting an equivalence of their complete interfaces. **Coefficients.** Restrict the scalar real-time coefficient to $[0,1)$; conversely, choose an extension compatible with the scalar right-continuity predicate. Prove equality almost everywhere of the coefficients used by each payoff and penalty. The scalar endpoint and exterior values are unconstrained by the shape conditions, so two extensions need not be literally equal. **Brownian space.** Bundle or unbundle the same sample space, sigma algebra, probability law and Brownian process. Identify the natural filtration and every elapsed-increment filtration. Equality in law alone does not identify admissible controls on a chosen space. **Controls and payoffs.** Bundle an admissible scalar control as a support control and conversely. With $s=t+r$, prove equality between the absolute integral over $[t,1]$ using $\alpha(s-t)$ and the elapsed integral over $[0,1-t]$ using $\alpha(r)$. Preserve progressive measurability and the pointwise bound $|\alpha|\le1$. **Value and minimizer.** Equality of the payoff sets gives equality of their suprema for every $x$ and $0\le t<1$. Only then identify the first and second spatial derivatives and the Parisi penalties. Transport minimality against every admissible competitor, including restriction or extension of that competitor. **Diffusion and moments.** Reindex the same process between nonnegative and real time, and stop it at one where required. Transport the integral equation on one full-measure event for all $t\in[0,1]$, path continuity, initial value, gradient and moment integrals. The diffusion comparison has a version issue. The support predicate asks for a globally progressive process; the scalar predicate asks for adaptedness of the stopped process and almost-sure continuity on $[0,1]$. There is a concrete ordinary construction of the needed progressive version. For $t\ge0$ and $k=0,1,\ldots$, put $$ X_t^{(k)}=X_{\min(2^{-k}\lfloor2^k t\rfloor,1)}. $$ Each left-step process is progressive: on every bounded time interval, its value on a step is measurable at that step's left endpoint. Define $\bar X_t$ as the pointwise limit where the sequence converges, and zero elsewhere. The convergence set and this limit are progressively measurable. On the single event where $X$ is continuous on $[0,1]$, the equality $\bar X_t=X_{\min(t,1)}$ holds for every $t\ge0$. Thus stopping and reindexing preserve paths, time integrals and moments on that event; no completion of the natural filtration is needed merely to construct this version. The initial value follows from the scalar equation at zero and $B_0=0$ on their common full-measure event. This settles the version construction at the ordinary mathematical level. Its implementation in the two formal predicates, and the coefficient, filtration and value identifications listed above, remain separate obligations. In particular, equality of values for every $x$ is needed before transporting their derivatives; agreement at $(0,0)$ is insufficient. Once those obligations are proved, an application must use the same transported minimizer and associated diffusion in all premises. No such cross-model transport theorem is supplied here. The manuscript proof in §§3–7 and the scalar implementation's independent argument remain available without it. These distinctions come from the defining [support model][support-model] and [scalar model][value-model], rather than from their endpoint names.

Also $\mathbb E[M_Ng_j]=\sqrt\Delta/c_j$ by orthonormality. Bessel's inequality applied separately to the orthonormal family $(g_j)$ and to the family $(Z_i)$ gives the vector estimates. Their union need not be orthogonal: $$ (A_j)_{j=1}^N=(\sqrt\Delta/c_j)_{j=1}^N+o_{\ell^2}(1), $$ $$ (B_i)_{i=1}^N= (\sqrt\Delta\,\mathbb E a(t_{i-1},Y_{i-1}))_{i=1}^N+o_{\ell^2}(1). $$ Coordinatewise errors would not control a sum of growing length. Put $$ e_N=\|u(T,Y_N)-M_N\|_2,\quad \alpha_j=\sqrt\Delta/c_j,\quad \beta_j=\sqrt\Delta\,\mathbb E a(t_{j-1},Y_{j-1}) \quad(1\le j\le N). $$ The fixed-$T$ Euler argument gives $e_N\to0$. Bessel's inequality gives $\|A_{1:N}-\alpha\|_2,\|B_{1:N}-\beta\|_2\le e_N$. Also $\|B_{1:N}\|_2\le1$ and $\|\alpha\|_2\le C_T$ for sufficiently large $N$, with $C_T$ independent of the mesh. Cauchy–Schwarz gives $$ \begin{aligned} \left|\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}(A_jB_{j+1}-\alpha_j\beta_{j+1})\right| &\le\|A-\alpha\|_2\|B_{2:N}\|_2 +\|\alpha_{1:N-1}\|_2\|B-\beta\|_2\\ &\le(1+C_T)e_N. \end{aligned} $$ The unindexed differences in this inequality use coordinates $1,\ldots,N$; restricting to the indicated subvector only decreases their norms. The rounding coordinate contributes at most $|A_NB_{N+1}|\le e_N+\sqrt\Delta/c_N$. Thus the dimension-free estimate is $$ \left|\sum_{j=0}^NA_jB_{j+1} -\Delta\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\frac{\mathbb E a(t_j,Y_j)}{c_j}\right| \le(2+C_T)e_N+\frac{\sqrt\Delta}{c_N}\longrightarrow0. $$ The index shift selects the Hessian at $t_j$; $Z_{N+1}$ serves rounding rather than another Euler increment. This estimate is a fixed-strip scalar correspondence, not a circuit energy identity. Hence $$ \sum_{j=0}^NA_jB_{j+1} =\Delta\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\frac{\mathbb E a(t_j,Y_j)}{c_j}+o(1) \longrightarrow\int_0^T\mathbb E a(t,X_t)\,dt. $$ The same vector estimates also give an unshifted sum with this limit: $$ \left|\sum_{j=1}^N A_jB_j-\sum_{j=1}^N\alpha_j\beta_j\right| \le(1+C_T)e_N\longrightarrow0, $$ $$ \sum_{j=1}^N A_jB_j =\Delta\sum_{j=1}^N \frac{\mathbb E a(t_{j-1},Y_{j-1})}{c_j}+o(1) \longrightarrow\int_0^T\mathbb E a(t,X_t)\,dt. $$ The latter is a left Riemann sum: $c_j\to1$ uniformly and the Euler coupling replaces $Y_{j-1}$ by $X_{t_{j-1}}$. Equal continuum limits therefore do not identify the finite expression needed by the circuit. The mesh count $N$ is unrelated to the spin-system size $n$. rows.text: #### 10.2.2 Adaptive directions and a finite-spin inequality Choose each zero-or-unit direction measurably from columns already revealed. Conditional on that history, the current residual candidate vectors and offsets are fixed, so the preceding recursion applies. More precisely, conditional on the revealed history, the expected next continuation value, including its accumulated offsets, equals the current one. Iteration therefore preserves the initial expected maximum. For any measurable choice of a candidate from the final history, its accumulated offset is bounded by the remaining conditional expected maximum. Hence $$ \mathbb E\,d_{s(\mathrm{history})}^{\rm final} \le\mathcal V(w,0). $$ Contraction of each residual, the finite candidate set and Gaussian column moments justify the expectations. Adaptivity does not turn a future column into part of the conditioning history. [Scalar implementation, adaptive recursion][scalar-adaptive]. Take all spins $w_s\in\{-1,1\}^n$ as candidates. The full quadratic matrix has off-diagonal coefficients $(G_{ij}+G_{ji})/\sqrt2$, which are independent standard normals, and a centered diagonal contribution common to every spin. Thus $$ \mathcal V(\mathrm{spins},0)=\sqrt n\,\mathbb E\max_\sigma H_n(\sigma). $$ Dividing the offset inequality by $n\sqrt n$ gives a bound by $e_n$. The implementation proves this normalization through equality of Gaussian increment distances in [the finite adaptive SK comparison][scalar-finite-adaptive]. rows.text: #### 10.4.1 The same test at every mesh size For the nonminimizing coefficient $\gamma=0$, Euler sampling is exact: $Y_j=B_{t_j}$. The curvature moment in §10.3 gives $$ c_j=\sqrt{\pi/2}(1-t_{j-1}^2)^{1/4}. $$ Monotonicity and symmetry of the Gaussian CDF turn the rounded spin into $$ F_N=\operatorname{sgn}(B_T+\sqrt{1-T}\,Z_{N+1}) \quad\hbox{almost surely}. $$ The argument of this sign is standard normal. Gaussian regression gives $B_i=\sqrt{2/\pi}\sqrt\Delta$ for $1\le i\le N$ and $B_{N+1}=\sqrt{2/\pi}\sqrt{1-T}$. To calculate $A_j$, condition on Brownian motion through $t_j$ and use the heat martingale. Gaussian integration by parts then gives $$ \mathbb E[Z_j u_0(t_j,x+\sqrt\Delta Z_j)] =\sqrt\Delta\,a_0(t_{j-1},x). $$ Multiplication by $c_ja_0(t_{j-1},B_{t_{j-1}})$ and expectation yield $A_j=c_j\sqrt\Delta\,\mathbb E a_0(t_{j-1},B_{t_{j-1}})^2 =\sqrt\Delta/c_j$. Consequently, for every $N\ge1$, $$ S_{T,N}=\sqrt{\frac2\pi} \left(\Delta\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\frac1{c_j} +\frac{\sqrt{\Delta(1-T)}}{c_N}\right). $$ The one-step value above is its $N=1$ case. At fixed $T<1$, its limit is $$ \frac2\pi\int_0^T(1-t^2)^{-1/4}\,dt, $$ whereas the unnormalized candidate covariance is $I_0(T)=T\sqrt{2/\pi}$. The subsequent $T\uparrow1$ limit is $4\Gamma(3/4)/(\sqrt\pi\,\Gamma(1/4))\approx0.76275976$, distinct from $\mathcal P(0)=\sqrt{2/\pi}\approx0.79788456$. The general predictable comparison of [§10.2](#independent-scalar-lower-bound) turns this limit into a lower bound for $P_*$, as shown next. It is not a numerical determination of $P_*$ or the value of the zero coefficient. Exact Euler simulation, orthonormal predictable increments and correct rounding all hold here. The missing identity is $\mathbb E a_0(t,B_t)^2=1$; consequently the normalizers do not approach one. This calculation extends the heat and rounding derivations of §§10.3–10.4 and isolates the role of minimality in the convergence theorem.

rows.text: #### 10.2.1 Revealing one Gaussian column For $w\in\mathbb R^n$, put $Q(w)=w\otimes w/\sqrt2$. An independent standard Gaussian matrix $G$ gives a centered field $\langle Q(w),G\rangle$ with covariance $\langle w,w'\rangle^2/2$. Given a unit vector $v$, define $$ R_vw=w-\langle v,w\rangle v,\qquad C_v(w)=\langle v,w\rangle R_vw+ \frac{\langle v,w\rangle^2}{\sqrt2}v. $$ Write $\alpha=\langle v,w\rangle$, $\beta=\langle v,w'\rangle$ and $r=\langle R_vw,R_vw'\rangle$. For an independent standard Gaussian column $Z$ and matrix $G'$, the covariance of $\langle C_v(w),Z\rangle+\langle Q(R_vw),G'\rangle$ is $$ \alpha\beta r+\frac12\alpha^2\beta^2+\frac12r^2 =\frac12(r+\alpha\beta)^2 =\frac12\langle w,w'\rangle^2. $$ Thus the new field has the old joint Gaussian law. The same statement holds for $v=0$: then $R_v$ is the identity and $C_v=0$. Allowing that case will avoid assuming empirical linear independence. For a finite nonempty family of candidates $w_s$ and offsets $d_s$, define $$ \mathcal V(w,d)=\mathbb E_G\max_s \{\langle Q(w_s),G\rangle+d_s\}. $$ The covariance identity and Fubini give the exact recursion $$ \mathcal V(w,d)=\mathbb E_Z\mathcal V \bigl((R_vw_s)_s,(d_s+\langle C_v(w_s),Z\rangle)_s\bigr). $$ Also $d_s\le\mathcal V(w,d)$ for each $s$, since the residual Gaussian term has mean zero. These are the two facts needed for adaptive choices. The source derives the equality by Gaussian comparison in both directions and proves the required integrability in [the one-column decomposition][scalar-column].

rows.text: ### 7.1 Error estimates at a fixed cutoff Fix the minimizer first and then $T<1$. The bounds below have constants depending on that minimizer and strip; they give an $N^{-1/2}$ rate there, not a rate uniform as $T\uparrow1$. Those derivative bounds are finite but have not been supplied as numerical inputs to an algorithm for choosing a mesh. The calculation is an ordinary deduction from the source's strip estimates, beyond the qualitative selected formal statement. Write $S_{T,N}=\sum_{j=0}^N A_jB_{j+1}$ and $f(t)=\mathbb E a(t,X_t)$, so $0\le f(t)\le1$. On the fixed strip let $K_T=\sup_{t\le T,x}|a(t,x)|$ and choose a spatial Lipschitz constant $L_T$ for $a$. Define $$ \delta_N=\max_{0\le j\le N}\|Y_j-X_{t_j}\|_2,\qquad d_N=\max_{1\le j\le N} \left|\mathbb E a(t_{j-1},Y_{j-1})^2-1\right|. $$ These errors have a rate at each fixed strip, even if $\gamma$ has jumps. Put $\Gamma=\gamma(T)$ and $V=\gamma(T)-\gamma(0)$. Bounded spatial derivatives and the PDE give temporal Lipschitz constants $$ J=\tfrac12\|u_{xx}\|_\infty+\Gamma K_T,\qquad H=\tfrac12\|a_{xx}\|_\infty+\Gamma(K_T^2+L_T) $$ for $u$ and $a$, respectively, on this strip. No derivative of $\gamma$ is used. Brownian coupling gives $\|X_s-X_{\pi_N(s)}\|_2\le\sqrt\Delta+\Gamma\Delta$. Subtract the Euler and diffusion equations and split the drift difference on $[t_j,t_{j+1}]$ as $$ \gamma(s)\bigl(u(s,X_s)-u(t_j,Y_j)\bigr) +\bigl(\gamma(s)-\gamma(t_j)\bigr)u(t_j,Y_j). $$ Put $A_T=\int_0^T\gamma(s)\,ds\le1$ and $w_j=\int_{t_j}^{t_{j+1}}\gamma(s)\,ds$. Taking a pathwise maximum over grid times, Minkowski and discrete Gronwall give, with $$ R_N=A_TK_T\sqrt\Delta+ [A_T(J+\Gamma K_T)+V]\Delta, $$ the bound $$ \delta_N\le\left\|\max_{j\le N}|Y_j-X_{t_j}|\right\|_2 \le e^{K_TA_T}R_N\le e^{K_T}R_N. $$ The recurrence weights the preceding maximal norm on interval $j$ by $K_Tw_j$; their sum is $K_TA_T$. The term $V\Delta$ is the monotone quadrature bound for the coefficient. For the martingale residual, Itô isometry and the same increment estimate give $$ e_N\le K_T\delta_N+ \sqrt T\{L_T\delta_N+L_T\sqrt\Delta+(H+\Gamma L_T)\Delta\}. $$ Thus $\delta_N,e_N=O_{\gamma,T}(\sqrt\Delta)$. These are deductions from the compact-strip bounds and stochastic identities, not quantitative clauses of the selected Lean statement. Since $a$ is bounded and Lipschitz, $d_N\le2K_TL_T\delta_N\to0$. Whenever $d_N\le1/2$, $$ \sqrt{2/3}\le c_j\le\sqrt2,\qquad |1/c_j-1|\le d_N,\qquad \|\alpha\|_2\le\sqrt{T(1+d_N)}. $$ These estimates give an explicit sufficient condition for all the required normalisers to be positive. They do not assume positivity for every coarse mesh. The first-moment identity in §6 makes $f=m$ nonincreasing, with $f(0)=1$. Its right Riemann sum therefore satisfies $$ 0\le I(T)-\Delta\sum_{j=1}^N f(t_j) \le\Delta\bigl(f(0)-f(T)\bigr). $$ Removing the last term adds $\Delta f(T)$, so $0\le I(T)-\Delta\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}f(t_j)\le\Delta$. The difference between the shifted interior sum and the integral is bounded by $$ \left|\Delta\sum_{j=1}^{N-1} \frac{\mathbb E a(t_j,Y_j)}{c_j}-\int_0^T f(t)\,dt\right| \le TK_Td_N+TL_T\delta_N+\Delta. $$ The first two terms replace the normalisers and Euler positions; the last is the preceding monotone quadrature estimate. Combining this with the vector and rounding-endpoint estimate gives $$ \begin{aligned} |S_{T,N}-P_*| \le{}&(1-T)m(T) +\bigl(2+\sqrt{T(1+d_N)}\bigr)e_N +\sqrt{\Delta(1+d_N)}\\ &+TK_Td_N+TL_T\delta_N+\Delta . \end{aligned} $$ In particular, for each fixed minimizer and $T<1$ there are finite $C_{\gamma,T}$ and $N_0(\gamma,T)$ such that $$ |S_{T,N}-P_*|\le(1-T)m(T)+C_{\gamma,T}\sqrt{T/N} \qquad(N\ge N_0(\gamma,T)). $$ The constants are not uniform as $T\uparrow1$. The [coefficient budget](#coefficient-budget) bounds $\int\gamma$ and $\gamma$ on each fixed strip, but numerical bounds for all strip derivative constants and an effective mesh threshold are not supplied. The scalar tail bound $(1-T)m(T)\le1-T$ uses only monotonicity of the first moment; Proposition 6.2 further makes it $o(1-T)$. All terms after this scalar tail tend to zero at each fixed $T<1$. Given a scalar tolerance $\zeta>0$, first choose $T$ with $1-T<\zeta/2$, then choose $N_0(\gamma,T,\zeta)$ so that their sum is below $\zeta/2$ for every $N\ge N_0$. This is the required finite choice of a Gaussian spin. The formula exposes the errors; it does not supply numerical values of $K_T,L_T,\delta_N,e_N$ or an effective mesh threshold. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 2.1][fs-reg]; [OpenAI (2026a), Proposition 7.2][fs-cons]. A diagonal can be chosen using these thresholds. For prescribed $T_m\uparrow1$, choose increasing $N_m$ large enough to make the mesh-dependent part of the fixed-$T_m$ bound less than $1/m$. An arbitrary increasing mesh schedule does not follow from the iterated limit alone. For example, the scalar array $$ h(T,N)=\min\{1,[N(1-T)]^{-1}\} $$ tends to zero in $N$ at every fixed $T<1$, but $h(1-1/N,N)=1$ for every $N\ge2$. This is an illustration of the quantifier issue, not an asserted error law for the SK construction.

The column formula gives $|E_{n,j}|\le1+\|\widehat z_{j+1,n}\|^2$. Define $$ c_n=\sum_{j0$ and positive active second moments, but no minimizer or diffusion. [Literal scalar specialization][scalar-literal-lower]. At a minimizer, the separate contact and diffusion arguments establish the fixed-strip inputs and eventual positivity. First take the mesh limit to obtain $I(T)\le P_*$, then let $T\uparrow1$. The scalar terminal assembly identifies that last limit with $\mathcal P(\gamma)$; together with $P_*\le\mathcal P(\gamma)$ this proves equality.
