rows.text: ### 10.4 An exact one-step calculation For a finite check of the definitions, use the admissible heat coefficient $\gamma_0\equiv0$, whose solution has $$ u_0(t,x)=2F_{\rm G}\bigl(x/\sqrt{1-t}\bigr)-1,\qquad a_0(0,0)=\sqrt{2/\pi}. $$ This coefficient is not a minimiser; the calculation tests the construction and its indices, not the minimiser-dependent convergence theorem. Take $T=4/5$ and $N=1$. Then $$ Y_1=\frac2{\sqrt5}Z_1,\qquad c_1=\sqrt{\pi/2},\qquad g_1=Z_1,\qquad m_1=u_0(T,Y_1)=2F_{\rm G}(2Z_1)-1. $$ Strict monotonicity and symmetry of the Gaussian distribution function give $$ F_1=\operatorname{sgn}\bigl(F_{\rm G}(2Z_1)+F_{\rm G}(Z_2)-1\bigr) =\operatorname{sgn}(2Z_1+Z_2) $$ almost surely. Thus the additional Gaussian is visibly the rounding coordinate. Set $V=(2Z_1+Z_2)/\sqrt5$, a standard normal. Gaussian regression gives $\mathbb E[Z_1\mid V]=2V/\sqrt5$ and $\mathbb E[Z_2\mid V]=V/\sqrt5$. Since $\mathbb E|V|=\sqrt{2/\pi}$, $$ A_0=0,\qquad A_1=B_1=2\sqrt{\frac{2}{5\pi}},\qquad B_2=\sqrt{\frac{2}{5\pi}}. $$ Consequently $$ \sum_{j=0}^1A_jB_{j+1}=\frac4{5\pi} \quad\hbox{whereas}\quad A_1B_1=\frac8{5\pi}. $$ Dropping the index shift changes the answer by a factor of two. At $N=1$ the interior Riemann sum is empty and the entire product comes from the rounding endpoint. Its later disappearance is an asymptotic statement, not an exact finite-mesh identity. The displayed coefficients follow from exact Gaussian regression; no numerical quadrature or finite computation is needed for this example.

rows.label: gaussian-sanity-check
rows.text: ### 10.3 The zero coefficient The admissible coefficient $\gamma_0=0$ makes the use of minimality in the normalization step explicit. Its diffusion is $X_t=B_t$, and the [zero-coefficient heat formula][fs-reg] gives $$ u_0(t,x)=2F_{\mathrm G}\!\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-t}}\right)-1, \qquad a_0(t,x)=\sqrt{\frac2\pi}\frac{e^{-x^2/(2(1-t))}}{\sqrt{1-t}}. $$ Since $\mathbb E e^{-\lambda B_t^2}=(1+2\lambda t)^{-1/2}$, $$ \mathbb E a_0(t,B_t)=\sqrt{\frac2\pi},\qquad \mathbb E a_0(t,B_t)^2=\frac2{\pi\sqrt{1-t^2}},\qquad q_0(t)=\frac2\pi\arcsin t. $$ The last identity follows by integrating $q_0'=\mathbb E a_0^2$ from $q_0(0)=0$. This heat and late-step variation argument is the zero-field specialization of [Chen, Handschy and Lerman, Theorem 6 and its proof, arXiv:1609.04368v4, pp. 13–16](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.04368v4). Strict convexity of $\arcsin$ gives $q_0(t)

rows.label: gibbs-comparison
rows.text:
### 11.1.2 Finite-temperature values and exact Gibbs samples

This comparison samples the exact Gibbs distribution. The QAOA Born law
in §11.2 is a separate distribution; none of the following bounds identifies
the two. For one fixed instance, let $L_n=\max_\sigma H_{n,J}(\sigma)/n$,
$\mathcal F_{n,\beta}=(n\beta)^{-1}\log\sum_\sigma e^{\beta H_{n,J}(\sigma)}$,
and let $\mathcal U_{n,\beta}$ be the mean energy per spin under the
Gibbs law proportional to $e^{\beta H_{n,J}(\sigma)}$. Then
$$
0\le\mathcal F_{n,\beta}-L_n\le\frac{\log2}{\beta},\qquad
0\le L_n-\mathcal U_{n,\beta}\le\frac{\log2}{\beta}.
$$
The first is the log-sum bound. The second uses
$\mathcal F=\mathcal U+S/(n\beta)$, where the Gibbs entropy satisfies
$0\le S\le n\log2$, together with $\mathcal U\le L_n\le\mathcal F$.
Thus both disorder averages approach $P_*$ along every joint
$n\to\infty$, $\beta\to\infty$, by the already established
convergence of $\mathbb E L_n$.

There is also a finite probability estimate. Every configuration has
Gaussian coefficient-vector norm $\sqrt{(n-1)/(2n^2)}$ after division
by $n$, and their maximum has the same Lipschitz bound. Gaussian
concentration gives, for $n\ge2$,
$$
\Pr_J(|L_n-\mathbb E L_n|>s)
\le2\exp\{-n^2s^2/(n-1)\}.
$$
For an exact Gibbs draw $\Sigma^{\rm G}$, count the at most $2^n$
configurations with deficit at least $s$ and bound the partition sum
below by its maximal term. This gives, for every instance,
$$
\Pr\{H_{n,J}(\Sigma^{\rm G})/n\le L_n-s\mid J\}
\le\min\{1,e^{n(\log2-\beta s)}\}.
$$
The lower tail below $P_*-s$ is bounded by
$\Pr_J(L_n<P_*-s/2)+\min\{1,e^{n(\log2-\beta s/2)}\}$;
the upper tail is at most the upper tail of $L_n$. Hence an exact
Gibbs sample also approaches $P_*$ in joint probability. These are
elementary scalar consequences of the Gibbs law, entropy and Gaussian
concentration. They supply neither an efficient sampler nor QAOA angles.

rows.label: heat-lower-bound
rows.text: **Corollary 10.2 (the heat test).** In this normalization, $$ P_*\ge\frac{4\Gamma(3/4)}{\sqrt\pi\,\Gamma(1/4)} \approx0.7627597635. \tag{10.2} $$ For each fixed $T<1$ and $N\ge1$, the heat normalizers $c_j$ are positive. The increments $g_j$ have unit second moments and are orthogonal, since their multipliers depend only on preceding Gaussians. The rounded $F_N$ is a measurable spin after an arbitrary choice on its null tie event. Thus Proposition 10.1 applies with $K=N$, $z_j=Z_{j+1}$ and $f_j=g_{j+1}$, giving $S_{T,N}\le P_*$. First let $N\to\infty$ at fixed $T$, using the displayed exact sum, and then let $T\uparrow1$. The integrand is nonnegative and its endpoint singularity has exponent $1/4<1$. Substitution $s=t^2$ yields $$ P_*\ge\frac2\pi\int_0^1(1-t^2)^{-1/4}\,dt =\frac1\pi B\!\left(\frac12,\frac34\right) =\frac{4\Gamma(3/4)}{\sqrt\pi\,\Gamma(1/4)}. $$ This is a consequence of the heat calculation and the general Gaussian comparison. Minimality is unnecessary for the inequality; it is what made the different, optimizing construction converge to $P_*$ itself.

rows.label: model
rows.text:
For independent standard Gaussian couplings $J_{ij}$, put

$$
H_n(\sigma)=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}\sigma_i\sigma_j,\qquad
\sigma\in\{-1,1\}^n,\qquad
P_*=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\mathbb E\max_\sigma H_n(\sigma).
$$

For overlap $R_{12}=n^{-1}\sum_i\sigma_i^1\sigma_i^2$, the covariance is
$nR_{12}^2/2-1/2$. Thus the convention is $\xi(t)=t^2/2$, with
$\xi''=1$. A centered Gaussian of variance $1/2$, common to all
configurations, removes the final constant without changing the expected
maximum. Every normalization below uses this convention.

Let $\mathcal U$ consist of nonnegative, nondecreasing, right-continuous
functions $\gamma:[0,1)\to[0,\infty)$ with
$\int_0^1\gamma(t)\,dt<\infty$. Their Stieltjes measures satisfy
$\mu_\gamma([0,t])=\gamma(t)$, including
$\mu_\gamma(\{0\})=\gamma(0)$. They are locally finite, but need not be
probability measures or have finite total mass. Support is relative to [0,1).

Let $B$ be standard Brownian motion. The control value and Parisi
functional are

$$
\Phi_\gamma(t,x)=\sup_{|\alpha|\le1}\mathbb E\left[
 \left|x+B_1-B_t+\int_t^1\gamma(s)\alpha_s\,ds\right|
 -\frac12\int_t^1\gamma(s)\alpha_s^2\,ds\right],
$$
$$
\mathcal P(\gamma)=\Phi_\gamma(0,0)-\frac12\int_0^1t\gamma(t)\,dt.
$$

Controls are progressively measurable for Brownian increments after $t$.
For a general admissible coefficient, the solution and its spatial derivatives
are locally absolutely continuous in time on compact strips; the time equation
holds almost everywhere. The control formula fixes the solution. The PDE is
$\Phi_t=-\tfrac12(\Phi_{xx}+\gamma\Phi_x^2)$, with
$\Phi(1,x)=|x|$. Auffinger and Chen's zero-temperature Parisi formula and
attainment identify $P_*$ with $\min_{\gamma\in\mathcal U}\mathcal P(\gamma)$.
The support theorem itself assumes a minimizer and proves a property of it;
it does not separately supply one. See [OpenAI (2026a), §§1–2][fs-main]
and [Auffinger and Chen (2017), Theorem 1 and proof of Lemma 3][ac2017].

rows.label: obligations
rows.text:
The full-support theorem and scalar-value theorem use related but
different formal representations. Their mathematical conclusions can be
discussed together, but a direct formal implication would require the
coefficient, Brownian law, control value and diffusion translations
described in §12, with common witnesses. The finite Gaussian result
also needs its rooted energy identification before it says anything
about a QAOA circuit. The boundedness, regularization, synthesis and
transfer estimates in §8 are additional steps, with temperature-specific
hypotheses where the positive-temperature route is used.

Infinite support allows gaps. An indefinite curvature identity does not imply
strict convexity before expectation is controlled. An algebraic certificate
does not establish its analytic hypotheses. Coordinatewise convergence does
not control a growing coefficient sum. A finite-dimensional Gaussian law
does not identify an energy observable without its operator argument.
Separate witnesses cannot be merged silently. The order
$\forall\varepsilon\ \exists\text{finite word}\ \lim_{n\to\infty}$
cannot be replaced by a fixed-instance depth limit.

The local comparison in §11.1 concerns two printed finite-step displays;
it neither replaces the cited theorem's hypotheses nor supplies the
remaining circuit estimates.

rows.label: overlap-pairs
rows.text: Choose one minimizer supplied by the attained Parisi formula, and apply the full-support theorem to that same coefficient. The external landscape theorem below then applies at every point of its Stieltjes support. For every fixed $r\in[0,1)$ and $\varepsilon,\eta>0$, there is a constant $K=K(r,\varepsilon,\eta)>0$, independent of $n$, such that $$ \mathbb P\left(\exists\sigma,\tau\in\{-1,1\}^n: \left|\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_i\tau_i-r\right|<\varepsilon, \quad \frac{H_n(\sigma)}n,\frac{H_n(\tau)}n\ge P_*-\eta\right) \ge1-Ke^{-n/K},\qquad n\ge1. $$ The probability is over the SK couplings; the configurations may depend on them. This is the specialization of [Auffinger–Chen–Zeng, Proposition 1, equation (5), p. 5][acz] to the full-support minimizer above. Their theorem applies to each point of its Stieltjes support. Its proof, on pp. 15–16, uses the coupled free energy constrained to a neighbourhood of that overlap, passes to the coupled maximum and applies Gaussian concentration. The coupled maximum approaches $2P_*$, while the unrestricted maximum approaches $P_*$; these two facts force both members of a maximizing pair to be near ground energy. The covariance normalization needs one small adjustment. Writing $R=n^{-1}\sum_i\sigma_i\tau_i$, our Hamiltonian has covariance $nR^2/2-1/2$. Adjoin a common independent Gaussian $C$ of variance $1/2$. Then $\widetilde H_n(\sigma)=H_n(\sigma)+C$ has covariance $n\xi(R)$ with $\xi(t)=t^2/2$, as in the cited mixed-spin theorem. Its expected maximum equals that of $H_n$, so its ground-state limit is the same $P_*$. Apply the theorem with energy tolerance $\eta/2$. On $|C|\le\eta n/2$, the resulting pair also satisfies the displayed energy inequalities for $H_n$. The omitted event has probability at most $2e^{-\eta^2n^2/4}$, which can be absorbed into $Ke^{-n/K}$ by enlarging $K$. Since the conclusion for $H_n$ depends only on its couplings, this also removes the auxiliary Gaussian from the probability statement. The pointwise result also gives a simultaneous statement at any fixed positive resolution. Given $\varepsilon,\eta>0$, choose finitely many centres $r_j\in[0,1)$ whose open $\varepsilon/2$-neighbourhoods cover $[0,1]$. Apply the preceding result at each centre with overlap tolerance $\varepsilon/2$ and energy tolerance $\eta$. A finite union bound gives constants $C,c>0$, depending only on these tolerances, such that $$ \mathbb P\!\left(\forall r\in[-1,1]\ \exists\sigma,\tau\in\{-1,1\}^n: |R(\sigma,\tau)-r|<\varepsilon,\quad H_n(\sigma)/n,H_n(\tau)/n\ge P_*-\eta\right) \ge1-Ce^{-cn}. \tag{9.1} $$ Indeed, on the event where every centre has a suitable pair, choose a nearest centre and use the triangle inequality. For negative targets, reverse one spin configuration: the pure two-spin Hamiltonian preserves its energy and changes the overlap's sign. The finite net covers the endpoints as well, with centres strictly below one. There is a useful contrast at a fixed finite size. If $\sigma,\tau$ differ at $k$ sites, precisely the $k(n-k)$ edges crossing that set change their spin product. Their independent Gaussian contributions give $$ \operatorname{Var}(H_n(\sigma)-H_n(\tau))=\frac{4k(n-k)}n. $$ For $0

rows.label: overview
rows.text:
The full-support manuscript proves that an admissible integrable minimizer
of the zero-temperature Parisi functional for the pure zero-field
Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model has Stieltjes support equal to every overlap
scale in [0,1). The proof turns a hypothetical support gap into a constant
interval for the order parameter. Variational contact at the ends of that
interval conflicts with a strict curvature inequality inside it. Along the
auxiliary diffusion, the spatial gradient of the value function is a bounded
martingale. Full support makes this martingale's second moment equal to time;
its terminal correlation with Brownian motion gives the ground-state value.
The manuscript's further argument gives a smooth Stieltjes density, strictly
positive on $(0,1)$, and no atom at zero. Sections 9.1–9.2 derive this stronger
ordinary conclusion separately from the selected formal support statement.

This record reconstructs those arguments and follows the finite Gaussian
approximation into the separate QAOA manuscript. The latter claims that
finite deterministic circuits approach the SK optimum when system size tends
to infinity before circuit depth increases. Its circuit construction needs
additional approximation, synthesis, seed-removal and transfer arguments.
The two formal statements concern full support and scalar value
consequences; neither states QAOA circuit convergence. Their verification
scope is described at the end. See [OpenAI (2026a), §§1–2][fs-main] and
[OpenAI (2026b), Theorem 1.1][q-intro].

rows.label: qaoa
rows.text:
On a single spin, let $Z=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$ and
$X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$; $Z_i$ and $X_i$ act on spin $i$
and as the identity on the other spins. Also set
$Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$ and
$|\pm\rangle=(|0\rangle\pm|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$.
Then $X|\pm\rangle=\pm|\pm\rangle$ and $Z|+\rangle=|-\rangle$. The cost and mixer are
$$
C_{n,J}=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}Z_iZ_j,\qquad B_n=\sum_iX_i.
$$
The two evolutions act differently:
$$
e^{-i\theta C_{n,J}}|\sigma\rangle
 =e^{-i\theta H_n(\sigma)}|\sigma\rangle,
\qquad
e^{-i\beta B_n}=\prod_{i=1}^n(\cos\beta\,I-i\sin\beta\,X_i).
$$
The cost evolution changes phases while preserving spin-basis probabilities;
the mixer combines amplitudes of different spin configurations. Cost evolution
alone leaves the initial uniform probabilities unchanged, and a mixer applied
first only multiplies $|+\rangle^{\otimes n}$ by $e^{-in\beta}$.
Alternating them lets the cost-dependent phases change subsequent measurement
probabilities. [Farhi, Goldstone, Gutmann and Zhou (2022), §2,
equations (1)–(6)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.08187v4).

A depth-$p$ state, with $p$ counting cost–mixer pairs, is
$$
|\psi_{n,p,J}(\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta)\rangle
=e^{-i\beta_pB_n}e^{-i\gamma_pC_{n,J}}\cdots
 e^{-i\beta_1B_n}e^{-i\gamma_1C_{n,J}}|+\rangle^{\otimes n}.
$$
Here the real angle vectors $\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta$ are
deterministic; $\boldsymbol\gamma$ is separate from the Parisi coefficient
$\gamma(t)$. A *word* means a finite ordered product of cost and mixer
exponentials. Its pattern and angles are fixed independently of $n,J$;
its cost operator depends on $n,J$. Define
$$
v_p(\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta)
=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\mathbb E_J
 \langle\psi_{n,p,J}|C_{n,J}|\psi_{n,p,J}\rangle,
\qquad Q_p=\sup_{\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^p}v_p.
$$
The fixed-depth, fixed-angle infinite-size limit is the input from
Farhi, Goldstone, Gutmann and Zhou; it does not contain the later depth
conclusion; see [Farhi, Goldstone, Gutmann and Zhou (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.08187v4).
The source target is $\lim_{p\to\infty}Q_p=P_*$. Its needed lower
bound has the literal quantifiers
$$
\forall\varepsilon>0\quad\exists p\in\mathbb N,
\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^p:
\quad\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\mathbb E_J
\langle\psi_{n,p,J}|C_{n,J}|\psi_{n,p,J}\rangle
\ge P_*-\varepsilon.
$$
The same finite list of gates and angles is used for every $n,J$; this is
a limiting expected-energy conclusion. A cost expectation is bounded above by its
maximum eigenvalue, and zero-angle padding makes $Q_p$ nondecreasing.
It therefore suffices to construct one finite word for every accuracy.
Fixed-instance convergence at increasing depth is a different quantifier
order. Farhi, Goldstone and Gutmann's original QAOA argument obtains that
convergence by adiabatic evolution and its Trotter approximation, with depth
allowed to depend on the instance; it does not supply the size-independent
word required here. [Farhi–Goldstone–Gutmann (2014), equation (10) and
§VI, pp. 10–11](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.4028v1);
[OpenAI (2026b), Theorem 1.1][q-intro].

The construction first describes local operations on a large tree, where
neighbouring subtrees supply Gaussian inputs. Temporary random labels let
those operations implement the finite classical function of §7. The hard
steps are to implement its aggregations using cost and mixer gates, and
then to replace every use of the labels by ordinary gates while preserving
the energy. Only the resulting ordinary word is transferred to SK.

The choices are nested: fix $\varepsilon$, choose $T<1$, choose a finite
mesh, fix the bounded classical formula and helper probabilities, then
choose the finite gate approximations and remove the seeds. The constants
in a replacement may depend on the surrounding word and on those positive
helper probabilities. [§8.6](#qaoa-assembly-detail) collects the error
allocation before the final $n\to\infty$ limit.
The principal circuit inputs can be read as four local lemmas. Their
proofs remain in the cited manuscript; §§8.2–8.5 reconstruct the
mechanisms and show where each hypothesis enters.

**Smooth replacement.** Fix the height, a finite expression and channel
list, and the required derivatives. Uniform recursive weighted bounds,
convergence of operators and adjoints, and strongly commuting signals with
the stated joint exponential bounds permit substitution inside a fixed
surrounding sequence in the exclusion-gate class defined in §8.2. Constants depend on that fixed family. This is the input
used in §8.3 to replace classical aggregates by finite gates; see
[the foundations, smooth topology and gate calculus][q-gate-calculus].

**Helper contraction and synthesis.** Fix a bounded, finite, type-excluded
odd formula, zero on helpers, and positive helper masses. The contraction
converges smoothly at every cut and for the specified responses. For each
$\eta>0$, finite seeded synthesis gives
$$
\mathcal E(v)\ge\mathcal E(m)-2\eta-2\sqrt{p_H}.
$$
Section 8.4 receives this one fixed seeded word. The source inputs are the
[synthesis statements][q-synthesis-statement] and
[helper theorem][q-helper-statement].

**Seed removal.** Fix that finite seeded word and an energy tolerance.
Reuse the same Gaussian at every occurrence on a vertex. Packet control and
the one-particle comparison then produce one finite ordinary word with the
required energy error. The [seed-removal theorem][q-seed-statement] supplies
an energy conclusion, not merely convergence of seed marginals. It makes the
ordinary-word transfer in §8.5 applicable.

**Fixed-word transfer.** Fix one ordinary word and all its angles before
either size or degree varies. Its positive tree scaled-edge limit equals
its SK expected-energy limit, with the convention conversion in §8.5.
This [fixed-word transfer][q-transfer] closes the thermodynamic-first
theorem in §8.6.

rows.label: qaoa-assembly
rows.text: ### 8.6 Fixing the word before the thermodynamic limit **Approximating a specified finite observable.** First fix $T,N$ and the positive finite normalizers in §7. The rooted construction in §8.1 has energy exactly $S_{T,N}$. Let $z$ be a smoothed version of its rounded spin $F_N$, let $m=\sin(2\theta)$ be the bounded formula's spin output, and let $m^{\mathrm{col}}$ be its color-excluded approximation. Write $$ \delta_s=\|z-F_N\|_2,\qquad \delta_b=\|m-z\|_2,\qquad \delta_c=\|m^{\mathrm{col}}-m\|_2. $$ These measure errors of the spin outputs, not of the angles. The rooted shift is a contraction, so $$ |\mathcal E(f)-\mathcal E(g)| \le(\|f\|_2+\|g\|_2)\|f-g\|_2. $$ All these outputs have norm at most one. Apply synthesis with tolerance $\eta_s$ and total helper probability $p_H$, then remove the seeds with energy tolerance $\eta_r$. The source's absolute synthesis bound and seed-removal theorem, followed by fixed-word transfer, give one ordinary word $W$ with $$ |v(W)-S_{T,N}| \le2(\delta_s+\delta_b+\delta_c) +2\eta_s+2\sqrt{p_H}+\eta_r. \tag{8.2} $$ The bounded formula is chosen before the colors and helper law. The excluded receiver and ancestor colors prevent a dependency from returning through a traversed branch; reserved helper colors are absent from every dependency and the output is zero on helpers. Color refinement and small positive helper probabilities jointly control $\delta_c$ and $p_H$. Only then is synthesis performed with that law fixed, using the same sitewise Gaussian seed at every seed gate. Each term in (8.2) can thus be made smaller than its allotted tolerance in this order. [OpenAI (2026b), Lemmas 3.1–3.4][q-classical]; [synthesis energy bound][q-synthesis-statement]; [seed removal][q-seed-statement]. This establishes an absolute approximation of each specified finite $S_{T,N}$ in the construction, without assuming it is already near $P_*$. It preserves the energy; it does not assert reproduction of the entire classical output law. Near-optimality now adds the cutoff and mesh choices. Allocate errors after choosing the desired $\varepsilon>0$. Apply the classical near-optimality proposition with the two tolerances $\varepsilon/4$ and $\eta_H=(\varepsilon/8)^2$. It supplies one formula and its helper law together, with classical loss below $\varepsilon/4$ and $0P_*-3\varepsilon/4. $$ Seed removal uses less than $\varepsilon/4$. The resulting fixed ordinary word therefore satisfies $v_W>P_*-\varepsilon$ after the fixed-word transfer. Its thermodynamic limit is taken only after all approximation choices have been made. Since $Q_p\le P_*$ and zero padding makes $Q_p$ nondecreasing, this proves the source's thermodynamic-first conclusion from its stated analytic inputs. [OpenAI (2026b), §6][q-assembly]. The order is: accuracy; minimizer and fixed $T<1$; finite scalar mesh; smoothing and bounded approximations; finite types and positive helper masses; exact helper contractions and finite commutator products; one fixed seeded word; initialization size; generic angle perturbation; finite selective pulse lists; sufficiently small $r$; one ordinary word; its $n\to\infty$ limit. The degree limits identify the rooted calculus and the transferred value for each already fixed word; they do not license changing that word with the finite instance. The reconstruction makes the source's circuit mechanisms explicit, but the evidence classes remain separate. The scalar construction and its formal interfaces in §§6–7 and 12 do not by themselves establish the weighted unitary calculus, simultaneous helper contraction or seed removal. Those analytic theorems are additional inputs from the QAOA manuscript, with the domain, commutation and uniformity hypotheses specified above. No quantitative depth bound, finite-size rate, efficient angle-selection procedure, or independent formal verification of this entire circuit construction follows from the selected formal statements. This completes the main support-to-circuit proof. The later comparisons have separate purposes: [§11.1](#positive-temperature-route) gives another classical input; [§11.2](#fixed-word-probability) adds a second-moment sampling theorem; and [§§11.3–11.5](#depth-quantifiers) compare quantifiers, other models and later finite-size estimates. They are not further premises of the proof just completed.

rows.label: qaoa-depth
rows.text: ### 11.3 Depth, angle choice and the order of quantifiers The complete witness is a finite ordered word, including every real angle. Its existence for each error tolerance asserts uniformity in system size and disorder that fixed-instance convergence does not provide. The quantifiers should be read literally. The source theorem says that for every $\varepsilon>0$, there is one finite word $W_\varepsilon$ such that $$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb E E_n(W_\varepsilon)\ge P_*-\varepsilon. $$ The cost operator uses $J,n$, but this word and its angles do not. In fixed-instance QAOA convergence, by contrast, the chosen depth and angles may depend on the fixed finite cost matrix and the requested accuracy. The performance of a prescribed family of nonzero angles with $p=p(n)\to\infty$ needs further estimates. A depth allowance alone can be met by the padded existence construction below. The distinction already occurs for the elementary array $a_{n,p}=p/(n+p)$. For each fixed $n$, its limit as $p\to\infty$ is one; for each fixed $p$, its limit as $n\to\infty$ is zero. This is a quantifier example, not a model of QAOA. The finite-dimensional convergence theorem of [Binkowski, Koßmann, Ziegler and Schwonnek, arXiv:2302.04968v1, Theorem 12][binkowski] fixes the optimization problem before selecting a sufficiently long circuit. It does not replace the construction of a size-independent word here. **An existential schedule under a prescribed depth allowance.** There is a narrower diagonal consequence for sampled output. Choose $W_k$ with $P_*-1/k\le v_{W_k}\le P_*$. Fixed-word second-moment convergence supplies $N_k$ so that, for every $n\ge N_k$, $\mathbb E(E_n(W_k)-v_{W_k})^2\le k^{-2}$. Given any prescribed integer depth allowance $d(n)\to\infty$, enlarge these strictly increasing thresholds until $d(n)\ge\operatorname{depth}(W_k)$ for every $n\ge N_k$. On $N_k\le n **Computational meaning of a finite word.** Nor does a supremum over angles assert that an optimizing angle vector exists at any particular depth. The proof constructs a sufficiently good word directly; monotonicity from identity padding then gives the limit of $Q_p$. Each QAOA round contains a full cost evolution and a mixer evolution. In the dense SK model a cost evolution involves all $\binom n2$ pair couplings, so the round count is not itself a bound on two-qubit gate depth, connectivity cost, precision or physical runtime. Three computational questions remain distinct. Evaluating the limiting energy at supplied angles is one task; finding suitable angles is another; implementing and sampling the resulting quantum circuit is a third. The [Basso et al. iteration][bfmvz] evaluates the fixed-angle limit in $O(p^2 4^p)$ arithmetic time. That is not a bound on the search needed to find the existence theorem's angles. Spin–boson representations provide another route to evaluation. The earlier [Boulebnane et al. mapping, arXiv:2505.07929v2][spin-boson], and the later [mixed-spin decoupling paper, arXiv:2609.40309v1, §§II–III and Supplement S2.1][decoupling], must be distinguished: the latter is a separate work, not the reference called BKL2026 in the original QAOA manuscript. Its fixed-depth mapping and numerical tensor-network performance do not supply an efficient angle-selection theorem for the present construction. Its discussion also gives fixed-word finite-size estimates; the absence of a finite-size rate **in the construction here** is not a claim that the wider literature contains none. **Why the two-spin hypothesis matters.** The statement is specific to the quadratic, zero-field SK model. The pure even higher-spin model has a different thermodynamic-first conclusion. For every even interaction order $q\ge4$, [Basso, Gamarnik, Mei and Zhou, arXiv:2204.10306v2, Theorem 4, (3.15), and its proof in §4.2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.10306v2) show $$ v_p^{(q)}(\boldsymbol\theta,\boldsymbol\beta) \le\eta_{\mathrm{OGP}}(G_q)<\eta_{\mathrm{OPT}}(G_q) $$ for every finite $p$ and every fixed angle vector, in that source's normalization. The same ceiling bounds their supremum over all finite $p$ and angles. The proof combines its dense–sparse value identity with the coupled-overlap-gap obstruction of [Chou, Love, Sandhu and Shi, arXiv:2108.06049v3, Parameter 4.1 and Corollary 4.4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.06049v3). That local-algorithm obstruction applies to sparse random signed Max-$q$-XOR for even $q\ge4$, at sufficiently large fixed degree and under the source's logarithmic-depth bound. The Basso–Gamarnik–Mei–Zhou transfer above only needs the resulting obstruction at each fixed depth. It requires no interchange of depth and system size. The exclusion $q\ge4$ is essential; this is not an obstruction for the SK two-spin model treated here. For comparison, [Goh, arXiv:2404.06087v6, Theorem 4.2 and Corollary 4.2.1][goh], treats even interaction order at least four. Its logarithmic-depth obstruction concerns sparse random-regular Max-q-XORSAT; the dense spin-glass corollary is explicitly conditional on swapping limits. The source states on p. 12 that its sparse/dense equivalence is only established at fixed depth, so it does not prove a dense logarithmic-depth obstruction. These hypotheses do not include quadratic SK. Neither a conclusion for all mixed spin glasses nor a general quantum advantage follows from §8. ### 11.4 The regular-MaxCut consequence has its own limits The original manuscript also gives a consequence for MaxCut. For each $\eta>0$ it selects one finite depth and normalized angles, and then a degree threshold, such that every finite simple unweighted $(D+1)$-regular graph of girth greater than $2p+1$ has expected cut fraction at least $$ \frac12+\frac{P_*-\eta}{\sqrt D} $$ for all sufficiently large $D$. The usual MaxCut cost is $H_{\rm MC}=\frac12\sum_{\{i,j\}}(I-Z_iZ_j)$, so its angles are $2\boldsymbol\gamma/\sqrt D$: the normalized angles are fixed, while these physical cost angles depend on degree. The sign conversion uses a bipartition of the relevant tree neighbourhood of each edge; the whole graph need not be bipartite. The further optimality comparison is for a uniform simple labelled $(D+1)$-regular graph $G_{n,D+1}$, along sizes with $n(D+1)$ even. Write $\operatorname{OPT}(G)$ for the maximum cut size divided by $|E(G)|$, $q_{p,G}$ for the circuit's expected cut fraction, and $\Delta_D(G)=\operatorname{OPT}(G)-q_{p,G}(2\boldsymbol\gamma/\sqrt D, \boldsymbol\beta)$. The same word can be chosen so that $$ \lim_{D\to\infty} \limsup_{\substack{n\to\infty\\n(D+1)\ \mathrm{even}}} \Pr_G\{\sqrt D\,\Delta_D(G_{n,D+1})>\eta\}=0. $$ Size goes to infinity first at fixed degree and word. The probability is over the random graph; the cut fraction has already averaged the quantum measurement. For fixed $D,p$, [McKay, Wormald and Wysocka (2004), Theorem 1](https://doi.org/10.37236/1819), gives tight counts of cycles of lengths at most $2p+3$. Every edge with a nontree neighbourhood is within bounded distance of one of these cycles, so their fraction tends to zero. The optimum is supplied separately by [Dembo, Montanari and Sen, arXiv:1503.03923v2, Theorem 1.6(b)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.03923v2): dividing their cut size per vertex by $(D+1)/2$ gives the leading cut fraction $1/2+P_*/\sqrt{D+1}$, with an error $o(D^{-1/2})$ in the stated iterated regime. A high-girth lower bound alone would not prove optimality on every high-girth graph. See [OpenAI (2026b), Corollary 1.2 and its complete proof][q-maxcut]. This separate consequence is recorded to preserve the source's scope; it is not a new selected formal endpoint or a joint size–degree limit.

rows.label: qaoa-depth-one
rows.text: #### 8.1.1 The same energy in the rooted representation We return to the value $\theta e^{-2\theta^2}\sin(4\beta)$ obtained in [the finite-SK and tree calculation](#depth-one-calibration). Retain its cost angle $\theta$, mixer angle $\beta$, $c=\cos(2\beta)$ and $s=\sin(2\beta)$. Here $\Omega$ is the Fock vacuum, $\mathrm{vac}=|+\rangle\otimes\Omega$, and $q(e)=a^*(e)+a(e)$. The root shift $\mathsf L$ defined in §8.1 creates one child excitation and puts the receiving root in its vacuum. Let $e=Z\mathrm{vac}=|-\rangle\otimes\Omega$ and $Q=q(e)$ in the rooted description. Its vacuum law is standard normal. The depth-one root operation is $u=e^{-i\beta X}e^{-i\theta ZQ}$. Using $Y|+\rangle=-i|-\rangle$, its insertion is $$ v=u^*Zu\,\mathrm{vac} =|-\rangle\otimes[c-is\cos(2\theta Q)]\Omega +|+\rangle\otimes s\sin(2\theta Q)\Omega. $$ The root shift retains only the plus-root, one-particle component. The first-chaos coefficient of the sine is $\mathbb E[G\sin(2\theta G)]=2\theta e^{-2\theta^2}$, so $$ \mathsf L^*v=2\theta s e^{-2\theta^2}e,\qquad \operatorname{Re}\langle v,\mathsf Lv\rangle =2\theta sc e^{-2\theta^2} =\theta e^{-2\theta^2}\sin(4\beta). $$ Here $\operatorname{Re}\langle e,v\rangle=c$ supplies the final factor. Thus the observable, not just the Gaussian law, agrees in all three representations. The example uses the [ordinary root updates][q-ordinary-updates] and [root shift][q-root-energy]. It calibrates one depth; the higher-depth occupation and replacement hypotheses remain necessary.

rows.label: qaoa-depth-one-pauli
rows.text: **One cost–mixer pair.** A single cost–mixer pair fixes the energy normalization before we introduce the rooted representation. Use the positive cost $C_{n,J}$ of §8 and $U=e^{-i\beta B_n}e^{-i\theta C_{n,J}}$; the symbol $\theta$ here is a cost angle, not the Parisi coefficient. Put $c=\cos(2\beta)$ and $s=\sin(2\beta)$. The Pauli identities are $$ e^{i\beta X}Ze^{-i\beta X}=cZ+sY,\qquad e^{i\alpha Z_iZ_j}Y_je^{-i\alpha Z_iZ_j} =Y_j\cos(2\alpha)+Z_iX_j\sin(2\alpha). $$ The mixed term $Z_iY_j$ therefore has cost-state expectation $$ \sin(2\theta J_{ij}/\sqrt n) \prod_{k\ne i,j}\cos(2\theta J_{jk}/\sqrt n). $$ The other mixed term exchanges $i$ and $j$. The $Z_iZ_j$ term has zero expectation. The $Y_iY_j$ term can be nonzero on an individual complete graph, but its expectation after the cost gate is independent of $J_{ij}$: $Y_iY_j$ commutes with that edge cost. Multiplying by $J_{ij}$ and averaging therefore removes it, even in the presence of triangles. For a standard Gaussian $J$, $$ \mathbb E\cos(aJ)=e^{-a^2/2},\qquad \mathbb E[J\sin(aJ)]=ae^{-a^2/2}. $$ Averaging the mixed terms and summing the $n(n-1)/2$ unordered edges gives $$ \frac1n\mathbb E_J\langle C_{n,J}\rangle =\frac{n-1}{n}\,\theta\sin(4\beta) e^{-2\theta^2(n-1)/n}. $$ This agrees with [Farhi et al., equation (62)][fggz]. With energy maximization, $\theta=1/2$, $\beta=\pi/8$ gives the limiting value $1/(2\sqrt e)$; their minimization example uses $\beta=-\pi/8$ and the negative value. For the positive cost $D^{-1/2}\sum_{\{i,j\}}Z_iZ_j$ on the $(D+1)$-regular tree, each endpoint has $D$ other neighbours. The same calculation now has no common-neighbour contribution and yields $$ \langle Z_oZ_v\rangle =\sin(4\beta)\sin(2\theta/\sqrt D) \cos^D(2\theta/\sqrt D). $$ Multiplying by $\sqrt D/2$ and letting $D\to\infty$ gives $\theta e^{-2\theta^2}\sin(4\beta)$, the same limit as finite SK. This checks the factor $1/2$ and the degree convention in §8.5. The value just obtained will be recovered once more from the [rooted insertion in §8.1.1](#depth-one-rooted). That calculation explains which part of the limiting state carries the energy.

rows.label: qaoa-finite-size
rows.text: ### 11.5 A later finite-size estimate and its limited depth consequence A separate, later source gives a quantitative comparison with the fixed-angle limit. Boulebnane, Khan, Subrahmanya, Herman, Farhi, Villalonga and Shaydulin, [arXiv:2609.40309v1, Corollary S3.1, pp. 46–47][decoupling], use the ordered-tuple Gaussian mixed-spin cost with covariance polynomial $\xi(t)=\sum_q c_q^2t^q$ of finite degree. Let $\Gamma>0$ bound every cost angle in a depth-$p$ word. Choose $x>0$ bounding $\xi(2),\xi'(1),\xi''(33)$, with $\Gamma^2p^2x\ge1$. No bound on the mixer angles is needed. Set $$ B_p=256p^4(2e\Gamma^2p^2x)^p,\qquad E_p=70\Gamma^2p^2x+p\log2,\qquad R_p=(2E_p/\log2)^{2p}. $$ For $$ 0<\varepsilon\le4\Gamma px \min\{e^{-1/2},2^{-(8p^2+3)/100}\}, $$ the source asserts $|\nu_n-\nu_\infty|\le\varepsilon$ whenever $$ n\ge T_p:=\max\left\{ 2^{8p^2+3}B_p \left(\frac{2^{\deg\xi+4}\Gamma^2p^2x^2}{\varepsilon^2}\right)^{R_p} \left[2\log_2\frac{4\Gamma px}{\varepsilon}+\deg\xi\right]^2, \frac{16\Gamma px}{\varepsilon}\right\}. $$ Here $\nu_n$ is the disorder-averaged energy per spin. The estimate applies to each near-optimal word from §8.6 separately. Given $\zeta>0$, choose a finite word $W_\zeta$ with $\nu_\infty(W_\zeta)\ge P_*-\zeta/2$. Its depth $p_\zeta$ and cost angles are finite; pad by a zero layer if needed and take $\Gamma_\zeta=\max\{1,\max_j|\theta_j(W_\zeta)|\}$. Choose a positive $\varepsilon_\zeta\le\zeta/2$ satisfying the displayed small-error condition. With these fixed parameters, the threshold gives $$ \nu_n(W_\zeta)\ge P_*-\zeta\qquad(n\ge T_{p_\zeta}). $$ The threshold is explicit in the chosen word and error. The existential construction supplies no quantitative bounds for $p_\zeta$ or $\Gamma_\zeta$ as $\zeta\downarrow0$, so it does not yield a bound in accuracy alone. A common angle bound is needed for the uniform growing-depth consequence below, not for this fixed-word application. For SK take $c_2=1/\sqrt2$. Combining the two ordered off-diagonal couplings recovers our standard Gaussian $J_{ij}$; the diagonal adds an independent scalar Gaussian of variance $1/2$. That scalar changes the circuit by a global phase and has zero mean, so the expected-energy comparison uses the same normalization. A fixed $x\ge\max\{2,\Gamma^{-2}\}$ satisfies the above bounds for every $p\ge1$. For fixed mixture, $\Gamma$ and $x$, put $\varepsilon_p=e^{-p^2}$. The small-error condition holds eventually, and direct logarithms give $$ \log R_p=4p\log p+O(p),\qquad \log\log T_p=4p\log p+O(p+\log p). $$ Consequently, for any deterministic sequence of words $W_n$ with depths $p(n)\to\infty$, one common cost-angle bound $\Gamma$, and $p(n)\log p(n)=o(\log\log n)$, the displayed hypotheses hold and $|\nu_n(W_n)-\nu_\infty(W_n)|\le e^{-p(n)^2}$ eventually. This is a uniform comparison along that specified bounded-angle class. It gives neither an efficient way to find near-optimal angles nor concentration of a quantum measurement in this growing-depth regime. The fixed-word second-moment theorem in §11.2 has separate quantifiers.

rows.label: qaoa-quantifiers
rows.text: ### 11.2 What is averaged, and a fixed-word probability consequence The probability conclusion here uses an additional fixed-word second-moment theorem, beyond the expected-value construction of §§8.1–8.6. The theorem in §8 is an existence statement about limiting expected energy. There are two random choices behind that expectation. First the couplings $J$ are sampled; then a computational-basis measurement of the state produces a spin string $\Sigma$. For the single word $W$ already chosen, put $$ E_n(J,\Sigma)=H_{n,J}(\Sigma)/n,\qquad \overline E_n(J)=\mathbb E[E_n(J,\Sigma)\mid J]. $$ The quantity defining $v_W$ is $\mathbb E_J\overline E_n(J)$. It is neither the energy of every measured string nor a worst-disorder guarantee. The temporary Gaussian labels used during synthesis are not an extra source of randomness in the final angle vectors. Farhi, Goldstone, Gutmann and Zhou supply that additional input. They prove, with the same Hamiltonian and gate-sign convention, that for every fixed word $$ \mathbb E_{J,\Sigma}E_n\longrightarrow v_W, \qquad \mathbb E_{J,\Sigma}E_n^2\longrightarrow v_W^2. $$ Their second expression is the quantum expectation of $(C_{n,J}/n)^2$ averaged over disorder, not merely the square of the conditional mean. Consequently $$ \mathbb E_{J,\Sigma}(E_n-v_W)^2\longrightarrow0, \qquad \Pr_{J,\Sigma}(|E_n-v_W|>s)\longrightarrow0 \quad(s>0). $$ The law of total variance separates what vanishes: $$ \mathbb E(E_n-v_W)^2= \mathbb E_J\operatorname{Var}(E_n\mid J) +\mathbb E_J(\overline E_n(J)-v_W)^2. $$ Both terms are nonnegative and hence tend to zero. Concentration of the conditional mean alone would not control a measured string. This is the elementary second-moment deduction from [Farhi et al., arXiv:1910.08187v4, §4, equations (13)–(22)][fggz]. Now run the circuit construction with accuracy $\varepsilon/2$ and freeze its resulting word. Since $v_W\ge P_*-\varepsilon/2$, $$ \Pr_{J,\Sigma}\{E_n0$, $$ \Pr_J\{b_n(J)>\tau\} \le\mathbb E_J b_n(J)/\tau\longrightarrow0. $$ Thus the same word also has small conditional measurement-failure probability for most disorder instances, in this precise sense. No claim is made for every instance, for arbitrarily varying depths, or with a quantitative size threshold. For $K$ fresh state preparations at the same disorder instance, the conditional failures are independent, so their joint failure probability is $\mathbb E_J b_n(J)^K$, not $(\mathbb E_J b_n(J))^K$. A fraction $\alpha$ of instances that always fail gives $\alpha$ for the former at every $K$. A bound $b_n(J)\le\tau$ on a particular instance does give $\tau^K$ there. Repeatedly measuring an already collapsed state is a different experiment.

rows.label: qaoa-regularization
rows.text: ### 8.2 Finite regularisation and the calculus needed for compilation Fix $T,N$ first. The independent continuous rounding coordinate makes the event at the sign discontinuity null. Bounded continuous odd approximations to that sign therefore converge in $L^2$ by dominated convergence. If the bounded output is $m^*$, shrink it to $(1-\kappa)m^*$, with fixed $0<\kappa<1$, before taking $\theta_\kappa=\tfrac12\arcsin((1-\kappa)m^*)$. This margin keeps the derivative of inverse sine bounded on its used range; the output loss is at most $\kappa$ in $L^2$. Then truncate the transmitted functions and approximate the resulting bounded maps by trigonometric polynomials. The source makes these choices from output toward leaves: each outer Lipschitz function is fixed before its inputs are approximated. The Gaussian isometry above converts an error in a transmitted child vector into the same $L^2$ error in its receiving position. Energy continuity then bounds the accumulated loss. The bounded output has the form $m=\sin(2\theta)$; it is the transmitted columns that are bounded, while the Gaussian fields themselves remain unbounded. [OpenAI (2026b), §3, bounded trigonometric approximation][q-bounded-classical]. **The formulas to be synthesized.** A mask is an event in the local seed space invariant under seed reversal. Fix a finite partition into masks, and write $p_R$ for the probability of mask $R$; probabilities used as denominators are positive. For disjoint masks $R,S$, aggregation on the finite regular tree means $$ (A_{RS}f)_i=\mathbf1_R(i)D^{-1/2} \sum_{j\sim i}\mathbf1_S(j)f_j. $$ A formula has a finite expression tree, with bounded measurable functions of the local seed as leaves. Internal operations are such aggregations or pointwise functions of previously formed quantities. Pointwise functions are smooth in their aggregate arguments, with polynomial bounds on all derivatives, uniformly in the seed. Seed dependence itself need not be smooth. Transmitted quantities are odd under simultaneous seed reversal; sent nonlinear functions and output angles are bounded, while aggregate Gaussian fields may be unbounded. An aggregation from $S$ to $R$ excludes $R$ if its transmitted formula uses no vertex of type $R$ below that call. All ancestor exclusions are retained, so a mask cannot recur on one active expression branch. It may recur on a different branch, and distinct branches may share descendants; exclusion asserts no independence between them. Gate targets are likewise excluded from the cross-edge dependencies of their parameters. This makes the physical all-neighbour calculation agree with the intended descendant calculation. For synthesis, reserve disjoint helper masks of positive mass, one per positive aggregation depth, absent from the output dependencies; the bounded odd output angle vanishes on their union. [OpenAI (2026b), Definition 3.3][q-formula-definition]; [Theorem 4.1][q-synthesis-statement]. The types can be encoded together with a Gaussian seed in one raw Gaussian variable: its sign supplies the odd symmetry, while disjoint binary digits of a uniform transform of its absolute value supply independent coordinates. The resulting finite type label is even and the Gaussian seed is odd under reversal. The associated pullback preserves vacuum, parity and $\mathsf L$. Thus adding types preserves the energy identification, rather than assuming an additional circuit resource. [OpenAI (2026b), §3, colours, exclusions and helpers][q-colors]. For the already fixed formula, the exclusion estimate is $$ \|m^{\rm col}-m\|^2\le C(\alpha+p_H), $$ where $\alpha$ is the largest nonhelper type mass and $p_H$ is the total helper mass. Its constant is independent of the number of types. The proof uses orthogonality of the disjoint masks before applying the Lipschitz estimate in the original, fixed list of formula coordinates. Treating the refined types as an arbitrary growing list of independent arguments would not provide this bound. The resulting classical near-optimality proposition supplies a finite bounded odd formula, zero on helpers, with energy as close to $P_*$ as required. [OpenAI (2026b), §3, “Type exclusion at small cost” and “Classical near-optimality in synthesis form”][q-colors]. **Which convergence permits the later substitutions?** The gate calculus uses recursive weights $\mathsf W_{h+1}=\mathsf W_0+d\Gamma(\Lambda_h)$, where $\Lambda_h$ is the previous weight restricted to the centred child space. The local weight includes the unbounded raw seed when needed. Its smooth domain is the intersection of all weighted domains. Smooth bounds mean polynomial bounds, with a finite loss of weight powers, for the maps, their adjoints and every specified parameter derivative. The finite height, fixed expression and fixed number of channels matter in these estimates. Strong convergence together with uniform stronger weighted bounds gives convergence in each weaker weighted norm by a spectral cutoff. This is the topology in which one replaces a gate inside a fixed surrounding circuit. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, weights and the topology of convergence][q-weights]. More precisely, the imported smooth-convergence contract is: for each output power $m$ and parameter multi-index $\alpha$, there are an input power $r$, exponent $k$ and constant $C$ such that $$ \|\mathsf W_D^m\partial_x^\alpha F_D(x)\xi\| \le C(1+|x|)^k\|\mathsf W_D^r\xi\|, \qquad \xi\in\bigcap_{q\ge0}\operatorname{Dom}(\mathsf W_D^q). $$ The bound is uniform in degree $D$ and parameter $x$. The same bound and strong convergence on smooth inputs are required for the adjoints and all specified parameter derivatives, with compatible limiting adjoints. Constants may depend on the fixed expression, height, channel list and derivative order. Bounded adjoint derivatives alone do not supply their convergence. At bounded local seeds $\mathsf W_0=1$; for polynomial Gaussian growth the source uses the vacuum-preserving weight $P_0+Q_0(1+|s|)Q_0$, where $P_0$ projects to the local vacuum and $Q_0=1-P_0$. These recursive weights control every generation. They differ from the top-generation number weight in §8.4's packet argument. No uniformity in growing word length, vanishing helper mass or the later seed-removal parameter is implicit in this contract. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, smooth-family bound][q-weights]. One of the essential inputs retains a term beyond the Gaussian field. Let $K_D(x)$ be a smooth unitary family with $K_D(0)=1$, uniformly controlled derivatives and adjoint derivatives that converge smoothly in the stated weighted topology to those of a limiting family $K$, and centred first vacuum derivatives. Write $K_\alpha=\partial_\alpha K(0)=iT_\alpha$ and $K_{\alpha\lambda}=\partial_\alpha\partial_\lambda K(0)$. For a fixed finite parameter list $a$, the source proves $$ K_D(a/\sqrt D)^{\otimes D}\longrightarrow \exp\!\left\{ i\sum_\alpha a_\alpha q(T_\alpha\mathrm{vac}) +\frac12\sum_{\alpha,\lambda}a_\alpha a_\lambda \left\langle K_{\alpha\lambda} +\tfrac12\{T_\alpha,T_\lambda\}\right\rangle_0 \right\}. $$ The second term is imaginary by unitarity. It survives because a second-order change of size $D^{-1}$ occurs in each of $D$ children. Its scalar coefficients become a possibly nonconstant controlled operator when commuting signals replace $a$. For example, $K(x)=e^{ix^2}$ has zero first derivative at zero but $K(a/\sqrt D)^D=e^{ia^2}$ exactly. Keeping only the first derivative would miss even this elementary contribution. The example explains why the term is necessary; the source's weighted product lemma supplies the general convergence and domain bounds. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, “Products of small unitaries”][q-unitary]. The smooth-substitution lemma makes the required joint control explicit. For a fixed finite list of strongly commuting self-adjoint signals $S_D=(S_{D,1},\ldots,S_{D,b})$, their polynomials must converge smoothly, and their joint exponentials must converge strongly on smooth inputs and satisfy, for every output weight $m$, $$ \|\mathsf W_D^m e^{it\cdot S_D}\xi\| \le C_m(1+|t|)^{k_m}\|\mathsf W_D^{r_m}\xi\|, $$ uniformly in $D$ and $t\in\mathbb R^b$. The coefficient family $F_D(x)$ and its adjoint obey the smooth bounds above and converge with all their jets on compact parameter sets. Each coefficient must commute with the signals' spectral projections; for unbounded coefficients this means commutation in the closed-operator sense. Seed-dependent substitution also requires strong commutation with the receiving seed multiplication algebra. These hypotheses permit the joint spectral and Fourier calculation of $F_D(S_D)$, including its derivatives and adjoints. A formal commutator identity on a single domain would not supply them. No nonsingular covariance matrix or inverse Gram matrix is required. [OpenAI (2026b), Lemma 2.10, “Smooth commuting substitution”][q-substitution]. For the formula fixed here, its finite expression tree supplies the finite channel list. Exclusion supplies the commuting physical control algebra; normalized-sum limits and the preceding product estimates supply the signal limits and weighted bounds. Conjugation by the already fixed preceding circuit preserves strong commutation, including when signals share descendants. The gate-calculus theorem applies these facts inductively to the formula and its adjoints, at each cut and inside the fixed surrounding sequence. It is this theorem, with these constructed inputs, that licenses the later replacements. Its conditional root-seed bounds also give the masked-column estimates used in §8.3. [OpenAI (2026b), Theorem 2.12][q-gate-calculus]. The exact cut recursion records the effect of such shared lower calculations. Let $y$ be the incoming boundary data, $V(y)$ the root matrix, and $m(y)$ its outgoing signals in the current frame. Factoring out the operations wholly inside each child gives $$ E^{[d]}(y)=V(y)\prod_{j\ \mathrm{child}} K_j^{[d-1]}(D^{-1/2}m(y)),\qquad K^{[d]}(y)=u^*E^{[d]}(0)^*E^{[d]}(y)u. $$ Every ratio $K^{[d]}$ equals one at zero. Nevertheless $m(0)$ generally does not vanish, because removing the parent input leaves the root's own signals. The actual zero-boundary root update is $u_{\rm new}=E^{[d]}(0)u$. It is not recovered by setting the entire ratio to one and discarding the baseline operation. Applying the unitary product lemma to this recursion, and then commuting substitution, is the source's smooth gate calculus. Its replacement statement covers a fixed finite surrounding sequence and its required parameter derivatives; it does not assert uniformity for arbitrary sequences whose length or channel count grows. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, smooth gate calculus and its cut recursion][q-gate-calculus].

rows.label: qaoa-rooted
rows.text: ### 8.1 Rooted realisation and the observable it preserves The fixed-depth spin–boson representation has an antecedent in [Boulebnane et al., Theorem 2 (informal), equations (10)–(11), p. 3][spin-boson]: as the degree grows with depth fixed, the symmetric tree state converges to a spin coupled to finitely many bosonic modes. The manuscript credits that representation, then proves the occupation, insertion and surrounding-circuit estimates needed below. Its additional task is to control the energy observable and substitutions inside a circuit, beyond identifying a limiting state. [OpenAI (2026b), §2][q-fock]. The immediate task is to realise the finite Gaussian spin from §7 in a space where its shifted correlation sum becomes an energy observable. We will identify that sum with a rooted quadratic form, then relate the same form to the scaled edge energy of a fixed circuit; §8.5 supplies the final transfer to SK. For an ordinary depth-$p$ word, this tree calculation uses only finitely many spins. Conjugate $Z_iZ_j$ backwards through the circuit. A mixer rotates the spins already in its support without enlarging that support. In a cost layer all edge factors commute, so factors disjoint from the current support commute past the other factors and cancel. The remaining factors enlarge support by at most one graph step. After $p$ pairs, the edge expectation therefore depends only on its radius-$p$ backward light cone. On the $(D+1)$-regular tree this contains at most $2\sum_{r=0}^pD^r$ vertices; the spins outside factor out of the product-state expectation. Thus fixed depth gives fixed tree height, although the number of children grows with $D$. This locality explains the finite tree calculation; the equality with dense SK is the separate transfer theorem in §8.5. [Farhi, Goldstone and Gutmann (2014), §II, equations (14)–(26)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.4028v1). On a rooted tree, factor a circuit as $U=(\bigotimes_jU_j)u$, where each $U_j$ contains operations wholly in child subtree $j$. Conjugating a root observable $P$ reduces to $u^*Pu$; its insertion vector is $u^*Pu\,\mathrm{vac}$, centered when its vacuum mean is zero. This factorization is why child operations enter the recursion below. The first change of setting preserves a specified quadratic form. At height zero the pointed space is $\mathsf k=\mathbb C^2\otimes L^2(\text{seed})$, with distinguished vector $\omega=|+\rangle\otimes1$. Recursively, $$ \mathcal H_0=\mathsf k,\qquad \mathcal H_{h+1}=\mathsf k\otimes\Gamma_s(\mathcal H_h^\circ), $$ where $\mathcal H_h^\circ$ is the orthogonal complement of the vacuum and $\Gamma_s$ is symmetric Fock space. A particle here is one child subtree whose state differs from its vacuum. It is not one physical spin. The occupation embedding identifies a symmetric state with $m$ nonvacuum children among $D$ available children with its $m$-particle vector, using the factor $\binom Dm^{-1/2}$. Adding empty descendants gives compatible embeddings between heights. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, pointed spaces and occupation embeddings][q-fock]. For a child direction $f$, write $q(f)=a^*(f)+a(f)$ and $W(f)=e^{iq(f)}$. Explicitly, $\Gamma_s(H)=\bigoplus_{m\ge0}H^{\otimes_s m}$, with vacuum $\Omega$ in sector zero. On sector $m$, $a^*(f)\psi=\sqrt{m+1}\operatorname{Sym}(f\otimes\psi)$, and $a(f)$ is its adjoint. The number operator is multiplication by $m$; more generally $d\Gamma(A)$ sums $A$ over those $m$ child factors. The vacuum characteristic function $\langle\Omega,e^{itq(f)}\Omega\rangle=e^{-t^2\|f\|^2/2}$ fixes the Gaussian normalization. For any finite list of fixed centred real child vectors, their parent positions $\mathsf G(f)=q(f)$ are jointly centred Gaussian; for $f,g$, $$ \mathbb E[\mathsf G(f)\mathsf G(g)]=\langle f,g\rangle, \qquad \|[\mathsf G(f)-\mathsf G(g)]\mathrm{vac}\|=\|f-g\|. $$ The directions are fixed elements of the child space, even when their values depend on the child's Gaussian coordinates. The receiving root's own seed is a separate, independent tensor factor. The root shift $$ \mathsf Lf=\omega\otimes a^*(f)\Omega $$ is an isometry on centred vectors, and is extended by zero on the vacuum. Its adjoint extracts the root-vacuum, one-child component, including a constant receiving-root seed. For a classical function of orthonormal Gaussian positions, this is its first Gaussian chaos. These covariance, independence and projection properties have distinct roles in the next calculation. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, root shift and classical first chaos][q-root-energy] [OpenAI (2026b), §2, classical Gaussian positions][q-gaussian]. Start with the standard root seed $g_0=S$ and recursively set $Z_{j+1}=\mathsf G(g_j)$. Suppose $g_0,\ldots,g_{j-1}$ are centred orthonormal vectors. The joint Gaussian law of their lifts and the covariance identity give independent standard normals $Z_1,\ldots,Z_j$. In the scalar construction of §7, the multiplier of $Z_j$ in $g_j$ depends only on its predecessors. Conditional centring therefore makes $g_j$ orthogonal to $g_1,\ldots,g_{j-1}$, and the chosen normaliser $c_j$ gives unit norm. Independence of the receiving-root seed gives orthogonality to $g_0$. This closes the induction. Compatible height embeddings ensure that the earlier variables are the same variables when the formula is embedded at greater height. Oddness of $u$ and evenness of $a$ make $Y_j$ and $g_j$ odd under simultaneous seed reversal. The extra centred rounding variable $2F_{\rm G}(Z_{N+1})-1$ is odd as well, so $F_N$ is centred. It is independent of the receiving-root seed, hence $\langle F_N,g_0\rangle=0=A_0$. With $A_j,B_{j+1}$ as in §7, first-chaos projection gives $$ \mathsf L^*F_N=\sum_{j=0}^NB_{j+1}g_j,\qquad \mathcal E(F_N):=\operatorname{Re}\langle F_N,\mathsf LF_N\rangle =\sum_{j=0}^NA_jB_{j+1}. $$ Thus the construction identifies both the scalar law and the required rooted energy. The Gaussian covariance rule does not declare distinct calculations on shared descendant subtrees independent. [OpenAI (2026b), §3, “A finite Gaussian formula and its rooted energy”][q-rooted-classical]. The connection to an edge observable is another statement. Let $f_D$ be centred, invariant under rooted permutations of complete child subtrees, and supported at a fixed finite radius. Suppose its occupation embedding converges strongly to $v$, with a uniformly bounded expected top-generation occupation $\langle f_D,\mathsf Nf_D\rangle$. Put $M=D+1$ and $R_M=\sqrt{1-\mathsf N/M}$. To see the decomposition, delete the distinguished edge and project onto the vacuum on either resulting half-tree. There are four pairings. The vacuum–vacuum pairing is zero by centring. If only one side is excited, the other side forces the root and all remaining branches into their vacuum; root symmetry gives the term $M^{-1/2}\langle\mathsf L^*f_D,R_Mf_D\rangle$ or its conjugate. In the pairing where both sides are excited, each projected vector has squared norm $M^{-1}\langle f_D,\mathsf Nf_D\rangle$ by symmetry among the $M$ branches. Cauchy–Schwarz bounds their pairing by that same quantity. Finally, deleting one vacuum child multiplies the $m$-particle sector by $\sqrt{\binom{M-1}{m}/\binom{M}{m}}=\sqrt{1-m/M}$, which identifies $R_M$. Thus the exact edge decomposition is $$ \langle f_{D,i},f_{D,j}\rangle =\frac2{\sqrt M}\operatorname{Re}\langle\mathsf L^*f_D,R_Mf_D\rangle +\varepsilon_D, \qquad |\varepsilon_D|\le\frac{\langle f_D,\mathsf Nf_D\rangle}{M}. $$ Vacuum deletion also gives $\|R_Mf_D-f_D\|^2\le M^{-1}\langle f_D,\mathsf Nf_D\rangle$. Consequently, $$ \lim_{D\to\infty}\frac{\sqrt D}{2} \langle f_{D,i},f_{D,j}\rangle=\mathcal E(v). $$ Strong convergence alone does not control the scaled remainder. The occupation estimate is supplied later for the relevant finite circuits. The occupation assumption cannot be dropped merely because vectors converge in norm. For orthogonal unit vectors $e_m$ in sector $m$, $\psi_k=\sqrt{1-1/k}\,\Omega+k^{-1/2}e_{k^2}$ tends to $\Omega$ in norm, whereas $\langle\psi_k,\mathsf N\psi_k\rangle=k$. The elementary continuity bound $$ |\mathcal E(v)-\mathcal E(w)| \le(\|v\|+\|w\|)\|v-w\| $$ will control every subsequent approximation after the observable has been identified. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, “Energy as a root shift,” including its exact finite-degree decomposition][q-root-energy]. The three identifications use different information: First, passing from the finite Gaussian formula to the rooted classical sector preserves the joint Gaussian law and the same $F_N$. This uses covariance, conditional centring and independence of the receiving-root seed. Second, the root-vacuum and first-chaos projection identify the energy itself: $\mathcal E(F_N)=S_{T,N}$. Third, for a finite-degree circuit insertion tending to $v$, root invariance, fixed radius, strong convergence and uniform occupation control imply that the scaled edge expectation tends to $\mathcal E(v)$. The first two calculations were given above. The third uses the source's edge decomposition; the requisite circuit estimates enter in §8.2.

rows.label: qaoa-seed
rows.text: ### 8.4 Removing the seed controls without changing their joint law Seed removal must simulate one Gaussian variable per vertex, reused at all seed gates. Replacing each occurrence with a fresh independent Gaussian would change the circuit. The source proves a theorem for any already fixed finite seeded word and any energy tolerance, producing one finite ordinary word. Its proof works in the fixed-word tree limit; it does not take a degree limit simultaneously with its small parameter. [OpenAI (2026b), §5, “Removal of seed controls”][q-seed-statement]. **A small component supplies a large response.** Fix $b>0$ and $01$. The right side is $o(r)$: within each ordinary packet the relevant Hermitian expectation is real, distinct packet centres have overlap $O(r^M)$, and terms containing only special packets have size $O(r^2)$. The norm remainder is carried by unitarity; it receives no unproved occupation bound. The exact zero clocks then cancel the first-order displacement on ordinary packets, leaving $o(r)$ error there. The prescribed action on a normalized special packet has $o(1)$ error, multiplied by its $O(r)$ amplitude. These are the unequal accuracy requirements that the next echo uses. [OpenAI (2026b), §5, accuracy of selective probes][q-seed-selective]. **The estimates must hold on the next input.** The repeated echo uses more than the initial special norm in (8.1). Let $\mathsf N$ count particles in the top child Fock space. Call a family $(\eta_r)$ bounded smooth when $\sup_r\|(1+\mathsf N)^k\eta_r\|<\infty$ for every fixed $k$. At each stage between simulated gates, the source propagates a linear ordinary/special decomposition on every such family, with $$ \begin{aligned} u_r\eta_r&=\Psi_{O,r}(\eta_r)+\Psi_{S,r}(\eta_r),\\ \|\Psi_{S,r}(\eta_r)\|&=r\|\eta_r\|,\\ \Psi_{O,r}(\eta_r)&=\zeta_r A_r\eta_r+o(r). \end{aligned} $$ Here $|\zeta_r|=1$, and the low unitary $A_r$ and its adjoint preserve all these seminorms uniformly. A separate part of the induction transports the special insertion: $$ u_r^*Z\psi_{S,r}/r=w_r+o(1), $$ with the negative sign between a selective flip and its undoing. The norm remainders remain separate from the designated smooth tails; no occupation estimate is imposed on them. This forward estimate gives the insertion approximation used at the next gate. For $P=Y,Z$, the vector $\widehat v_{P,r}=A_r^*PA_r\mathrm{vac}$ is itself a bounded smooth family. Since $A_r\widehat v_{P,r}=PA_r\mathrm{vac}$, unitarity gives $$ \begin{aligned} \|u_r^*Pu_r\mathrm{vac}-\widehat v_{P,r}\| &=\|Pu_r\mathrm{vac}-u_r\widehat v_{P,r}\|\\ &\le\|P(u_r-\zeta_r A_r)\mathrm{vac}\|\\ &\quad+\|(u_r-\zeta_r A_r)\widehat v_{P,r}\|=O(r). \end{aligned} $$ The second term explains why an estimate on the vacuum alone would not suffice: its input changes with $r$. The scalar phase cancels in this comparison. This $O(r)$ estimate supplies smooth approximants for actual insertions; it is not divided by $r$. The singular echo instead uses the more accurate difference derived next. [OpenAI (2026b), §5, packet invariant and insertion-approximation lemma][q-seed-echo]. **The echo amplifies a controlled difference.** Consider a forward cost $t/r$, a selective flip of the special component, the reverse cost $-t/r$, and a selective undoing of that flip. The packet invariant transports the special component so that its contribution to the insertion changes sign. For the actual insertion directions before and after the first flip, it gives $$ v'_r-v_r=-2r\,w_r+o(r). $$ The Weyl product of the two costs is formed with these actual directions before making any approximation. Their large centres cancel, leaving a bounded displacement $$ \frac tr(v'_r-v_r)=-2t\,w_r+o(1). $$ Approximating each direction by a low component with merely $O(r)$ error before this subtraction would leave an uncontrolled order-one error. The remaining scalar Weyl phase is independent of the root spin and cancels in insertions; it need not itself converge. The second flip restores the transported special component so that the same construction can be used again. Mixers receive analogous selective compensations. [OpenAI (2026b), §5, packet invariant, insertion approximation and “One echo”][q-seed-echo]. In the limit, $\ell_r$ and $w_r$ become two orthogonal external real Gaussian modes at each root. The initialization uses $q(\ell)$ and every simulated seed gate uses the same $q(w)$: choosing $t=\sigma/2$ implements $e^{-i\sigma Zq(w)}$. Different vertices have independent local copies. This is the required joint law of the seeded word. A finite induction uses the Weyl identity $$ \langle W(f)\Omega,W(g)\Omega\rangle =\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12\|g-f\|^2 +i\operatorname{Im}\langle f,g\rangle\right) $$ to match the relevant finite Gram matrices. Escaping high directions supply precisely the vanishing pairings between the new external modes and endogenous child directions. [OpenAI (2026b), §5, external-mode limit][q-seed-gram]. **The energy pairing after seed removal.** Matching the seed law and its finite Gram matrices is not yet enough. For a centred low insertion $h=\sum_j s_j\otimes W(f_j)\Omega$, the one-particle coefficient of $W(f_j)\Omega$ is $i e^{-\|f_j\|^2/2}f_j$. Hence $$ \langle h,\mathsf Lh\rangle =-i\sum_j\langle s_j,+\rangle e^{-\|f_j\|^2/2} \langle f_j,h\rangle. $$ In the seeded representation, $\mathsf L$ places the root-seed factor in its vacuum and creates $h$ only in the endogenous child space. External components therefore contribute zero to the last pairing. The high-direction estimate yields the same zeros in the actual limit. The actual insertion differs from its low insertion by $O(r)$, so energy continuity completes the comparison. Matching Gram matrices without this one-particle calculation would not identify $\mathsf L$ or its energy. [OpenAI (2026b), §5, “Finite Gram induction,” including the energy calculation][q-seed-gram]. **Why the selective rotations are available at every required stage.** The limiting projection of each special centre must be nonzero. The source imposes finitely many visibility conditions on the angles of the formal seeded word. At each relevant standard stage they have form $$ -2\operatorname{Im}\langle v_Z^{\rm form}, -2bz\,e+yD^{\rm form}\rangle\ne0, \qquad z,y\in\{\pm1\}, $$ where $e=Z\mathrm{vac}$ and $D^{\rm form}$ accumulates echoes whose reverse costs have already occurred. These functions are real analytic by the finite Weyl formulas. Setting all target angles to zero, while retaining initialization, gives $4bz e^{-8b^2}\ne0$, so none is identically zero. An arbitrarily small angle perturbation avoids their finite union of zero sets and the zero echo-time hyperplanes. The huge-cost stages need a separate transverse-projection estimate; their limiting projection pairs then also have a nonzero coordinate. Finite pulse lists can now be chosen successively from limits already established at earlier stages. No list is chosen from a limit that assumes its own successful implementation. [OpenAI (2026b), §5, huge-stage transverse projection, visibility and construction order][q-seed-visibility]. The choices are therefore nested: make $b$ small to control initialization; perturb the fixed target angles to ensure visibility; choose all finite probe lists; finally choose $r$ small. A value of $r$ fixes every large angle and every finite product. The theorem allows those angles to be large or negative. It makes no claim of uniform bounds as the target word length grows or as the tolerance tends to zero. [OpenAI (2026b), §5, proof of seed removal][q-seed-visibility].

rows.label: qaoa-synthesis
rows.text: ### 8.3 Seeded synthesis: helper contraction and nested responses Temporarily add longitudinal seed gates $\exp(-it\sum_i s_iZ_i)$, using an independent Gaussian $s_i$ at each vertex and reusing that same variable whenever a later seed gate acts there. The synthesis theorem turns the finite classical formula into a finite word of these gates, costs and mixers. Its ideal local $Y$ rotations have $Z$ insertion $$ v_{\rm cl}=|+\rangle m+|-\rangle n,\qquad m=\sin(2\theta). $$ Here $n$ is the remaining seed-dependent coefficient of the $|-\rangle$ component, not the number of spins. Both coefficients may depend on descendant seeds. The second term does not contribute to $\mathcal E$: $\mathsf L$ puts the root spin in $|+\rangle$, and shifting the $|-\rangle$ term puts a spin excitation into a child, orthogonal to the classical sector. Thus $\mathcal E(v_{\rm cl})=\mathcal E(m)$. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, classical rotations][q-root-energy] [OpenAI (2026b), §4, “Classical synthesis”][q-synthesis-statement]. There are two different approximation operations. First, seed conjugations of $X$ generate $\cos(2ts)X$ and $\sin(2ts)Y$. Trigonometric approximation and matrix commutators give the required bounded measurable masked spin controls. Sign averaging of masked $X$ flips isolates an interaction between chosen types; the cost terms commute, so this isolation is exact. This sign averaging is the refocusing method of [Jones and Knill (1999), §II, p. 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9905008v1): orthogonal sign rows cancel unwanted Ising couplings, while identical rows retain a selected coupling. The source applies it to the finite partition of seed masks. Finite commutator products then approximate the desired pointwise matrices with smooth bounds. They can be substituted after the surrounding circuit has been fixed. The local masks are measurable functions of the seed; smoothness is required in the continuous aggregate inputs, not in the mask labels. [OpenAI (2026b), §4, elementary masked controls and matrix products][q-masked-controls]. The second operation implements an aggregation. Let $I$ be the receiver region, $J$ the sender region, and $K$ an unused helper region of fixed positive probability $p_K$. They are disjoint. The lower seed-only formula $f$ excludes these regions along its cross-edge paths. With $A_{ij}=D^{-1/2}1_{i\sim j}$, the desired propagation has generator $$ H=\sum_{i\in I,j\in J}P_iA_{ij}f_j. $$ Partition $J$ into parts $J_l$ of probabilities $p_l$. Two levels of spin commutators generate the commuting Hamiltonian $$ \widetilde H_{\mathcal P} =\frac1{p_K}\sum_l\sum_{i\in I,\,j,j'\in J_l,\,k\in K} P_iA_{ij}X_jA_{jk}X_kA_{kj'}X_{j'}f_{j'}. $$ For a fixed receiver–sender edge $i\sim j$, the terms with $j=j'$ contain $X_j^2=1$; $f_j$ is seed-only and commutes with these spin factors. On helper-pinned states $X_k=1$, so their sum is exactly $$ \frac1{p_K}P_iA_{ij}f_j \sum_{k\in K}A_{jk}A_{kj} =P_iA_{ij}f_j\frac{N_K(j)}{Dp_K}, $$ where $N_K(j)$ counts helper neighbours of $j$. Conditional on the receiver edge, its endpoint $i\in I$ is not a helper and the other $D$ neighbours have mean helper count $Dp_K$. Its binomial variance is $Dp_K(1-p_K)$, so the ratio tends to one in $L^2$ at fixed $p_K>0$. Terms with $j\ne j'$ are simple paths and must disappear under partition refinement. The factor $1/p_K$ is harmless only after a positive helper mass has been fixed. [OpenAI (2026b), §4, helper generators and contraction][q-helper-statement]. Helper pinning is a statement about every helper spin in the light cone. Its finite-degree projection is $$ \Pi_{K,V}=\prod_{v\in V} \left[1-1_K(s_v)\frac{1-X_v}{2}\right]. $$ It retains the seed variables and helper-labelled descendant spaces while fixing the helper spins in $|+\rangle$. The ideal propagation, the exact Hamiltonian $\widetilde H_{\mathcal P}$, and the surrounding gates that avoid $K$ preserve this compressed space. Multiplying an insertion by $1_{K^c}(s_o)$ only masks the root label and does not impose this descendant condition. Individual finite commutator factors may leave the compressed space. Accordingly, the proof first establishes the exact contraction there, then chooses finite commutator products on the full space to approximate it. [OpenAI (2026b), §4, “Simultaneous helper contraction”][q-helper-statement]. The estimate controlling a growing partition is $$ \rho^2=\sum_l p_l^2\le p_J\max_l p_l\longrightarrow0. $$ At a helper root, each part supplies two commuting fields with columns $d_l,e_l$ on disjoint sender masks, of weighted norm at most $C\sqrt{p_l}$. The remaining correction is a sum of centred quadratics $$ \sum_l\bigl[q(d_l)q(e_l)-\langle d_l,e_l\rangle\bigr]. $$ Normal ordering and disjoint-mask orthogonality bound its quadratic kernels by $C\rho$ in Hilbert–Schmidt norm. The source separately bounds the exponentials in the weighted topology, uniformly in the number of parts. Smallness of the generator on smooth vectors alone would not justify inserting its exponential into the surrounding circuit. [OpenAI (2026b), §4, “Quadratics with many orthogonal columns”][q-helper-quadratics]. The helper estimate alone does not control all cuts. Put $\epsilon_{\mathcal P}=\max_l\sqrt{p_l}$. The receiver and helper corrections have weighted size $O(\rho)$; a sender correction is $O(\sqrt{p_l})$ conditional on its label. The remaining lower-formula responses have size $O(\epsilon_{\mathcal P})$. Both quantities tend to zero with $f$, the number of lower channels and $p_K>0$ fixed. There remains a response inside the lower formula $f$. A cut can pass through a descendant used to compute $f$, rather than through one of the displayed three-edge paths. The source first writes the exact difference of the affected Hamiltonian terms before applying the preceding subtree circuit. That circuit is fixed with respect to the new cut input. Exclusions ensure that the downward coefficients are independent of that active boundary argument. The resulting additive cut-response rule retains both first derivatives and mixed second derivatives: $$ \sum_\alpha a_\alpha q(H_\alpha\mathrm{vac}) +\frac12\sum_{\alpha,\lambda}a_\alpha a_\lambda \langle H_{\alpha\lambda}\rangle_0. $$ Here $H_\alpha$ is centred by parity; no limit of the extensive zero-input Hamiltonian is required. The self-adjoint generator is obtained from the limiting time group of cut ratios. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, “Additive cut responses”][q-additive-response]. After substituting the signals of a lower formula, a boundary difference contains, in particular, $$ \begin{aligned} &\sum_\alpha[m_\alpha(y)-m_\alpha(0)]q(r_\alpha)\\ &\quad+\frac12\sum_{\alpha,\lambda} [m_\alpha(y)m_\lambda(y)-m_\alpha(0)m_\lambda(0)] c_{\alpha\lambda}. \end{aligned} $$ The mixed coefficients $c_{\alpha\lambda}$ must remain even when two channels share descendants. A bounded scalar example makes the issue visible: for a shared standard normal $Q$, take $H(y_1,y_2)=\cos(Q+y_1+y_2)-\cos Q$. At zero both first derivatives are $-\sin Q$ and are centred, but $\mathbb E H_{12}=-e^{-1/2}$. The two cross terms in the half-sum therefore contribute $-e^{-1/2}a_1a_2$. Centred first responses do not remove a mixed second response. This example checks the algebraic reason for retaining the term; the cut-response theorem supplies the operator and domain justification. At the actual root there is no parent input to subtract: the corresponding unsubtracted $m(0)$ terms enter the root update. The source propagates small terminal responses through the fixed depth and fixed list of lower channels. It refines the calling sender mask while keeping those lower formulas fixed. This is what controls all cuts in a simultaneous replacement of several calls. A root-seed scalar phase may remain on helper labels; it cancels in insertions and child conjugations. [OpenAI (2026b), §4, lower-formula responses and completion of the contraction proof][q-helper-responses]. Compilation now proceeds from outer aggregations to inner ones. Reserve a separate unused helper type for each aggregation rank. At a given rank, establish the simultaneous exact contraction, fix the sender partitions, and only then choose finite commutator approximations. Subsequent inner calls use their own helpers, which remain unused. Each inner accuracy is chosen after its surrounding finite sequence is fixed. This order avoids assuming uniformity over all helper masses, ranks or circuit lengths. [OpenAI (2026b), §4, order of compilation][q-compilation]. If the resulting insertion $v$ obeys $\|1_{H^c}(v-v_{\rm cl})\|<\eta$, seed commutation and unitarity give $\|1_Hv\|=\sqrt{p_H}$. First omit the helper part of $v$, at energy cost at most $2\sqrt{p_H}$. Compare the two insertions projected off helpers; their norm difference is below $\eta$, so their energies differ by at most $2\eta$. The projected classical insertion still has energy $\mathcal E(m)$ because $m=0$ on helpers. Thus $$ |\mathcal E(v)-\mathcal E(m)|\le2\eta+2\sqrt{p_H}. $$ All projected insertion vectors have norm at most one. This completes the interface from a bounded classical formula to a finite seeded word. It uses the source's smooth gate and helper-contraction theorems; it is not a consequence of the scalar theorem or of a finite-degree central limit theorem alone. [OpenAI (2026b), §4, synthesis statement and its proof][q-synthesis-statement].

rows.label: qaoa-transfer
rows.text: ### 8.5 Transfer of the resulting ordinary word After all these choices there is one finite ordinary word $W$, fixed independently of degree, size and disorder. On the $(D+1)$-regular tree use $C_D=D^{-1/2}\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}Z_iZ_j$, counting each edge once. The edge expectation is defined on the finite light cone described in §8.1. The source applies the fixed-word transfer theorem $$ v_W=\lim_{D\to\infty}\frac{\sqrt D}{2} \langle+|W_D^*Z_iZ_jW_D|+\rangle. $$ The [full preprint of Basso et al., arXiv:2110.14206v3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.14206v3), Theorem 1, equates the limiting tree recursion with the infinite-size SK recursion for every fixed depth and fixed angle vector. Its proof is in §6, especially (6.6)–(6.31), with the symmetry statement proved in Appendix B and the iteration stabilisation in Appendix A.4. The shorter proceedings edition states the theorem but refers to this full preprint for the proof. Basso et al. use a negative tree cost in (2.3). Let $V=\prod_{i\in A}X_i$ on one bipartition of the finite light cone. Every edge has exactly one endpoint in $A$, hence $$ VZ_iZ_jV=-Z_iZ_j,\qquad VB_DV=B_D,\qquad V|+\rangle=|+\rangle. $$ Consequently, if $C_D^-=-C_D$, then $VW(C_D^-,B_D)V=W(C_D,B_D)$ for the same fixed word and angles, while its measured edge expectation changes sign. This converts the negative cut convention in their (2.6) to the positive energy above. Their SK cost (6.1) already has the positive convention used here.
